blurb: Energia, calor e ondas no dia a dia.

lessons.title: Energia e calor
lessons.summary: Para onde vai a energia, como se move o calor e porque é que as bombas de calor ganham aos aquecedores.

cards.title: A energia muda de forma
cards.text:
A energia nunca se cria nem se destrói, apenas se converte. A energia química de uma pilha torna-se energia elétrica, que uma lâmpada transforma em luz e calor.

A eficiência é a parte útil. Uma lâmpada de filamento antiga convertia cerca de 5% em luz; um LED consegue várias vezes isso, por isso aquece menos para o mesmo brilho.

deep.x: The rule that energy is never created or destroyed is called the **conservation of energy**, or the first law of thermodynamics. It was pinned down in the 1840s, when James Joule showed that a fixed amount of mechanical work always produces the same amount of heat. Since then no experiment has ever broken it.
Where the energy ends up

Follow any chain of conversions far enough and it ends as low-grade heat, spread thinly through the surroundings. The light from a lamp hits the walls and warms them slightly. The energy still exists, but it is too spread out to do useful work again.
Efficiency

Efficiency is useful output divided by total input. A filament bulb gets about 15 lumens of light per watt; a good LED gets over 100. That is why switching a 60 W bulb for a 9 W LED gives the same light.
efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy in × 100%

v.unit: approx. % of input that is useful

x: Bulb uses 60 J each second
5% becomes light = 3 J
The other 57 J leaves as heat

deep.w: Energy gets "used up"
deep.r: It only changes form; what we lose is the useful, concentrated kind

deep.x: Energy is like money moving between accounts: the total never changes, but some of it always leaks into the "heat" account.
Nothing reaches 100%: even large electric motors, among the best machines we have, lose a few per cent as heat.

cards.title: Três formas de o calor se mover
cards.text:
Condução: o calor passa através de materiais em contacto, do bico do fogão para o fundo da panela.
Convecção: o fluido quente sobe e o frio desce, criando circuitos que agitam a água.
Radiação: a luz infravermelha atravessa um espaço sem qualquer material, como o calor que sentes ao pé de uma fogueira.

deep.x: Heat always flows from hotter to colder. The three routes differ in what carries the energy: vibrating particles, moving fluid, or light itself.
Conduction

In a solid, hot atoms vibrate harder and pass that jiggle to their neighbours. Metals conduct best because their free electrons carry energy quickly. Copper conducts heat about 16,000 times better than still air, which is why pan bases are metal and handles are often wood or plastic.
Convection

Liquids and gases expand when warmed, become less dense and rise; cooler fluid sinks to take their place. This sets up loops called convection currents. A radiator mostly heats a room this way, and the same process drives sea breezes and much of the weather.
Radiation

Every warm object gives off infrared light. It needs no material at all, which is how the Sun's heat crosses 150 million km of empty space. Dark, matt surfaces emit and absorb it well; shiny ones reflect it.
Conduction needs contact, convection needs a fluid that can flow, and radiation needs nothing at all.
A cool tiled floor and a rug at the same temperature feel different because tile conducts heat away from your feet much faster.

cards.title: As bombas de calor movem calor
cards.text:
Uma bomba de calor não produz calor; desloca-o. Um fluido refrigerante absorve calor do ar exterior (até o ar frio tem algum), o compressor comprime-o para que fique mais quente, e esse calor é libertado dentro de casa.

Como a maior parte do calor vem de fora, 1 kWh de eletricidade pode fornecer 3–4 kWh de calor. Essa razão é o COP.

deep.x: A heat pump is a fridge run in reverse for your house. Instead of pulling heat out of a small box and dumping it into the kitchen, it pulls heat out of the outside air, ground or water and dumps it indoors.
Why it beats a heater

An electric heater turns 1 kWh of electricity into exactly 1 kWh of heat. A heat pump uses that electricity only to move heat, so most of what it delivers is "free" heat taken from outside. The ratio of heat delivered to electricity used is the **coefficient of performance (COP)**.
COP = heat delivered ÷ electricity used

x: Heat pump uses 1 kWh
Takes 2.5 kWh from outside air
Delivers 3.5 kWh: COP = 3.5

v.unit: kWh of heat per kWh of electricity

deep.x: What lowers the COP

x: The bigger the gap between outside and inside temperature, the harder it works
Low-temperature radiators or underfloor heating suit heat pumps best
Portugal's mild winters are kind to air-source heat pumps; they are also widely used here for hot water

deep.w: Heat pumps don't work in winter
deep.r: Even air at −10 °C holds heat they can extract, though less efficiently

deep.x: A heat pump is cheaper than a heater because it moves heat rather than making it.

cards.title: Calor específico
cards.text: A energia para aquecer algo é massa × calor específico × subida de temperatura. O calor específico da água é elevado, cerca de 4186 J por kg por °C, e é por isso que demora a ferver e armazena tão bem o calor.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><rect class="w" x="112" y="82" width="86" height="66" rx="0"/><path class="s" d="M110 50 V150 H200 V50"/><path class="s" d="M240 40L240 128"/><circle class="s" cx="240" cy="140" r="10"/><circle class="fred" cx="240" cy="140" r="6"/><path class="r" d="M240 132L240 70"/></g><text class="" x="155" y="40" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">1 L de água</text><text class="r" x="250" y="30" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">20 → 100 °C</text><text class="a" x="160" y="172" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">Q = 1 × 4186 × 80 ≈ 335 kJ</text></svg>

deep.x: Specific heat capacity tells you how much energy one kilogram of a material needs to warm by one degree. Materials with a high value warm slowly and cool slowly; low-value ones change temperature fast.
Q = m × c × ΔT

x: Kettle with 1 kg of water, 20 → 100 °C
A 2 kW kettle needs about 170 s, nearly 3 minutes

deep.x: Water is a champion

Water's value is about four times that of air (per kilogram) and roughly ten times that of iron. Its molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds, which soak up energy before the molecules can move faster.
Why it matters

x: The sea warms slowly in spring and stays warm into autumn, which is why coastal towns like Viana do Castelo have milder winters than inland Trás-os-Montes
Central heating uses water to carry heat around the house
A hot-water bottle stays warm for hours

deep.x: High specific heat means slow to warm and slow to cool, which makes water a superb store of heat.
Hot oil in a pan heats up roughly twice as fast as the same mass of water on the same burner, because its specific heat is about half.

cards.title: Formas de energia
cards.text: A energia surge em muitas formas: cinética (movimento), potencial (altura, molas), térmica (calor), química (combustível, alimentos), elétrica, radiante (luz) e nuclear. A física acompanha como passa de umas para outras.

deep.x: Physicists group energy by where it is stored or how it moves. These labels are bookkeeping: the same joule can sit in one store and then shift to another.
Two formulas worth knowing
Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed, so doubling speed gives four times the energy. Gravitational potential energy grows simply with height.
kinetic energy = ½ × m × v²   |   potential energy = m × g × h

x: 1,000 kg car at 50 km/h (13.9 m/s)
Same as dropping it from about 10 m

deep.x: Following the energy

A hydroelectric dam, such as Alqueva in the Alentejo, shows a chain clearly. Water held high has potential energy; falling, it gains kinetic energy; turbines turn that into electrical energy; your kettle turns it into thermal energy.
Nuclear and mass

Einstein's E = mc² shows mass itself is a store of energy. Nuclear power stations release a tiny fraction of it; a uranium fuel pellet the size of a fingertip holds roughly as much energy as a tonne of coal.
Energy has many names but one currency: the joule.

deep.w: Heat and temperature are the same thing
deep.r: Temperature is how hot; heat is energy moving because of a temperature difference

cards.title: Energia dos alimentos
cards.text: A energia dos alimentos mede-se em quilocalorias (kcal), que nos rótulos aparecem como "Calorias". Uma kcal são cerca de 4,2 kJ. Uma dieta diária de 2000 kcal são cerca de 2,3 kWh, mais ou menos uma lâmpada de 100 W acesa o dia inteiro.

deep.x: A food "Calorie" with a capital C is a kilocalorie: the energy to warm 1 kg of water by 1 °C. In Europe labels must also show kilojoules, so a label might read "250 kcal / 1046 kJ".
1 kcal ≈ 4.2 kJ   |   1 kWh = 3,600 kJ ≈ 860 kcal

x: ÷ 3,600 = about 2.3 kWh per day
Spread over 86,400 s ≈ 97 W

deep.x: Where it goes

Most of the energy in food ends up as body heat. A resting adult gives off roughly 80–100 W, which is why a crowded room warms up quickly. Only a modest share goes into mechanical work, because muscles are only about 20–25% efficient.
Food versus fuel
Per kilogram, fats store about 37 kJ per gram, while carbohydrates and protein store about 17. Petrol stores about 46 kJ per gram, not that far above butter.
Food energy values were first measured by burning food in a sealed "bomb calorimeter" and measuring how much it warmed surrounding water.
Your body runs on about the same power as an old 100 W light bulb.

cards.title: Dilatação térmica no dia a dia

items: Carris e pontes precisam de folgas
Água quente solta tampas de frascos

cards.text: A maioria das coisas dilata quando aquece: os carris do comboio têm folgas, os cabos elétricos descaem no verão, a tampa presa de um frasco solta-se debaixo de água quente. A água é estranha: expande-se ao congelar, e é por isso que o gelo flutua e os canos rebentam.

deep.x: When a solid is heated its atoms vibrate harder and push each other slightly further apart, so it grows. The change is small per degree but adds up over long lengths and big temperature swings.
change in length = original length × expansion coefficient × temperature rise

x: 1 km of steel rail, coefficient ≈ 12 millionths per °C
Warms by 40 °C, cold morning to hot afternoon

deep.x: How engineers cope

x: Bridges have expansion joints, the toothed metal strips you drive over
Modern rails are welded and laid under tension, so they stretch rather than gap
Pyrex glass expands little, so it survives oven-to-table temperature changes

deep.x: Water's odd behaviour
Water is densest at about 4 °C. Cool it further and it expands; when it freezes it grows by about 9%. Ice therefore floats, and lakes freeze from the top down, letting fish survive underneath.
The Eiffel Tower is typically about 15 cm taller on a hot summer day than in winter.
Heat makes most things grow, so good engineering always leaves room to move.

cards.title: Isolamento e o termo
cards.text: Um termo trava os três tipos de transferência de calor: o vácuo bloqueia a condução e a convecção, e as paredes espelhadas refletem a radiação. É por isso que mantém o café quente ou as bebidas frias durante horas.

deep.x: The vacuum flask was invented by the Scottish scientist James Dewar in 1892 to keep liquefied gases cold. A German company sold it to the public from 1904 under the name Thermos, which became the everyday word.
How each layer works

x: **Vacuum**: with almost no gas molecules, there is nothing to conduct heat or to carry it by convection
**Silvered walls**: shiny surfaces reflect infrared radiation back towards the drink
**Stopper**: stops warm air rising out of the top

deep.x: The weak spots
Heat still leaks slowly through the neck, where inner and outer walls join, and through the stopper. That is why a good flask keeps tea hot for perhaps 12 hours but not for days.
Same ideas, bigger scale

House insulation uses the same tricks. Wool, foam and cork trap air in tiny pockets so it can't circulate. Double glazing traps a gas layer between panes. Portugal is the world's largest cork producer, and cork is an excellent natural insulator for exactly this reason.

deep.w: A Thermos keeps things hot
deep.r: It slows heat flow either way, so it keeps cold drinks cold too

deep.x: Stop conduction, convection and radiation together and heat barely moves.

cards.title: A evaporação arrefece
cards.text: Quando a água evapora, as moléculas mais rápidas escapam e levam energia consigo, por isso o que fica arrefece. O suor, as bilhas de barro e as torres de arrefecimento aproveitam isto.

deep.x: In any liquid, molecules move at a range of speeds. Only the fastest have enough energy to break free from the surface. When they leave, the average energy of those left behind drops, and lower average energy means lower temperature.
How much heat it takes
Evaporating water absorbs a lot of energy, about 2.4 million joules per kilogram at skin temperature. That is over five times the energy needed to heat the same water from 0 to 100 °C.

x: You sweat 1 litre on a hot walk
1 kg × 2.4 MJ/kg ≈ 2.4 MJ
About 0.67 kWh of heat removed from your body

deep.x: What speeds it up

x: Higher temperature
Wind or a fan, which carries away the moist air
Dry air: in humid weather sweat drips off instead of evaporating, so you feel hotter
Larger surface area, like a wet towel spread out

deep.x: Everyday examples

Traditional Portuguese clay water jugs seep a little water through their walls; as it evaporates, the water inside stays noticeably cooler. A dog pants because it has few sweat glands, so it evaporates water from its tongue instead.

deep.w: A fan cools the air
deep.r: It doesn't cool the room; it speeds up evaporation from your skin

deep.x: When water evaporates, it takes heat with it.

cards.title: De onde vem a energia da Terra
cards.text: Quase toda a energia que usamos tem origem no Sol: alimentos, vento, hídrica, solar e até combustíveis fósseis (luz solar antiga armazenada pelas plantas). As exceções são a energia nuclear, a geotérmica e a das marés.

deep.x: The Sun delivers about 170,000 terawatts to the top of Earth's atmosphere. Humanity's total energy use averages around 20 terawatts, so sunlight brings roughly 10,000 times what we use.
Fossil fuels are old sunlight
Coal formed mostly from swamp forests around 300 million years ago. Oil and gas formed mainly from marine plankton. In both cases the energy was originally captured from sunlight by photosynthesis.
The exceptions

x: Geothermal heat comes mostly from radioactive decay deep inside Earth, plus heat left over from its formation
The Azores use it: geothermal plants on São Miguel supply a large share of the island's electricity
France's La Rance tidal power station has run since 1966

deep.x: Even wind is solar

The Sun heats the equator more than the poles and land more than sea. These differences create pressure differences, and air moving between them is wind. Portugal now gets a large share of its electricity from wind and hydro, both driven by the Sun.
Uranium was forged in exploding stars before the Solar System existed, so nuclear power uses energy from older stars than ours.
Almost every joule you use started out as sunlight.

quiz.q: De que forma é que o calor do Sol te chega sobretudo?
quiz.explain: O espaço está quase vazio, por isso só a radiação o consegue atravessar.

quiz.q: Uma bomba de calor com COP de 3 consome 2 kWh de eletricidade. Quanto calor fornece?
quiz.explain: Calor fornecido = COP × eletricidade consumida = 3 × 2 = 6 kWh.

quiz.q: Aquecer 2 kg de água em 10 °C exige cerca de…
Porque é que o gelo flutua?
options: A água expande-se ao congelar, por isso o gelo é menos denso
Só por causa das bolhas de ar
quiz.explain: O gelo é cerca de 9% menos denso do que a água.

quiz.q: Como é que o suor te arrefece?
options: A evaporação leva energia da pele
quiz.explain: As moléculas mais rápidas escapam e levam calor consigo.

lessons.title: Ondas, som e luz
lessons.summary: Uma só equação que explica cordas de guitarra, Wi-Fi e trovoadas.

cards.title: Anatomia de uma onda
cards.text: Uma onda transporta energia sem transportar matéria. O comprimento de onda (λ) é a distância de uma crista à seguinte. A amplitude é a sua altura, que define o volume ou o brilho. A frequência é quantas cristas passam por segundo, em hertz (Hz).

deep.x: A wave is a travelling disturbance. The material it passes through only wobbles about a fixed position; it's the pattern and the energy that move along. A cork on the sea bobs up and down as waves pass but stays roughly where it is.
Frequency and period
Frequency and period are two views of the same thing. A wave with a frequency of 50 Hz completes one cycle every 1/50 s, or 0.02 s. The European mains supply alternates at exactly this rate.
period = 1 ÷ frequency
Amplitude and energy

The energy a wave carries goes up with the square of its amplitude. Double the height of a sea wave and it carries four times the energy, which is why storm waves on the Nazaré coast are so destructive.
One equation for all waves
wave speed = frequency × wavelength

deep.w: Waves carry water along with them
deep.r: The water mostly goes round in small circles; the energy travels on

deep.x: A wave moves energy from place to place while the medium stays put.

cards.title: Experimenta: que comprimento tem um som?
cards.text: A velocidade é a frequência vezes o comprimento de onda. O som viaja a cerca de 343 m/s no ar, por isso as notas graves têm ondas longas e as agudas têm ondas curtas.

deep.x: Rearranging the wave equation gives wavelength as speed divided by frequency. Because sound travels at a fixed speed in air, the frequency alone decides how long each wave is.
wavelength = speed ÷ frequency

x: Concert A at 440 Hz
Each wave is about the length of your arm

deep.x: From tiny to huge
The range of human hearing covers wavelengths from about 17 m down to about 1.7 cm, a factor of 1,000. Few other senses span such a range.
Why it matters

x: Big loudspeakers (woofers) are needed to push long bass waves; small tweeters handle short ones
Bass passes through walls and around corners more easily, so you hear the neighbours' music as a thump
Organ pipes must be roughly half a wavelength long, so the lowest notes need pipes several metres tall

deep.x: Temperature changes the answer
Sound travels faster in warm air, about 0.6 m/s faster per °C. At 0 °C it's about 331 m/s; at 20 °C it's 343 m/s. Wind instruments go slightly sharp as they warm up for this reason.
At a fixed speed, higher frequency always means shorter waves.
A bat's ultrasonic call at 50 kHz has a wavelength of under 7 mm, small enough to bounce off a moth.

cards.title: A que distância está a trovoada?
cards.text:
A luz do relâmpago chega-te quase instantaneamente; percorre cerca de 300 000 km por segundo. O som arrasta-se a cerca de 343 m/s, mais ou menos 1 km a cada 3 segundos.

Conta os segundos entre o relâmpago e o trovão e divide por 3 para obter a distância em quilómetros.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="s bgf" d="M40 62 q-2 -26 24 -24 q10 -22 36 -10 q22 -12 36 8 q22 2 18 26 Z"/><path class="r" d="M96 64 L80 100 H95 L82 136"/><path class="a" d="M122 108 q10 12 0 24"/><path class="a" d="M138 100 q16 20 0 40"/><path class="a" d="M154 92 q22 28 0 56"/><rect class="s bgf" x="250" y="112" width="42" height="38" rx="0"/><path class="s" d="M244 112 L271 88 L298 112"/></g><text class="r" x="218" y="60" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">luz ≈ instantânea</text><text class="a" x="212" y="80" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">som: 1 km / 3 s</text><text class="" x="160" y="172" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">segundos ÷ 3 = km</text></svg>

deep.x: Lightning and thunder happen at the same moment. Lightning heats a narrow channel of air to around 30,000 °C in a split second; the air expands explosively and makes the boom. The difference you notice is entirely down to travel time.
The 3-second rule
Light covers a few kilometres in about one hundred-thousandth of a second, so you can treat it as instant. Sound takes about 2.9 s per kilometre.

x: Flash, then you count 9 seconds
Storm is about 3 km away

deep.x: Safety

x: If the gap is under about 30 seconds (10 km), you're within reach of a strike
If the gap is shrinking, the storm is coming towards you
Wait about 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back outside

deep.x: Why thunder rumbles
A lightning bolt can be several kilometres long. Sound from the nearest part reaches you first and from the farthest parts later, so a single crack stretches into a long rumble.

deep.w: Lightning never strikes the same place twice
deep.r: Tall structures are hit many times a year

deep.x: Light arrives almost at once, so the delay before thunder is a measure of distance.
Thunder is rarely heard more than about 15–20 km away, so you can see "silent" lightning from storms far beyond that.

cards.title: O espetro eletromagnético
cards.text:
Rádio, micro-ondas, infravermelhos, luz visível, ultravioleta e raios X são todos a mesma coisa: ondas eletromagnéticas, todas a mover-se à velocidade da luz. Só o comprimento de onda muda.

Ondas mais curtas transportam mais energia por fotão. É por isso que os UV podem queimar a pele e os raios X a atravessam, enquanto a rádio é inofensiva. O Wi-Fi a 2,4 GHz tem um comprimento de onda de cerca de 12,5 cm.

deep.x: Electromagnetic waves are linked electric and magnetic fields that keep creating each other as they travel. They need no medium, which is why sunlight crosses space. James Clerk Maxwell predicted them in the 1860s; Heinrich Hertz made radio waves in his lab in 1887.
Same speed, different wavelength
All of them travel at about 300,000 km/s in a vacuum. Using v = f × λ, a higher frequency simply means a shorter wavelength.

x: Wi-Fi at 2.4 GHz
Wavelength = 0.125 m = 12.5 cm

deep.x: Energy per photon

Light comes in packets called photons, and each photon's energy rises with frequency. One UV photon has enough energy to break chemical bonds in DNA; a radio photon has millions of times too little, however many there are.
Uses across the spectrum

x: Radio: broadcasting, mobile phones, GPS
Microwaves: ovens (2.45 GHz), radar, satellite links
Infrared: remote controls, thermal cameras
X-rays: medical imaging, airport scanners

deep.w: Mobile phones and Wi-Fi emit dangerous radiation like X-rays
deep.r: They are non-ionising: each photon is far too weak to break chemical bonds

deep.x: Radio, light and X-rays are one family of waves; only the wavelength changes.

cards.title: Transversais e longitudinais
cards.text: Nas ondas transversais, o meio move-se perpendicularmente à onda (ondulações, luz). Nas ondas longitudinais, move-se para a frente e para trás na direção de propagação (som).

deep.x: Both kinds of wave carry energy forward, but the medium moves differently. Picture a Slinky: shake one end sideways and a transverse wave runs along; push and pull the end and a longitudinal wave of squashed and stretched coils travels along it.
Why sound can only be longitudinal in air
A gas can be squeezed, so it can carry pressure waves. It can't resist being sheared sideways, so it can't carry a transverse wave. Solids can do both.
Earthquakes show both kinds

x: **P-waves** (primary) are longitudinal, travel at around 6 km/s in rock and arrive first
**S-waves** (secondary) are transverse, slower, and cannot pass through liquid
Because S-waves vanish on the far side of the planet, seismologists deduced in the early 1900s that Earth's outer core is liquid

deep.x: Light is special

Light is a transverse wave, but nothing physical moves sideways: it's the electric and magnetic fields that oscillate at right angles to the direction of travel. That's why light can be polarised, the trick used by polarising sunglasses.
The great Lisbon earthquake of 1755 was felt across much of Europe and North Africa; studying its effects helped launch modern seismology.
Transverse waves wobble across their path; longitudinal waves squeeze along it.

cards.title: Reflexão e ecos

steps: Mede o tempo e obtém a distância

cards.text: As ondas ressaltam nas superfícies. Um eco é som refletido; o sonar e a ecografia cronometram ecos para medir distâncias e ver o interior das coisas.

deep.x: When a wave meets a boundary, part of it bounces back. Hard, smooth surfaces such as rock, concrete or water reflect sound strongly; soft, porous ones absorb it.
Hearing an echo
Your brain merges two sounds arriving less than about 0.1 s apart. In that time sound travels about 34 m, so a wall must be at least about 17 m away to give a separate echo.

x: Shout at a cliff, echo returns in 2 s
Sound went there and back: 343 × 2 = 686 m
Cliff is about 343 m away

deep.x: Using echoes
How ultrasound sees inside you

A probe sends pulses of a few million hertz into the body. Each time they cross a boundary between tissues, such as fluid and muscle, part reflects. A computer times all the echoes and builds an image. Because it uses sound, not radiation, it's safe for pregnancy scans.

deep.w: Echoes only happen in caves and canyons
deep.r: Every room reflects sound; most echoes are too quick to hear separately

deep.x: An echo is a reflected wave, and timing it tells you how far away the reflector is.

cards.title: Interferência
cards.text: Quando duas ondas se encontram, somam-se: cristas com cristas dão ondas maiores, cristas com vales anulam-se. Os auscultadores com cancelamento de ruído emitem uma cópia invertida do ruído exterior para o anular.

deep.x: When two waves overlap, their effects simply add at each point. This is called **superposition**. If crest meets crest, you get a bigger wave (constructive interference). If crest meets trough, they cancel (destructive interference).
Light is a wave: Young's experiment

In 1801 Thomas Young shone light through two narrow slits. Instead of two bright lines, he saw a pattern of bright and dark bands. Only waves could do this, as light from the two slits reinforced in some places and cancelled in others.
Noise-cancelling headphones
They work best on steady, low sounds such as aircraft engine drone, where the wave is predictable and long. Sudden or high-pitched sounds, like voices, are harder to cancel in time.
Everyday interference

x: The rainbow colours on soap bubbles and oil films
"Dead spots" in a room where two speakers' sounds partly cancel
Wi-Fi signals reflecting off walls and interfering, giving weak spots a metre away from strong ones
Musicians tuning by listening for "beats", a slow wobble when two notes are nearly the same

deep.x: Two sounds can add up to silence, but the energy isn't destroyed: it is redistributed to places where the waves reinforce.
Overlapping waves add: crests on crests build up, crests on troughs cancel out.

cards.title: Difração
cards.text: As ondas contornam obstáculos e espalham-se por aberturas comparáveis ao seu comprimento de onda. É por isso que consegues ouvir alguém do outro lado de uma esquina, mas não vê-lo: as ondas sonoras medem metros, as de luz menos de um micrómetro.

deep.x: Diffraction is the spreading of waves as they pass through a gap or around an edge. The effect is strongest when the gap is about the same size as the wavelength. Much bigger gaps let the wave pass almost straight through.
Seen in the harbour
Sea waves passing through a harbour entrance spread out in arcs on the other side, reaching boats tucked behind the harbour wall. You can watch this from above at many Portuguese fishing ports.
Radio and hills
Long radio waves bend around hills and over the horizon; short ones need a clearer line of sight. That's why AM stations reach further than FM, and why mobile networks need many masts.
A limit on seeing
Diffraction also limits how sharp an image can be. Light spreading through a lens or the pupil of the eye blurs fine detail. Telescopes are made wider partly to reduce this blurring.

deep.w: Light always travels in perfectly straight lines
deep.r: Light diffracts too, but only noticeably around very tiny gaps

deep.x: Waves bend around obstacles roughly their own size, which is why you can hear round corners but not see round them.
The rainbow sheen on a CD comes from diffraction by its tracks, which are only about 1.6 thousandths of a millimetre apart.

cards.title: Ressonância
cards.text: Todos os objetos têm frequências naturais. Empurra-os no ritmo certo e a vibração cresce, como quando empurras um baloiço. Os instrumentos musicais usam a ressonância; os engenheiros evitam-na em pontes e máquinas.

deep.x: Every object that can vibrate has one or more natural frequencies, set by its size, stiffness and mass. Push it in step with one of these and each push adds to the last, so the vibration builds up.
Useful resonance

x: A guitar body resonates to make the strings' quiet vibration loud
Radios are tuned by setting a circuit to resonate at one station's frequency
MRI scanners use resonance of atomic nuclei in a magnetic field
Microwave ovens heat food by making water molecules jiggle at about 2.45 GHz

deep.x: Dangerous resonance

In 1831 soldiers marching in step helped collapse the Broughton suspension bridge near Manchester, and armies have ordered troops to break step on bridges ever since. London's Millennium Bridge swayed alarmingly on opening day in 2000 as walkers fell into step with its motion; it was fixed with dampers.

deep.w: Tacoma Narrows Bridge fell from simple resonance
deep.r: It was aeroelastic flutter: wind and the twisting deck fed each other

deep.x: Small pushes at the right rhythm can build huge vibrations.
A trained singer can, occasionally, shatter a wine glass by holding its exact natural note loudly enough.

cards.title: O efeito Doppler
cards.text: Uma fonte em movimento comprime as ondas à sua frente e estica-as atrás. A sirene de uma ambulância soa mais aguda quando se aproxima e mais grave quando se afasta. Os radares da polícia e meteorológicos usam o mesmo efeito.

deep.x: Christian Doppler, an Austrian physicist, described the effect in 1842. If a source moves towards you, each wave crest is emitted a bit closer to you than the last, so crests arrive more often: higher frequency. Moving away, they're spread out: lower frequency.
Tested with a train
In 1845 the Dutch scientist Buys Ballot put trumpeters on a train and musicians by the track to judge the pitch change. It matched Doppler's prediction.
Uses
The expanding universe

Light from distant galaxies is shifted towards red, meaning longer wavelengths. In the 1920s Edwin Hubble and others found the farther the galaxy, the bigger the redshift. This was the key evidence that the universe is expanding.

x: Siren at 700 Hz, ambulance at 25 m/s

deep.w: The siren gets louder and that's the Doppler effect
deep.r: Doppler changes the pitch, not the loudness; loudness changes with distance

deep.x: Motion towards you squeezes waves to a higher frequency; motion away stretches them lower.

quiz.q: Um tom de 343 Hz no ar (343 m/s) tem um comprimento de onda de…
O trovão chega 9 segundos depois do relâmpago. A que distância caiu?
quiz.explain: O som percorre cerca de 1 km a cada 3 s, por isso 9 s ≈ 3 km.

quiz.q: Qual transporta mais energia por fotão?
quiz.explain: Comprimento de onda mais curto significa frequência mais alta e mais energia por fotão.

quiz.q: Os auscultadores com cancelamento de ruído funcionam…
options: Emitindo som que interfere destrutivamente com o ruído
quiz.explain: Ondas invertidas anulam-se.

quiz.q: Porque é que uma sirene soa mais aguda quando se aproxima?
quiz.explain: Comprimento de onda mais curto significa som mais agudo.

lessons.title: Descrever o movimento
lessons.summary: Rapidez, velocidade e aceleração.

cards.title: Rapidez
cards.text: A rapidez é a distância a dividir pelo tempo. Um carro que percorre 120 km em 1,5 horas faz uma média de 80 km/h. Para converter km/h em m/s, divide por 3,6.

deep.x: Speed tells you how much distance is covered in each unit of time. Most journeys speed up and slow down, so the simple formula gives an **average** speed. The speedometer shows your **instantaneous** speed, the speed at that very moment.
speed = distance ÷ time
Converting units
One kilometre per hour is 1,000 m in 3,600 s, which is 1 ÷ 3.6 m/s. So divide km/h by 3.6 to get m/s, and multiply m/s by 3.6 to go back.

x: Motorway limit in Portugal: 120 km/h
You cover a football pitch every 3 seconds

deep.x: Some speeds for scale
Usain Bolt's 9.58 s world record over 100 m, set in Berlin in 2009, averages about 37.6 km/h. His fastest stretch, mid-race, touched about 44 km/h.
Average speed can mislead
A trip from Viana do Castelo to Porto that takes an hour has an average of about 70 km/h, even if you spent time at 120 and time stuck at 0. Average speed says nothing about what happened in between.

deep.w: Average speed is the average of the speeds
deep.r: It's total distance ÷ total time; 60 km/h out and 40 km/h back averages 48, not 50

deep.x: Speed is distance per unit time, and km/h ÷ 3.6 gives m/s.

cards.title: Rapidez vs velocidade
cards.text: A velocidade é a rapidez com uma direção. Um carro a dar a volta a uma rotunda a rapidez constante tem uma velocidade variável, porque a direção está sempre a mudar.

deep.x: Speed is a **scalar**: just a size. Velocity is a **vector**: a size and a direction. "50 km/h" is a speed; "50 km/h heading north" is a velocity.
Why the difference matters

Physics cares about velocity because forces change velocity. Turning a corner at a steady 40 km/h still needs a force from the tyres, because your direction is changing. Without that force the car would carry straight on.
Round trips
If you run once round a 400 m track in 80 s, your average speed is 5 m/s. But you end where you started, so your displacement is zero and your average velocity is zero too.

x: 400 m lap in 80 s
Average speed = 400 ÷ 80 = 5 m/s
Average velocity = 0 ÷ 80 = 0 m/s

deep.x: Velocities add

On a moving walkway at an airport, your velocity relative to the floor is your walking velocity plus the walkway's. Pilots do the same sum with wind: a headwind of 100 km/h takes 100 km/h off their ground speed.
The Moon travels around Earth at roughly constant speed, about 3,700 km/h, yet its velocity is always changing because its direction keeps turning.
Velocity is speed with a direction, so changing direction means changing velocity.

cards.title: Aceleração
cards.text: A aceleração é a rapidez com que a velocidade muda. Um carro que vai de 0 a 100 km/h (27,8 m/s) em 8 segundos acelera a cerca de 3,5 m/s².

deep.x: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. Its unit, metres per second per second (m/s²), means "how many m/s faster each second". Speeding up, slowing down and turning are all accelerations.
acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time taken

x: Car 0 → 100 km/h in 8 s

deep.x: Feeling it in g
It's often handy to compare with gravity, g ≈ 9.81 m/s². An ordinary car pulls about 0.35 g; hard braking on a dry road reaches nearly 1 g.
Deceleration
Slowing down is just acceleration in the opposite direction to motion, often given a minus sign. A car braking from 27.8 m/s to rest in 4 s has an acceleration of about −7 m/s².

deep.w: A fast car is accelerating
deep.r: At a steady speed in a straight line, acceleration is zero, however fast you go

deep.x: Acceleration is how quickly velocity changes, not how fast you are going.
Trained fighter pilots, wearing special suits, can briefly tolerate around 9 g; untrained people tend to black out at around 4–6 g.

cards.title: Queda livre
cards.text: Perto da superfície da Terra, os objetos em queda ganham cerca de 9,81 m/s de velocidade a cada segundo, se a resistência do ar for desprezável. Ao fim de 1 s estás a cair a cerca de 35 km/h; ao fim de 3 s, a mais de 100 km/h.

deep.x: Near Earth's surface gravity gives every falling object the same acceleration, about 9.81 m/s², usually called g. Each second, the falling speed goes up by 9.81 m/s, but the distance fallen grows much faster, with the square of time.
speed = g × t   |   distance = ½ × g × t²

x: Drop a stone down a well, splash after 2 s
(A little less really, as the sound takes time to come back)

deep.x: Speeds pile up quickly
After 1 s you're falling at 9.81 m/s, about 35 km/h. After 3 s, 29.4 m/s, about 106 km/h. That's why even modest falls are dangerous.
g isn't quite the same everywhere

x: Near the equator it's about 9.78 m/s²; near the poles about 9.83 m/s²
It's slightly weaker on mountain tops, being further from Earth's centre
On the Moon it's 1.62 m/s², about a sixth of Earth's

deep.w: Things fall at a steady speed
deep.r: In free fall they speed up every second until air resistance catches up

deep.x: In free fall, speed grows steadily with time but distance grows with time squared.

cards.title: A intuição de Galileu
cards.text: Sem resistência do ar, objetos pesados e leves caem ao mesmo ritmo. Em 1971, astronautas na Lua mostraram-no ao largar um martelo e uma pena: chegaram ao chão juntos.

deep.x: For nearly 2,000 years people followed Aristotle, who taught that heavy objects fall faster than light ones. It seemed obvious: a stone drops quicker than a leaf. Galileo Galilei, working in Italy around 1590–1638, argued that the difference is caused by air, not weight.

items.w: A leaf is too light to fall fast

deep.x: How he tested it

Falling objects move too fast to time with the clocks of his day. Galileo rolled balls down gentle ramps to slow the motion, timing them with water clocks and musical beats. He found the distance grew with the square of the time, whatever the ball's mass.
A clever argument

Galileo also used pure reasoning. Tie a heavy and a light stone together. If light things fall slower, the light stone should hold back the heavy one, so the pair falls slower. But the pair is heavier, so it should fall faster. Both can't be true, so the idea must be wrong.
On the Moon
On 2 August 1971, Apollo 15 commander David Scott dropped a geologist's hammer and a falcon feather on the airless Moon. They hit the ground together, live on television.

deep.w: Galileo dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa
deep.r: The story comes from a later biographer; historians doubt it happened

deep.x: Without air, a hammer and a feather fall side by side.
In 2014 the BBC filmed a bowling ball and feathers dropped together inside the world's largest vacuum chamber, in Ohio, and they landed at the same instant.

cards.title: Velocidade terminal
cards.text: À medida que um objeto em queda acelera, a resistência do ar aumenta até igualar o peso. A partir daí deixa de acelerar. Um paraquedista de barriga para baixo chega a cerca de 200 km/h; o paraquedas reduz isso para cerca de 20 km/h.

deep.x: Air resistance, or drag, grows rapidly with speed, roughly with its square. A falling object speeds up until drag equals its weight. Then the forces balance, acceleration stops and it falls at a steady **terminal velocity**.
What sets it

x: Heavier objects need more drag to balance, so they fall faster
Bigger area facing the air means more drag and a slower terminal speed
Thinner air (higher up) means less drag and a faster fall

deep.x: Opening a parachute

A canopy has dozens of times the area of a body. When it opens, drag suddenly far exceeds weight, so the skydiver decelerates sharply until a new, much lower terminal velocity of about 20 km/h is reached.
In 2012 Felix Baumgartner jumped from about 39 km up. In the very thin air he reached around 1,350 km/h, faster than the speed of sound.

deep.w: Raindrops would kill us without air resistance
deep.r: True in theory, but drag limits even big drops to about 30 km/h

deep.x: Terminal velocity is reached when air resistance grows to match weight, so the fall stops speeding up.

cards.title: Distância de paragem
cards.text: A distância de paragem é a distância de reação mais a distância de travagem. A distância de travagem cresce com o quadrado da velocidade: o dobro da velocidade, quatro vezes a distância de travagem.

deep.x: Stopping a car happens in two stages. First your brain notices and your foot moves; the car is still at full speed. Then the brakes slow it. The total is the stopping distance.
stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance
Why braking distance grows with the square
The kinetic energy to get rid of is ½mv². Brakes remove energy at a roughly fixed rate per metre, so braking distance follows v². Double the speed and the braking distance quadruples.
braking distance = v² ÷ (2 × deceleration)

x: 50 km/h = 13.9 m/s, deceleration 7 m/s²
Braking: 13.9² ÷ 14 ≈ 14 m, thinking (1 s): 14 m
Total ≈ 28 m; at 100 km/h: 28 + 55 ≈ 83 m

v.unit: total stopping distance, m (dry, 1 s reaction)

deep.x: What makes it worse

x: Wet roads can roughly double braking distance; ice can make it ten times longer
Worn tyres and poor brakes
Tiredness, alcohol and phones lengthen thinking distance

deep.w: A little faster makes little difference
deep.r: At 60 instead of 50 km/h, braking distance rises by about 44%

deep.x: Braking distance grows with the square of speed, so small speed increases have big consequences.

cards.title: Tempo de reação

viz.unit: metros antes de travar (reação de 1 s)

cards.text: Um condutor típico demora cerca de 1 segundo a reagir. A 120 km/h, o carro percorre mais de 33 m antes de os travões começarem sequer a atuar. O telemóvel ao volante torna esse tempo muito maior.

deep.x: Reaction time is the delay between something happening and you responding. For a simple, expected signal, like a starting gun, it can be under 0.2 s. On the road, where you must notice a hazard, decide and move your foot, about 1 s is typical, and longer in real traffic.

x: Motorway at 120 km/h = 33.3 m/s
1 s reaction
33 m travelled before braking starts

v.unit: distance before braking, m (1.5 s reaction)

deep.x: Try the ruler test
Have a friend hold a 30 cm ruler above your open fingers and drop it without warning. The distance it falls before you catch it gives your reaction time, using the free-fall formula.

x: Ruler falls 20 cm = 0.2 m

deep.x: What slows reactions

items: Looking at or holding a phone

deep.x: In Portugal the drink-drive limit is 0.5 g/l of blood, and 0.2 g/l for new and professional drivers, reflecting how alcohol slows and blurs reactions.
Athletics rules treat any reaction under 0.1 s after the starting gun as a false start, on the basis that humans can't genuinely react faster.
In the second it takes to react, a car at motorway speed covers about a third of a football pitch.

cards.title: Movimento relativo
cards.text: O movimento depende do observador. Num comboio a 200 km/h, uma chávena de café está parada em relação a ti, mas move-se depressa em relação ao chão. Não existe "imobilidade" absoluta.

deep.x: Every measurement of motion is made relative to something. Usually we measure against the ground, but that is a choice, not a law of nature. Galileo made this point in 1632 with a ship: below decks, in a smoothly moving ship, flies, fish and dripping water all behave as on land.
Combining velocities
Relative velocities add or subtract. Two cars approaching head-on at 90 km/h each close the gap at 180 km/h. A car overtaking at 130 km/h past a lorry at 90 gains on it at only 40 km/h.
You are never still

Sitting in a chair in Portugal, you are carried round by Earth's rotation at about 1,300 km/h, and round the Sun at about 107,000 km/h. The Sun itself orbits the galaxy. You feel none of it, because steady motion can't be felt; only changes in motion can.
From Galileo to Einstein

Einstein's special relativity (1905) started from the same principle: the laws of physics are the same for everyone moving steadily. Adding one twist, that light has the same speed for everyone, led to time dilation and E = mc².

deep.w: There is one true "at rest"
deep.r: All steady motion is relative; no experiment can single out absolute rest

deep.x: Motion only makes sense relative to something, and steady motion feels exactly like standing still.

cards.title: Gráficos do movimento
cards.text: Num gráfico distância–tempo, o declive é a rapidez. Num gráfico velocidade–tempo, o declive é a aceleração e a área por baixo é a distância percorrida.

deep.x: Graphs turn a journey into a picture. Two kinds are used most: distance–time and velocity–time. They look similar but you read them in completely different ways.
Reading a distance–time graph

x: A straight sloping line means steady speed; steeper means faster
A flat line means not moving
A curve getting steeper means speeding up

deep.x: Reading a velocity–time graph

x: A flat line means steady velocity (zero acceleration)
A line sloping up means accelerating; down means braking
The area under the line is the distance travelled
Car goes 0 → 20 m/s in 10 s on a straight line
Area of triangle = ½ × 10 × 20
Distance = 100 m

deep.x: Where you see them
Fitness apps plot your pace through a run; car data loggers and train systems record speed against time; investigators use a vehicle's recorded speed graph to reconstruct crashes.

deep.w: A flat line always means stopped
deep.r: Only on a distance–time graph; on a velocity–time graph it means steady speed

deep.x: On a distance–time graph slope is speed; on a velocity–time graph slope is acceleration and area is distance.

quiz.q: 90 km/h em m/s são…
Se duplicares a velocidade, a distância de travagem passa a ser cerca de…
quiz.explain: Cresce com o quadrado da velocidade.

quiz.q: Sem ar, um martelo e uma pena caem…
quiz.explain: Demonstrado na Lua em 1971.

lessons.title: Leis de Newton
lessons.summary: As três regras por trás de cada empurrão e puxão.

cards.title: Primeira lei: inércia
cards.text: Um objeto continua a fazer o que está a fazer, parado ou a mover-se em linha reta a velocidade constante, a não ser que atue sobre ele uma força resultante. É por isso que os passageiros são projetados para a frente quando o autocarro trava.

deep.x: Inertia is an object's resistance to changes in its motion. The more mass, the more inertia. A full supermarket trolley is harder to start and to stop than an empty one.
A radical idea

Aristotle believed that moving things need a constant push to keep going. Galileo and then Descartes realised that, without friction, motion would simply continue. Newton made it his first law in 1687.
The key word is "net"

Many forces can act at once. If they balance, the net force is zero and the object behaves as if no force acts. A car cruising at a steady 100 km/h has engine force exactly balancing drag and friction.

items: Passengers lurch when a bus brakes

deep.x: Why headrests matter
In a rear-end crash, the seat shoves your body forward. Your head, by inertia, stays behind and snaps backwards. A headrest pushes your head along with your body, preventing whiplash.

x: Bus brakes from 50 km/h
Bus slows, your body keeps going at 50 km/h
You lurch forward until a seat or handle stops you

deep.w: Moving things naturally slow down and stop
deep.r: They slow because friction and drag act; with no net force they keep going

deep.x: Objects resist changes to their motion; only an unbalanced force changes it.
Voyager 1, launched in 1977, has been coasting for decades with its engine off, still moving at about 17 km/s.

cards.title: Segunda lei: F = m × a
example: Carro de 1500 kg, força resultante de 3000 N
cards.text: A aceleração de um objeto é proporcional à força que atua sobre ele e inversamente proporcional à sua massa. Empurra com o dobro da força e acelera o dobro; duplica a massa e a aceleração cai para metade.

deep.x: The second law gives a number to the first. It says exactly how much an object accelerates when a net force acts. In fact, it defines the unit of force: 1 newton (N) accelerates 1 kg at 1 m/s².
force = mass × acceleration

x: 1,500 kg car accelerating at 3 m/s²
4,500 N of net forward force

deep.x: How big is a newton?
A small apple of about 100 g weighs about 1 N. A typical adult weighs roughly 700 N. A family car's engine might deliver a few thousand newtons through the tyres.
Rearranging it

x: a = F ÷ m: a lighter car accelerates faster with the same engine
m = F ÷ a: astronauts measure their mass in orbit by timing how a known spring force accelerates them

deep.x: Net force, again
If you push a heavy box with 300 N and friction pushes back with 250 N, only the 50 N difference accelerates it. Push with 250 N and it moves at a steady speed or not at all.

deep.w: A constant force gives a constant speed
deep.r: A constant net force gives constant acceleration; speed keeps rising

deep.x: Force causes acceleration, and the more mass, the less acceleration for the same force.

cards.title: Terceira lei: ação e reação

items: para cima e para a frente

cards.text: Cada força tem uma parceira igual e oposta. Quando empurras uma parede, a parede empurra-te de volta. Os foguetões empurram gás para trás; o gás empurra o foguetão para a frente.

deep.x: Forces always come in pairs. If A pushes on B, then B pushes on A with the same strength in the opposite direction. The pair acts at the same instant; neither comes first.
Why they don't cancel

The two forces act on different objects, so they can't cancel each other out. When a horse pulls a cart, the cart pulls back on the horse. The horse still moves because the ground pushes it forward harder than the cart pulls back.
Equal forces, unequal effects

The force pair is equal but the masses aren't. When you jump, you and Earth push each other equally. You accelerate noticeably; Earth, about 10²³ times heavier, accelerates by an immeasurably small amount.
Walking needs friction
On ice you can't walk well because your foot can't push backwards on the ground, so the ground can't push you forwards. Grip is how you get the reaction force you need.

x: Skater (60 kg) pushes a friend (40 kg) on ice
Both feel the same force, say 120 N
She gets 2 m/s², he gets 3 m/s², in opposite directions

deep.w: The bigger object pushes harder
deep.r: A lorry and a car in a collision push on each other with equal force; the car's lower mass makes it suffer more acceleration

deep.x: Forces come in equal, opposite pairs acting on two different objects.

cards.title: Outra vez massa e peso

viz.unit: peso de uma pessoa de 70 kg (N)

cards.text: A massa (kg) é a quantidade de matéria e não muda. O peso é a força da gravidade sobre ela e depende de onde estás: na Lua pesarias cerca de um sexto.

deep.x: In everyday speech "weight" means kilograms. In physics weight is a force, measured in newtons, and mass is measured in kilograms. Mass tells you how much stuff there is and how hard it is to accelerate. Weight tells you how hard gravity pulls on it.
weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W = m × g)

x: A 70 kg person
On Earth: 70 × 9.81 ≈ 687 N
On the Moon: 70 × 1.62 ≈ 113 N

v.unit: weight of a 70 kg person, N

deep.x: Your bathroom scale

A bathroom scale actually measures force: how hard you press on it. It then divides by Earth's g to show kilograms. Take it to the Moon and it would claim you'd lost five-sixths of your "weight", though your mass hadn't changed.
Inertia doesn't change
On the Moon a loaded wheelbarrow is easier to lift, but just as hard to push sideways to get it moving, because that depends on mass, not weight.

deep.w: Astronauts in orbit have no weight
deep.r: Gravity still pulls them; they feel weightless because they are falling freely

deep.x: Mass is how much matter you have; weight is how hard gravity pulls on it.
Since 2019 the kilogram is defined using a fixed value of Planck's constant, replacing a metal cylinder kept near Paris since 1889.

cards.title: Cintos de segurança e airbags
cards.text: Num acidente, o teu corpo tem de perder a velocidade. Distribuir isso por mais tempo e mais distância significa uma força menor. Os cintos esticam um pouco e os airbags amortecem, reduzindo drasticamente a força máxima.

deep.x: In a crash, your body has to go from the car's speed to zero. Newton's second law can be written in terms of momentum: force equals the change in momentum divided by the time it takes. Stretch the time, and the force falls.
force = mass × change in velocity ÷ time taken

x: 70 kg person stops from 50 km/h (13.9 m/s)
In 0.01 s against the dashboard: 70 × 13.9 ÷ 0.01 ≈ 97,000 N
In 0.1 s with belt and airbag: ≈ 9,700 N

deep.x: How they work together

x: The belt spreads force across the strong bones of the pelvis and ribcage
Pre-tensioners pull the belt tight in the first milliseconds
Airbags inflate in about 30 thousandths of a second, then vent gas to cushion
Without a belt, an airbag can do harm: it's designed to work alongside one

deep.x: A gift to the world

Swedish engineer Nils Bohlin designed the three-point seat belt for Volvo in 1959. Volvo made the patent freely available, and the design is now standard worldwide. It's credited with saving a very large number of lives.

deep.w: You can brace yourself with your arms
deep.r: At 50 km/h the forces are many times your body weight; arms cannot hold them

deep.x: Seat belts and airbags save lives by making the stop take longer, which shrinks the force.

cards.title: Movimento circular
cards.text: Andar em círculo exige uma força dirigida para o centro (força centrípeta). Numa rotunda, vem do atrito dos pneus; no caso da Lua, da gravidade da Terra. Sem ela, os objetos saem disparados em linha reta.

deep.x: Moving in a circle at steady speed is still accelerating, because the direction changes all the time. That acceleration points towards the centre of the circle, and so must the net force causing it, the **centripetal force**.
centripetal force = m × v² ÷ r

x: 1,200 kg car at 36 km/h (10 m/s), bend radius 20 m
6,000 N from tyre friction

deep.x: Speed matters most

The force needed grows with the square of speed. Take a bend twice as fast and you need four times the grip. On a wet or icy road, available friction drops, so the car slides outwards along a straighter path.
Banked curves
Racing tracks and some motorway slip roads tilt inwards. Part of the road's push then points towards the centre, so cars rely less on friction to turn.

deep.w: Let go of a whirling ball and it flies outward
deep.r: It flies off in a straight line along the tangent, the way it was heading

deep.x: Circular motion needs a constant pull towards the centre; take it away and the object goes straight.
For a rotating space station to give "gravity" of 1 g with a radius of 100 m, it would need to turn about three times a minute.

cards.title: "Força centrífuga"

items.r: o corpo segue em frente enquanto o carro curva

cards.text: Num carro a curvar sentes-te empurrado para fora. Na verdade, o teu corpo está a tentar seguir em frente (inércia) enquanto o carro curva por baixo de ti. A "força centrífuga" é a forma como isso se sente dentro do referencial que roda.

deep.x: Sitting in a car as it turns left, you feel thrown to the right. Watched from outside, nothing pushes you outwards: your body is trying to continue in a straight line, and the car door swings into your path and pushes you round the corner.
A "fictitious" force

Physicists call centrifugal force a fictitious or inertial force. It appears only when you describe motion from a rotating viewpoint. Engineers sometimes use it as a handy shortcut, but there is no object producing it.
The spin dryer

In a washing machine's spin cycle, the drum pushes the clothes inwards, making them travel in a circle. Water drops pass through the holes, where nothing pushes them inwards, so they fly off in straight lines and leave the drum.
Other examples

x: Mud flying off a bicycle tyre leaves in a straight line from where it lets go
A salad spinner dries lettuce the same way
Centrifuges in labs separate blood into layers; denser parts move furthest out

deep.w: Centrifugal force throws things outward
deep.r: Nothing pulls them out; they just keep going straight while their surroundings turn

deep.x: The outward "force" you feel when turning is your own inertia seen from a turning seat.

cards.title: O atrito e Newton

items: o movimento parece precisar de empurrão

cards.text: Na Terra, as coisas abrandam por causa do atrito e da resistência do ar, não porque o movimento pare naturalmente. No espaço, um objeto empurrado continua a deslizar para sempre.

deep.x: Friction is the force that resists surfaces sliding over each other. Even surfaces that feel smooth have microscopic bumps that catch and briefly bond. Air and water resistance are the fluid versions.
Why Aristotle was fooled

Everything in daily life slows to a stop: a rolling ball, a pushed cart, a coasting bicycle. It's easy to conclude that rest is the natural state. Only by imagining away friction, as Galileo did, does the first law become visible.
How friction compares
The friction coefficient is roughly friction force divided by the force pressing the surfaces together. Lower numbers mean slipperier contact.
Friction we rely on

x: Tyres gripping the road, and brakes gripping discs
Shoes on pavements; Portugal's polished calçada stones become notoriously slippery when wet
Knots holding, nails staying in wood, matches lighting

deep.x: In space
With no air, a spacecraft keeps coasting after its engines stop. Probes travel for years using only short engine bursts to change course.

x: Ice hockey puck at 10 m/s on ice, μ ≈ 0.02
Deceleration ≈ 0.02 × 9.81 ≈ 0.2 m/s²
Glides about 10² ÷ (2 × 0.2) ≈ 250 m

deep.x: Things stop because friction and drag act on them, not because motion naturally fades.

cards.title: As leis de Newton no desporto

items: Acompanhar o gesto prolonga o contacto
Aterrar de joelhos fletidos reduz a força

cards.text: Os futebolistas empurram o chão para trás para acelerar para a frente; os jogadores mais pesados são mais difíceis de parar; um remate bem cronometrado transfere mais força através de um contacto mais longo.

deep.x: Every sport is applied Newtonian physics. Athletes and coaches use the three laws, often without naming them, to get more speed, power and control.
Kicking a ball

Foot and ball are in contact for only about a hundredth of a second. During that time the force on the ball can exceed a thousand newtons. Following through keeps the foot pushing slightly longer, giving more change in momentum.

x: 0.43 kg football kicked to 30 m/s (108 km/h)
Contact lasts 0.01 s
Average force = 0.43 × 30 ÷ 0.01 ≈ 1,300 N

deep.x: Sprint starts
Sprinters push hard backwards against starting blocks. The blocks push back, giving a large forward force from the very first step. Leaning forward helps direct that force horizontally.

items: Jumpers push down to go up

deep.x: Soft landings
Bending your knees when you land from a jump makes the stop take longer, so the force on your joints is smaller. Gymnastics mats, padded gloves and cushioned running shoes use the same idea.

deep.w: A bigger swing always means a harder hit
deep.r: Speed at impact and clean contact matter more than effort

deep.x: Sport is a contest of forces: push back to go forward, push longer to go faster, bend to land softly.

cards.title: Principia, 1687
cards.text: Isaac Newton publicou as suas leis do movimento e da gravitação universal nos "Principia Mathematica" em 1687. Explicavam a queda das maçãs e as órbitas dos planetas com as mesmas regras.

deep.x: The full title is *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica*, "Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy". Written in Latin, it set out three laws of motion and a law of universal gravitation, then used them to explain a huge range of phenomena.
How it came about

In 1684 the astronomer Edmond Halley asked Newton what path a planet would follow under an inverse-square pull. Newton said an ellipse, and that he had already calculated it. Halley urged him to publish and paid for the printing himself.
What it explained

x: Why planets follow Kepler's elliptical orbits
The tides, from the pull of the Moon and Sun
The paths of comets
The slightly flattened shape of the spinning Earth

deep.x: Its legacy
Newton's laws predicted the return of Halley's comet in 1758 and, in 1846, guided astronomers to discover Neptune from its pull on Uranus. They are still used to send spacecraft to other planets.

deep.w: An apple hit Newton on the head
deep.r: Newton said watching an apple fall made him think about gravity; nothing hit him

deep.x: The Principia showed that the same laws rule a falling apple and the orbiting Moon.
Newton later ran England's Royal Mint and personally pursued counterfeiters.

quiz.q: Um carro de 1000 kg com uma força resultante de 2000 N acelera a…
quiz.explain: a = F ÷ m.

quiz.q: Porque é que os airbags reduzem as lesões?
options: Prolongam a paragem no tempo, reduzindo a força máxima
quiz.explain: Mais tempo de paragem significa menos força.

quiz.q: Que lei explica a propulsão dos foguetões?
quiz.explain: Ação e reação.

lessons.title: Gravidade e órbitas
lessons.summary: Porque é que a Lua não cai (cai, mas falha).

cards.title: Gravitação universal
cards.text: Todas as massas se atraem umas às outras. A força aumenta com ambas as massas e diminui com o quadrado da distância: o dobro da distância, um quarto da força.

deep.x: Newton's great leap was to say that the force pulling an apple down is the same force holding the Moon in orbit, and that it acts between every pair of masses in the universe. He published this law in 1687.
F = G × m₁ × m₂ ÷ r²
The inverse square

Gravity spreads out in all directions, like light from a bulb. At twice the distance the same pull is spread over four times the area, so it's a quarter as strong. At ten times the distance it's a hundredth.
Gravity is very weak

G is tiny, so only enormous masses produce noticeable pulls. Two people standing 1 m apart attract each other with a force of about a third of a millionth of a newton. A small fridge magnet beats the whole Earth's pull on a paperclip.

x: Two 70 kg people, 1 m apart

deep.x: Weighing the Earth
In 1798 Henry Cavendish measured the tiny attraction between lead balls in his laboratory. That gave G, and with it the first accurate value for Earth's mass, about 6 × 10²⁴ kg.

deep.w: Gravity stops at some distance
deep.r: Its reach is unlimited; it just gets weaker and weaker

deep.x: Every mass pulls on every other, and the pull falls with the square of the distance.

cards.title: As órbitas são quedas

steps: Rápido o suficiente: a Terra curva-se

cards.text: Um satélite em órbita está constantemente a cair para a Terra, mas move-se de lado tão depressa que o chão se curva por baixo dele. Newton imaginou um canhão no alto de uma montanha a disparar cada vez mais depressa.

deep.x: An orbit isn't a balance between gravity and some outward force. It is pure falling. The satellite falls towards Earth all the time, but it's moving sideways so fast that Earth's surface curves away just as quickly as it falls.
Newton's cannon

Newton imagined a cannon on a very high mountain. Each faster shot lands further away, until at one speed the ball falls round the curve of the Earth and comes back to the mountain. He drew this in a work published in 1728, after his death.
The magic number

Earth's surface curves down by about 5 m for every 8 km you travel. In the first second of falling, anything drops about 5 m. So something moving sideways at about 8 km/s falls 5 m while the ground drops 5 m: it never gets closer.

x: Sideways speed 8 km/s
In 1 s it travels 8 km and falls 5 m
Ground has also dropped 5 m: it stays at the same height

deep.x: Why satellites still come down
Low satellites skim the outer edge of the atmosphere. The thin air drags on them, slowly lowering their orbit. Without occasional engine boosts, the ISS would fall back within a year or two.

deep.w: Satellites orbit because they're above gravity
deep.r: Gravity is what keeps them in orbit; without it they'd fly off in a straight line

deep.x: An orbit is a fall that keeps missing the ground.
The Moon is falling towards Earth too, by about 1.4 mm every second, while moving sideways about 1 km.

cards.title: Velocidades orbitais
cards.text: A Estação Espacial Internacional orbita a cerca de 400 km de altitude a cerca de 28 000 km/h, dando a volta à Terra mais ou menos a cada 90 minutos. A tripulação vê cerca de 16 nasceres do sol por dia.

deep.x: The closer a satellite is to Earth, the faster it must go to stay in orbit, because gravity is stronger there. Farther out, gravity is weaker, so orbits are slower and much longer.
The ISS in numbers

x: Orbit length ≈ 2π × (6,371 + 400) km ≈ 42,500 km
At 27,600 km/h

deep.x: Seeing it from Portugal

The ISS is the third brightest thing in the night sky after the Moon and Venus. Shortly after sunset or before sunrise it crosses the sky as a steady, bright point in about 5 minutes, lit by sunlight while the ground is already dark. Space agency websites list visible passes for your town.
A home in orbit

x: Built from 1998 and continuously crewed since November 2000
About as long as a football pitch, counting its solar panels
Partners include NASA, Russia, Japan, Canada and ESA, with European modules such as Columbus
Current plans are to bring it down into a remote part of the Pacific around 2030

deep.x: The lower the orbit, the faster the satellite must travel.

cards.title: Imponderabilidade
cards.text: Os astronautas em órbita não estão fora do alcance da gravidade: à altitude da ISS, a gravidade tem cerca de 90% da força que tem à superfície. Flutuam porque eles e a estação estão a cair juntos.

deep.x: The feeling of weight is really the feeling of the floor pushing up on you. In free fall, nothing pushes on you, because you and everything around you fall together. That's the floating feeling of orbit.

x: Earth's radius 6,371 km, ISS radius 6,771 km
Gravity there is about 89% of ground level

deep.x: Free fall on Earth

You feel brief weightlessness at the top of a rollercoaster hill or in a lift that drops suddenly. ESA trains astronauts and runs experiments on parabolic flights from Bordeaux in France: the aircraft flies arcs that give about 20 seconds of free fall each time.
Effects on the body

x: Without load, bones lose roughly 1% of their density per month in some areas
Muscles weaken, so ISS crews exercise about two hours a day
Fluid shifts to the head, giving a puffy face and blocked sinuses
The spine stretches, and astronauts can return a few centimetres taller, though this fades

deep.w: There's no gravity in space
deep.r: Gravity is almost as strong at the ISS; astronauts float because they are falling

deep.x: Weightlessness is what falling feels like when everything falls with you.

cards.title: Órbita geoestacionária
cards.text: A cerca de 35 786 km acima do equador, um satélite demora exatamente um dia a dar uma volta, por isso fica sempre sobre o mesmo ponto. Os satélites de televisão e meteorológicos usam-na.

deep.x: Orbits get slower as they get higher. At one particular height, about 35,786 km above the equator, one orbit takes exactly as long as one turn of the Earth. A satellite there seems to hang still in the sky.
Why it's so useful
A fixed dish on your roof can point at one satellite for years without moving. That's why satellite TV dishes in Portugal all point roughly south, towards the equator.
The catch: distance and delay

The signal has to travel up nearly 36,000 km and down again. Even at the speed of light that takes about a quarter of a second, which is why satellite phone calls and old satellite internet felt laggy.

x: ≈ 0.24 s delay each way

deep.x: A crowded ring
Because there is only one such ring, slots in it are allocated internationally. Europe's Meteosat satellites, run by EUMETSAT, sit there and provide the cloud images on weather forecasts.
The idea of using geostationary satellites for communication was popularised by science-fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke in 1945, nearly 20 years before the first one was launched.

deep.w: Geostationary satellites aren't moving
deep.r: They travel at about 11,000 km/h, exactly keeping pace with Earth's spin

deep.x: At one special height, an orbit lasts exactly a day, so the satellite stays over the same spot.

cards.title: Marés

steps: A Lua puxa mais o lado próximo
A Terra roda por baixo delas

cards.text: A gravidade da Lua puxa com mais força o lado da Terra mais próximo do que o lado oposto, esticando os oceanos em duas protuberâncias. À medida que a Terra roda, a maioria das costas tem duas marés altas por dia.

deep.x: The Moon's pull weakens with distance. The side of Earth facing the Moon is pulled harder than Earth's centre, and the centre harder than the far side. The result is a stretch: the oceans bulge towards the Moon and also on the opposite side.
Why tides come about 50 minutes later each day

Earth spins under the two bulges, giving two highs and two lows. But the Moon moves along its orbit too, so it takes about 24 hours 50 minutes to return overhead. High tides are about 12 hours 25 minutes apart.
Spring and neap tides

The Sun raises tides as well, a little under half as strong as the Moon's. When Sun and Moon line up, at new and full moon, their effects add: big **spring tides**. At half moon they partly cancel: small **neap tides**.
Range varies hugely
The shape of coasts and seabeds amplifies or damps tides. Portugal's Atlantic coast has moderate ranges; the nearly enclosed Mediterranean barely has tides at all.
Tidal friction is slowly braking Earth's spin, lengthening the day by roughly 2 thousandths of a second per century, while the Moon drifts about 3.8 cm further away each year.
Tides come from the difference in the Moon's pull across Earth, which stretches the oceans into two bulges.

cards.title: Velocidade de escape
cards.text: Para sair da Terra sem mais propulsão, precisarias de cerca de 11,2 km/s (40 300 km/h). Os foguetões não a atingem de imediato; queimam combustível durante minutos, subindo e acelerando.

deep.x: Throw a ball up and it comes back. Throw it faster and it goes higher. Escape velocity is the launch speed at which an object, with no further push, would keep slowing forever but never stop and fall back.
escape velocity = √(2 × G × M ÷ r)
It doesn't depend on your mass
A pebble and a spacecraft need the same speed to escape, because heavier things feel more gravity but also need more force to slow them down; the two effects cancel, just as in free fall.
Rockets don't need it at the start

Escape velocity is for something fired like a bullet and then left alone. A rocket keeps firing, so it can climb at any speed. In practice rockets rise slowly through the thick lower air, then accelerate horizontally for several minutes. Missions to the Moon or Mars burn up to nearly 11 km/s only once they're already in orbit.
Black holes
If an object is compact enough, its escape velocity exceeds the speed of light. Nothing, not even light, can get out: that's a black hole.

x: About 12 times faster than a rifle bullet

deep.w: You need escape velocity to reach space
deep.r: Reaching space or orbit needs less; escape is for leaving Earth's pull for good

deep.x: Escape velocity is the speed that lets an unpowered object coast away from a planet for ever.

cards.title: As leis de Kepler
cards.text: Os planetas movem-se em elipses com o Sol num dos focos; aceleram quando estão mais perto do Sol; e quanto mais longe está o planeta, mais longo é o seu ano, segundo uma regra precisa.

deep.x: Johannes Kepler worked with the most precise naked-eye observations ever made, collected by the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe. Struggling for years to fit the orbit of Mars, he finally abandoned perfect circles.
The third law in action
If distance is measured in astronomical units (Earth–Sun distance) and time in Earth years, the square of a planet's year equals the cube of its distance.

x: Mars is 1.52 AU from the Sun
A Martian year ≈ 1.88 Earth years

deep.x: Earth's own ellipse

Earth's orbit is nearly circular, but it's closest to the Sun in early January, about 147 million km, and farthest in early July, about 152 million km. Moving faster near the Sun, Earth crosses the winter half of its orbit quicker: the northern winter is a few days shorter than summer.

deep.w: Seasons happen because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer
deep.r: Earth is closest in January; seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis

deep.x: Kepler found the rules of planetary motion; Newton later showed gravity was the reason for them.

cards.title: Assistências gravitacionais

steps: Roubar-lhe um pouco de energia orbital

cards.text: As sondas espaciais passam junto a planetas para ganhar velocidade, como uma bola a ressaltar num comboio em movimento. A Voyager usou Júpiter e Saturno para chegar ao Sistema Solar exterior.

deep.x: Flying close to a planet, a spacecraft is pulled in and swung round. Relative to the planet it leaves at the same speed it arrived. But the planet itself is moving around the Sun, and the craft can borrow some of that motion.
The train analogy

Throw a ball at 30 km/h at a train coming towards you at 50 km/h. Relative to the train the ball hits at 80 km/h and bounces back at 80 km/h. Add the train's own 50 km/h and the ball now flies away at 130 km/h.

x: Ball 30 km/h, train 50 km/h towards it
Bounces off at 80 km/h relative to the train
80 + 50 = 130 km/h relative to the ground

deep.x: Nothing for free
The planet loses exactly the energy the probe gains, but a planet is so massive that its orbit changes by an immeasurably tiny amount.
The Grand Tour

A rare alignment of the outer planets, recurring roughly every 175 years, let Voyager 2 visit Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune using each as a slingshot to the next. Without assists, the trip to Neptune would have taken decades longer.
Braking too

Assists can also slow a craft down. ESA's BepiColombo, launched in 2018 to Mercury, used nine flybys of Earth, Venus and Mercury mostly to shed speed as it falls towards the Sun. ESA's JUICE is using several flybys on its way to Jupiter.
A gravity assist steals a sliver of a planet's orbital motion to speed up or redirect a probe.

cards.title: Ondas gravitacionais

events.l: prova indireta num par de pulsares

cards.text: Einstein previu que massas em aceleração criam ondulações no espaço-tempo. Em 2015, os detetores LIGO mediram estas ondas pela primeira vez, provenientes da fusão de dois buracos negros a mais de mil milhões de anos-luz.

deep.x: In 1916 Albert Einstein predicted that accelerating masses send out ripples in space-time itself. They travel at the speed of light, stretching and squeezing space as they pass. He doubted they could ever be detected, because the effect is so tiny.
How LIGO measures them

LIGO uses two L-shaped detectors in the USA, each with arms 4 km long. Laser beams bounce along the arms and recombine. A passing wave lengthens one arm and shortens the other by a minuscule amount, shifting how the beams interfere.
The first signal

On 14 September 2015, both detectors picked up a chirp lasting a fraction of a second. It came from two black holes, about 36 and 29 times the Sun's mass, spiralling together. About three Suns' worth of mass was converted into gravitational-wave energy.
A new kind of astronomy

x: Europe's Virgo detector near Pisa, Italy, joined the search in 2017
In August 2017 a merger of neutron stars was seen in both gravitational waves and light, and showed such collisions forge heavy elements like gold
ESA plans a space detector, LISA, with arms millions of kilometres long, for the 2030s

deep.w: Gravitational waves are just very strong gravity
deep.r: They're ripples in space-time itself, so faint that measuring them took a century

deep.x: Accelerating masses ripple space-time, and since 2015 we can hear those ripples.

quiz.q: Porque é que os astronautas flutuam na ISS?
options: Eles e a estação estão juntos em queda livre contínua
quiz.explain: A gravidade continua lá a cerca de 90%.

quiz.q: Duplica a distância entre duas massas e a atração gravitacional passa a ser…
quiz.explain: Lei do inverso do quadrado.

quiz.q: O que causa as marés?
options: A atração desigual da Lua (e do Sol) ao longo da Terra
quiz.explain: A diferença de gravidade cria duas protuberâncias.

lessons.title: Momento linear e colisões
lessons.summary: Porque é que coisas pesadas e rápidas são difíceis de parar.

cards.title: Momento linear
cards.text: O momento linear é a massa vezes a velocidade. Um camião lento e uma bala rápida podem ambos ter um momento linear grande.

deep.x: Momentum is "mass in motion": mass times velocity. Its unit is the kilogram metre per second (kg·m/s). Like velocity, it has a direction. Newton actually wrote his second law in terms of momentum: force is the rate at which momentum changes.
momentum = mass × velocity (p = m × v)
Big and slow vs small and fast

x: 40,000 kg lorry creeping at 1.4 m/s
A rifle bullet (0.01 kg at 900 m/s) has only 9

deep.x: Momentum vs kinetic energy

A bullet has small momentum but a lot of energy concentrated in a tiny area, which is why it does damage. A slow lorry has huge momentum, which is why it takes so long to stop and can push almost anything aside. Momentum grows with v; kinetic energy grows with v².

deep.w: A bullet has more momentum than a car
deep.r: A 50 km/h car has nearly 2,000 times a bullet's momentum; the bullet has concentrated energy

deep.x: Momentum is mass times velocity: the harder something is to stop, the more momentum it has.

cards.title: Conservação do momento linear
cards.text: Numa colisão sem forças exteriores, o momento linear total antes é igual ao momento linear total depois. É assim que os peritos reconstituem acidentes.

deep.x: Newton's third law says colliding objects push on each other equally and oppositely for the same time. So whatever momentum one gains, the other loses. Add them up and the total never changes, as long as no outside force interferes.
total momentum before = total momentum after

x: 1,000 kg car at 20 m/s hits a stopped 1,500 kg car; they lock together

deep.x: Crash investigation

Police crash investigators work backwards. Skid marks and final resting positions give speeds just after impact; the masses are known; momentum conservation, applied in two directions, reveals speeds before the crash.
Directions matter
Momentum to the right counts as positive, to the left negative. Two identical cars hitting head-on at the same speed have a total momentum of zero, so if they lock together the wreck stops dead.
Why "no outside force"

Friction from the road acts during a crash, but the collision itself lasts only a fraction of a second while the impact forces are huge. Over that brief moment, outside forces are tiny in comparison, so momentum is very nearly conserved.
Conservation of momentum is one of the deepest laws in physics: it follows from the fact that the laws of nature are the same everywhere in space.
In any collision, the total momentum is the same before and after.

cards.title: Elásticas e inelásticas
cards.text: Nas colisões elásticas, os objetos ressaltam e a energia cinética conserva-se (bolas de snooker, quase). Nas inelásticas, deformam-se ou ficam colados e a energia transforma-se em calor e som (acidentes de carro).
