deep.x: Momentum is always conserved in collisions, but kinetic energy isn't. The difference between collisions is how much kinetic energy survives as motion, and how much turns into heat, sound and bent metal.
A spectrum, not two boxes
Truly elastic collisions only happen between atoms and molecules. Everything else loses some energy. How much is captured by how well things bounce.
Where the energy goes in a crash

x: Car crash from the previous card
Before: ½ × 1,000 × 20² = 200 kJ
After: ½ × 2,500 × 8² = 80 kJ, so 120 kJ became heat, sound and damage

deep.x: Why it matters

x: In car crashes, inelastic is good: the car absorbs energy instead of bouncing the passengers
Sports balls are tested for bounce: official tennis balls dropped from 2.54 m must bounce to about 1.35–1.47 m
Gas molecules collide elastically, which is why a gas doesn't simply run down and settle

deep.w: In inelastic collisions momentum is lost
deep.r: Momentum is always conserved; only kinetic energy is lost

deep.x: Elastic collisions keep the kinetic energy; inelastic ones turn some of it into heat, sound and deformation.

cards.title: Impulso
cards.text: Mudar o momento linear exige uma força aplicada durante algum tempo: o impulso. A mesma variação pode vir de uma força grande durante pouco tempo ou de uma força pequena durante muito tempo.

deep.x: Impulse is force multiplied by the time it acts. It equals the change in momentum. It's measured in newton seconds (N·s), which is the same as kg·m/s.
impulse = force × time = change in momentum
Same change, different force

To stop a moving thing, you must remove all its momentum. You choose how: a big force briefly or a gentle force for longer. When you want to protect something, stretch the time. When you want a big force, shorten it.

x: Catch a 0.15 kg cricket ball at 30 m/s
Change in momentum = 4.5 N·s
Stiff hands (0.01 s): 450 N; hands moving back (0.1 s): 45 N

deep.x: When you want a short time

A hammer delivers its momentum to a nail in a millisecond or two, giving a force of thousands of newtons with a modest swing. Karate breaks and the "thwack" of a golf drive both rely on very short contact times.
Follow-through
In tennis, golf and football, coaches stress following through. Keeping the racket or foot pushing for longer increases the impulse, so the ball leaves faster.

deep.w: Catching something gently is about reflexes
deep.r: It's about stretching the stopping time to shrink the force

deep.x: The same change in momentum can come from a big force briefly or a small force for longer.

cards.title: Zonas de deformação
cards.text: A frente dos carros é concebida para se deformar, prolongando o choque de poucos milissegundos para cerca de um décimo de segundo, o que reduz a força sobre os passageiros.

deep.x: The front and rear of a modern car are designed to collapse in a controlled way, folding like a concertina. This lengthens the time and distance over which the passenger compartment stops, so the force on the people inside is much smaller.
Numbers

x: Car at 50 km/h (13.9 m/s) stops in 0.6 m of crumpling
Deceleration = 13.9² ÷ (2 × 0.6) ≈ 160 m/s² ≈ 16 g
Stopping in 5 cm instead would mean about 190 g

deep.x: Strong in the middle

Crumple zones only work if the passenger cell itself stays intact. The middle of the car uses high-strength steel so that the energy is absorbed in front of you, not by you. The engine is often designed to drop down under the cabin rather than push into it.
History

Hungarian-born engineer Béla Barényi at Mercedes-Benz patented the idea in 1952, and it reached production cars in 1959. Today the independent Euro NCAP programme, started in 1997, crash-tests new cars sold in Europe and rates how well they protect occupants.

deep.w: Old, rigid cars were safer because they didn't dent
deep.r: They passed the force straight to the people inside

deep.x: A car that crumples protects its passengers by taking longer to stop.
A crumpled car after a minor crash may look worse than an older car's, but that damage is energy that didn't go into its occupants.

cards.title: Recuo
cards.text: Disparar um canhão empurra-o para trás: o momento do projétil para a frente é equilibrado pelo momento do canhão para trás. O canhão, mais pesado, move-se muito mais devagar.

deep.x: Before a cannon fires, the cannon and shell are at rest: total momentum zero. After firing, the shell has forward momentum, so the cannon must have equal backward momentum to keep the total at zero.
mass of gun × recoil speed = mass of shell × shell speed

x: 1,000 kg cannon fires a 10 kg ball at 300 m/s
Ball's momentum: 10 × 300 = 3,000 kg·m/s
Cannon recoils at 3,000 ÷ 1,000 = 3 m/s

deep.x: Taming the kick

Old warship cannons rolled back on wheeled carriages, held by thick ropes. Modern artillery uses hydraulic recoil systems that let the barrel slide back and return. Rifles are held firmly against the shoulder so the shooter's body adds mass and absorbs the kick.

items: Garden hose pushing back on you

deep.x: Jumping from a boat
Step from a small rowing boat onto a jetty, and the boat shoots backwards. Your forward momentum must be matched by the boat's backward momentum. Many people have ended up in the water this way.
The same equation lets a squid escape predators: it squirts water backwards and shoots forwards.

deep.w: Recoil means the gun pushes harder than the bullet
deep.r: The forces are equal and opposite; the gun moves slower only because it's heavier

deep.x: When something is pushed out one way, whatever pushed it moves the other way with equal momentum.

cards.title: O pêndulo de Newton
cards.text: Levanta uma bola, larga-a, e sai disparada uma bola do outro lado. O momento e a energia passam pelas bolas paradas quase na perfeição.

deep.x: Despite the name, Newton didn't invent it. The desk toy became popular in the late 1960s. It's a neat demonstration of two conservation laws at work together.
Why only one ball flies out

In principle, two balls could leave at half the speed and still carry the same momentum. But that would halve the kinetic energy. The only outcome that conserves both momentum and kinetic energy for steel balls is one ball out at the same speed.

x: One 0.1 kg ball at 1 m/s
Momentum 0.1, energy 0.05 J
Two balls at 0.5 m/s: momentum 0.1 ✓, energy 0.025 J ✗

deep.x: Why it eventually stops

Each collision loses a little energy as sound (the clicks), heat and slight deformation of the steel. Over time the motion spreads out, the balls start moving together and eventually they all come to rest.
The snooker version
Hit a snooker ball dead centre into a stationary ball of the same mass, with no spin, and the first stops dead while the second moves off at the same speed. Players call it a stun shot.

deep.w: Momentum travels by the balls moving
deep.r: The middle balls barely move; a compression wave passes through them

deep.x: Newton's cradle obeys both momentum and energy conservation, which is why exactly as many balls fly out as went in.

cards.title: Momento angular
cards.text: Os objetos em rotação têm momento angular. Uma patinadora que encolhe os braços gira mais depressa, porque o momento angular se conserva enquanto o corpo fica mais compacto.

deep.x: Angular momentum is the rotational version of momentum. It depends on how fast something spins and how its mass is arranged around the axis. Mass far from the axis counts for much more than mass near it.
angular momentum = moment of inertia × spin rate
The spinning skater

With no outside twisting force, angular momentum stays the same. Pulling the arms in reduces the moment of inertia, so the spin rate must go up to compensate. An ice skater can spin several times faster this way.
Everywhere you look

items: Office chair spins faster, arms in
Cats twist to land on their feet

deep.x: Stars that spin hundreds of times a second
When a massive star's core collapses to a neutron star only about 20 km across, its spin speeds up enormously. Some pulsars rotate over 700 times a second.
Earth and Moon
Tides are slowly transferring angular momentum from Earth's spin to the Moon's orbit. Earth's day gets slightly longer, and the Moon moves about 3.8 cm further away each year.

deep.w: A spinning skater speeds up by pushing harder
deep.r: No push is needed; drawing mass inward alone makes the spin faster

deep.x: Bring mass closer to the axis and a spinning body spins faster, because angular momentum is conserved.
A helicopter needs its tail rotor because the main rotor's spin would otherwise make the body spin the opposite way.

cards.title: Giroscópios
cards.text: As rodas em rotação resistem a mudanças do seu eixo. As bicicletas estabilizam-se em parte assim; os giroscópios guiam navios, aviões e telemóveis (como minúsculos sensores vibratórios).

deep.x: A gyroscope is a spinning wheel or disc mounted so its axis can point freely. Because of angular momentum, a fast-spinning gyroscope keeps pointing in the same direction in space unless a twisting force acts on it.
Precession

Push on a spinning gyroscope's axis and it doesn't simply tip over. It swivels sideways at right angles to your push. A spinning top leaning over traces a slow circle instead of falling for this reason.
Uses

x: French physicist Léon Foucault named the gyroscope in 1852, using one to show Earth's rotation
Ship gyrocompasses, from the early 1900s, point to true north and ignore magnetism
The Hubble Space Telescope uses gyroscopes to hold its aim steady
Your phone's gyroscope is a tiny vibrating structure on a chip, not a spinning wheel; it senses rotation from the Coriolis effect

deep.x: And bicycles?

A spinning wheel resists tipping a little, but research shows the main reasons a moving bicycle stays up are its steering geometry and the rider steering into any lean. In 2011, researchers built a bike with no gyroscopic effect that still balanced itself.

deep.w: Gyroscopes are what keep bicycles upright
deep.r: They help slightly; steering geometry and the rider do most of the work

deep.x: A spinning object resists having its axis turned, which makes gyroscopes superb direction-keepers.

cards.title: Foguetões no espaço

steps: Expelir gases para trás a alta velocidade

cards.text: Os foguetões não precisam de ar onde se apoiar: empurram os gases de escape para trás e ganham igual momento para a frente. É por isso que funcionam ainda melhor no vácuo do espaço.

deep.x: A rocket carries both fuel and oxidiser. Burning them makes hot gas that shoots out of the nozzle at several kilometres per second. By conservation of momentum, the rocket gains equal momentum in the opposite direction. No air is needed.
Even better in a vacuum

In the lower atmosphere, air pressure pushes back on the exhaust and air resistance drags on the rocket. In space neither happens, so the same engine produces more thrust, and every bit of it goes into speed.
Mostly fuel

items.l: of a launch rocket is fuel

deep.x: A rocket must carry fuel to accelerate fuel it will burn later. The Russian teacher Konstantin Tsiolkovsky worked out the rocket equation in 1903: final speed depends on exhaust speed and on how much of the starting mass is fuel. That's why rockets are built in stages, dropping empty tanks along the way.
Gentle but efficient
Ion engines push out charged atoms at around 30 km/s. Their thrust is tiny, about the weight of a sheet of paper, but they run for months. ESA's SMART-1 probe used one to reach the Moon in 2004.

deep.w: Rockets push against the air
deep.r: They push against their own exhaust; in 1920 a newspaper mocked this idea and only corrected itself in 1969

deep.x: A rocket moves forward by throwing mass backward, so it needs nothing to push against.

quiz.q: Uma bola de 0,5 kg a 10 m/s tem um momento linear de…
Porque é que os patinadores giram mais depressa quando encolhem os braços?
options: O momento angular conserva-se à medida que o corpo fica mais compacto
quiz.explain: Raio menor, rotação mais rápida.

quiz.q: Para que servem as zonas de deformação?
options: Aumentar o tempo do choque para reduzir as forças
quiz.explain: A mesma variação de momento, menos força.

lessons.title: Gases e pressão
lessons.summary: Porque é que os pneus, os balões e o tempo se comportam como se comportam.

cards.title: Moléculas em movimento
cards.text: Um gás são milhares de milhões de moléculas a voar a centenas de metros por segundo, a chocar umas com as outras e com as paredes. Os seus impactos nas paredes são a pressão.

deep.x: The idea that a gas is a swarm of tiny, fast-moving particles is called the **kinetic theory of gases**. It explains pressure, temperature and much more with one simple picture.

items.l: molecules in a litre of air

deep.x: Faster than a jet airliner

At room temperature an average nitrogen molecule moves at about 500 m/s, faster than a cruising passenger jet. But it never gets far: in air at sea level it hits another molecule after travelling only about 70 nanometres, billions of times a second.
Pressure is countless tiny impacts
Each molecule bouncing off a wall gives it a minute push. Billions upon billions of pushes every second add up to a steady force. Pressure is that force per square metre, measured in pascals (Pa).
pressure = force ÷ area

x: Sea-level pressure ≈ 101,000 Pa = 101,000 N per m²
Like 10 tonnes resting on every square metre

deep.x: Why we aren't crushed

Air pushes equally in every direction, including from inside your body, lungs and ears. Forces balance, so we don't notice. Remove the air from one side, as in a vacuum-packed bag, and its force becomes obvious.
The jittery dance of pollen grains in water, seen by Robert Brown in 1827, was explained by Einstein in 1905 as molecules bombarding them; this helped convince scientists that atoms are real.
Gas pressure is the combined push of countless fast molecules hitting a surface.

cards.title: Temperatura e pressão
cards.text: Aquece um gás fechado e as moléculas movem-se mais depressa, batendo nas paredes com mais força e mais vezes, por isso a pressão sobe. É por isso que a pressão dos pneus sobe depois de uma longa viagem.

deep.x: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules. Warm a gas in a rigid container and its molecules hit the walls faster and more often, so pressure rises in proportion to the absolute temperature.
pressure ÷ absolute temperature = constant (fixed volume)
Kelvin, the absolute scale

The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, −273.15 °C, where molecular motion is at its minimum. Gas law calculations must use kelvin: 20 °C is about 293 K. Using Celsius gives nonsense, because 0 °C isn't "no heat".
Tyres after a long drive

x: Tyre at 2.2 bar on the gauge, 15 °C
Absolute pressure 3.2 bar × (313 K ÷ 288 K) ≈ 3.48 bar
Warm tyre at 40 °C reads about 2.5 bar

deep.x: This is why manufacturers tell you to check pressures with cold tyres. Letting air out of hot tyres leaves them under-inflated once they cool.

items: Footballs go soft in the cold

deep.w: Absolute zero is like a very cold freezer
deep.r: It's −273.15 °C, a limit that can be approached but never quite reached

deep.x: Heat a sealed gas and its pressure rises in step with the absolute temperature.

cards.title: Lei de Boyle
cards.text: A temperatura constante, comprimir um gás para metade do volume duplica a sua pressão. As bombas de bicicleta e as seringas mostram-no.

deep.x: In 1662 Robert Boyle, working with his assistant Robert Hooke, showed that if you squeeze a fixed amount of gas at constant temperature, its pressure rises in exact proportion. Half the volume, double the pressure.
pressure × volume = constant (fixed temperature)
Why it works
Squeeze the same molecules into half the space and each square centimetre of wall gets hit twice as often. Their speed hasn't changed, because the temperature hasn't.
Diving
Water adds about 1 bar of pressure for every 10 m of depth. A breath of air shrinks as a diver descends and expands as they rise.

v.unit: volume of 1 litre of surface air, L

deep.x: Scuba divers breathing compressed air must never hold their breath while surfacing: the air in their lungs would expand and could cause serious injury. The rule taught in every diving course is to breathe normally and ascend slowly.
Everyday Boyle

x: Ears pop on a plane or in a fast lift as air pressure changes
A sealed bag of crisps puffs up on a flight or a mountain road
A bicycle pump squeezes air until its pressure exceeds the tyre's and the valve opens
Syringe holds 20 ml of air at 1 bar
Push plunger (outlet blocked) to 10 ml
Pressure rises to 2 bar

deep.x: Halve the space a gas has and its pressure doubles, as long as the temperature stays the same.

cards.title: A lei dos gases ideais
cards.text: A pressão, o volume e a temperatura estão ligados numa só equação para a maioria dos gases em condições do dia a dia.

deep.x: Three separate discoveries, Boyle's law (1662), Charles's law (1787, volume and temperature) and Gay-Lussac's law (1802, pressure and temperature), combine into one equation. Avogadro's idea, that equal volumes of gas hold equal numbers of molecules, completes it.
pV = nRT
What's a mole?

A mole is a fixed count of particles, about 6 × 10²³. One mole of air molecules has a mass of about 29 g. The ideal gas law says one mole of any gas takes up about 24 litres at room temperature and normal pressure, whether it's hydrogen or carbon dioxide.

x: V ≈ 0.024 m³ = 24 litres

deep.x: Why "ideal"?

The law assumes molecules are points that don't attract each other. That's an excellent approximation for air in everyday conditions. It breaks down at very high pressures or near the temperature where a gas turns liquid, when molecules are close and start to stick.
Who uses it
Engineers size gas cylinders and car airbags with it; meteorologists use it in weather models; chemists use it to count molecules by measuring volume.
A typical car airbag fills with around 60 litres of gas in about 30 milliseconds, produced by a rapid chemical reaction.
Pressure, volume, temperature and amount of gas are tied together by one simple equation.

cards.title: Pressão do ar e altitude

viz.unit: % da pressão ao nível do mar

cards.text: A pressão do ar cai para metade mais ou menos a cada 5,5 km de altitude. No alto da Serra da Estrela (1993 m) é cerca de 80% da do nível do mar; no Evereste, cerca de um terço.

deep.x: Air pressure is the weight of all the air above you pressing down. Climb higher and there's less air above you, so pressure falls. Air is compressible, so the lower layers are squeezed denser and pressure drops fastest near the ground.
Pascal's mountain

In 1648 Blaise Pascal asked his brother-in-law to carry a mercury barometer up the Puy de Dôme in France. The mercury column was several centimetres shorter at the top, proving that air has weight and thins with height.
Breathing up high

The air at altitude is still about 21% oxygen, but each breath holds fewer molecules. On Everest each breath brings in only about a third as much oxygen as at sea level, which is why most climbers there use bottled oxygen.
Planes
Airliners cruise at about 11 km, where pressure is under a quarter of sea level. Cabins are pressurised to the equivalent of roughly 1,800–2,400 m, a bit higher than the top of Serra da Estrela.

x: Pressure halves every ≈ 5.5 km

deep.w: Mountain air has less oxygen in it
deep.r: It has the same 21% oxygen; there's simply less air in each breath

deep.x: Air pressure is the weight of the air above you, so it falls as you climb.

cards.title: Ebulição e altitude
cards.text: A água ferve quando a sua pressão de vapor iguala a pressão do ar. No alto de uma montanha a pressão do ar é mais baixa, por isso a água ferve abaixo dos 100 °C e a massa demora mais a cozer. As panelas de pressão fazem o contrário.

deep.x: A liquid boils when bubbles of vapour can form inside it. That needs the liquid's vapour pressure to equal the pressure of the air above. Lower the air pressure and the water reaches that point at a lower temperature.
Cooking up a mountain

Cooking depends on temperature, not on bubbles. At about 93 °C on the top of Serra da Estrela, pasta and eggs take noticeably longer. On Everest, water boiling at about 71 °C barely cooks food at all.
The pressure cooker
A sealed pressure cooker lets steam build up to about 1 bar above atmospheric pressure. Water then boils at about 120 °C, so beans, stews and chickpeas cook in perhaps a third of the usual time.
History
The French physicist Denis Papin invented the "steam digester", the ancestor of the pressure cooker, in 1679. Its safety valve inspired later steam engines.

deep.w: Turning up the heat makes boiling water hotter
deep.r: Open-pan boiling water stays at its boiling point; more heat just boils it away faster

deep.x: Water boils when its vapour pressure matches the surrounding pressure, so lower pressure means a lower boiling point.
In a vacuum chamber, a glass of room-temperature water will boil, and cool itself until it freezes.

cards.title: Balões e densidade
cards.text: O ar quente é menos denso do que o ar frio, por isso um balão de ar quente sobe. O hélio é mais leve do que o ar, por isso os balões de hélio flutuam. Um submarino muda a sua densidade com tanques de lastro.

deep.x: Any object in a fluid feels an upward push, or **upthrust**, equal to the weight of the fluid it pushes aside. This is Archimedes' principle. If the upthrust beats the object's weight, it rises.
Hot-air balloons
Heating air makes it expand, so a cubic metre of it weighs less. The difference from the surrounding air gives the lift. That's why balloons fly best on cold, calm mornings.

x: Each m³ of 100 °C air is ≈ 0.25 kg lighter than 20 °C air
Balloon of 2,800 m³
Lift ≈ 700 kg for basket, burner, envelope and people

deep.x: A Portuguese first

In 1709 the Portuguese-Brazilian priest Bartolomeu de Gusmão demonstrated a small hot-air balloon to King João V in Lisbon, more than 70 years before the Montgolfier brothers' famous crewed flight in Paris in 1783.
Floating in water

x: A submarine floods ballast tanks to sink and blows them out with compressed air to rise
Fish adjust gas in a swim bladder
Ships float because their hulls displace a large volume of water

deep.w: Helium balloons are pulled up
deep.r: They're pushed up by the heavier air around them

deep.x: Things rise when they're less dense than the fluid around them.

cards.title: Sugar não é puxar

steps: O ar empurra a superfície da bebida

cards.text: Uma palhinha não "puxa" a bebida para cima. Tu baixas a pressão na boca e a atmosfera empurra o líquido pela palhinha acima. É por isso que uma palhinha não consegue elevar água mais de cerca de 10 m.

deep.x: Gases can only push; there's no such thing as a pulling force from a vacuum. "Suction" always means lowering the pressure on one side so that the higher pressure on the other side pushes.
The 10-metre limit
Even a perfect vacuum at the top of a straw can only let the atmosphere push water up until the water column's weight matches air pressure. That happens at about 10.3 m.

x: Atmospheric pressure ≈ 101,000 Pa
≈ 10.3 m of water

deep.x: How it was discovered

In the 1600s, Italian well-diggers found their suction pumps couldn't lift water more than about 10 m. Evangelista Torricelli realised why and in 1643 replaced water with mercury, which is 13.6 times denser. The mercury stood about 76 cm high: the first barometer.
Magdeburg's hemispheres
In 1654 Otto von Guericke pumped the air out of two joined copper hemispheres. Teams of horses pulling in opposite directions couldn't separate them. Let the air back in, and they fell apart.

deep.w: Vacuum cleaners suck up dirt
deep.r: A fan lowers the pressure inside, and outside air rushes in, carrying dust

deep.x: Suction is really the atmosphere pushing into a region of lower pressure.

cards.title: Ar comprimido
cards.text: Comprimir o ar aquece-o (o cilindro da bomba da bicicleta fica quente); deixá-lo expandir arrefece-o (as latas de spray ficam frias). Os frigoríficos e as bombas de calor aproveitam isto com fluidos refrigerantes especiais.

deep.x: Pushing a piston into a gas does work on the molecules: each one bounces off the advancing piston faster than it arrived, so the gas heats up. When a gas expands and pushes something outwards, its molecules lose speed and it cools.
Diesel engines
Rudolf Diesel patented his engine in the 1890s. It squeezes air to roughly a fifteenth or twentieth of its volume, heating it to over 500 °C. Fuel sprayed in then ignites without any spark.
Weather
Rising air expands and cools by roughly 10 °C per kilometre until it becomes saturated. That cooling turns water vapour into the droplets of clouds.
Fridges and heat pumps

A refrigerant is compressed (getting hot) and gives its heat away through coils behind the fridge. It then passes through a valve, expands and turns cold, picking up heat from inside the fridge. The cycle repeats.
A CO₂ fire extinguisher's horn can frost over when used, because the escaping gas expands and cools dramatically.
Squeezing a gas warms it and letting it expand cools it, and that's the heart of every fridge.

cards.title: Tempo e pressão
cards.text: As zonas de alta pressão trazem ar descendente e normalmente tempo estável; as de baixa pressão trazem ar ascendente, nuvens e chuva. Os barómetros medem-na, muitas vezes em hectopascais (hPa).

deep.x: Average sea-level pressure is about 1013 hPa. Weather maps show lines of equal pressure called **isobars**. Regions of higher and lower pressure drive the winds and shape the weather.
Why the wind spirals

Air flows from high pressure towards low, but Earth's rotation deflects it. In the northern hemisphere winds circle clockwise around highs and anticlockwise around lows. Closely packed isobars mean strong winds.
Portugal's weather maker

The **Azores High** is a semi-permanent high-pressure area over the Atlantic. In summer it usually extends towards Iberia, blocking rain and bringing Portugal's dry, sunny months. In winter it often retreats south, letting Atlantic low-pressure systems bring rain.
Reading a barometer

x: A slow rise: improving, settled weather
A steady reading: little change
A fast fall, several hPa in three hours: wind and rain on the way
1 hPa = 100 Pa = 1 millibar
Sea-level pressure ≈ 1013 hPa
Strong storm centre ≈ 960 hPa or lower

deep.x: Since 2017 Portugal's weather service, IPMA, names major storms together with the Spanish and French services.
High pressure brings settled weather; low pressure brings rising air, cloud and rain.

quiz.q: Porque é que a água ferve abaixo dos 100 °C numa montanha?
options: Com menos pressão atmosférica, ferve a uma temperatura mais baixa
quiz.explain: A ebulição depende da pressão à volta.

quiz.q: Reduz para metade o volume de um gás a temperatura constante e a sua pressão…
quiz.explain: Lei de Boyle: p × V constante.

quiz.q: O que empurra a bebida pela palhinha acima?
options: A pressão atmosférica sobre a superfície da bebida
quiz.explain: Tu baixas a pressão, o ar empurra.

lessons.title: Luz e ótica
lessons.summary: Reflexão, refração, lentes e o olho.

cards.title: A luz viaja depressa e em linha reta
cards.text: A luz viaja a cerca de 300 000 km/s no vácuo e em linha reta (raios). Demora cerca de 8 minutos e 20 segundos a chegar até nós desde o Sol.

deep.x: The speed of light in a vacuum is exactly 299,792,458 m/s. It's exact because since 1983 the metre has been defined by it: a metre is the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
Measuring it

In 1676 the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer noticed that eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io came early when Earth was near Jupiter and late when far away. He realised light takes time to cross the extra distance. In 1849 Hippolyte Fizeau measured it on Earth using a spinning toothed wheel and a mirror 8 km away.
Straight lines make shadows

Because light travels in straight lines in a uniform material, opaque objects cast shadows with clear edges. Solar and lunar eclipses are shadows on a cosmic scale. A pinhole camera works the same way: rays from the top of a scene pass through the hole to the bottom of the screen, giving an upside-down image.
Slower in materials
Light slows down inside transparent materials: about 225,000 km/s in water and about 200,000 km/s in glass. This slowing is what makes lenses work.

x: Sun to Earth ≈ 150,000,000 km

deep.x: When you look at a star, you see light that left it years or even thousands of years ago; you see the past.
Light is the fastest thing there is, and it travels in straight lines unless something bends it.

cards.title: Reflexão
cards.text: A luz ressalta num espelho com o mesmo ângulo com que lhe bate: o ângulo de incidência é igual ao ângulo de reflexão. As superfícies rugosas espalham a luz em todas as direções, e é por isso que o papel não é um espelho.

deep.x: The law of reflection is simple: the angle at which light hits a surface equals the angle at which it leaves, both measured from a line at right angles to the surface (the "normal").
angle of incidence = angle of reflection
Why paper isn't a mirror

Every tiny bit of a surface obeys the same law. On paper, the fibres point every which way, so rays scatter in all directions. That diffuse reflection is actually what lets us see most objects from any angle.
Mirror images

A flat mirror's image appears as far behind the glass as you are in front. It looks left-right reversed, though strictly it's front-to-back reversed. To see your whole body, the mirror only needs to be half your height, wherever you stand.
Bouncing light back

x: Road cat's eyes and bike reflectors return light straight to its source
Apollo astronauts left reflectors on the Moon; observatories still bounce lasers off them to measure the Moon's distance to within millimetres
Fresh snow reflects so much sunlight that skiers need sunglasses

deep.w: A mirror swaps left and right
deep.r: It swaps front and back; your raised right hand stays on the right side of the image

deep.x: Light bounces off a surface at the same angle it arrives.

cards.title: Refração

steps: A luz entra na água inclinada

cards.text: A luz abranda na água ou no vidro e desvia-se quando entra com um ângulo. É por isso que uma palhinha parece torta num copo e as piscinas parecem menos fundas do que são.

deep.x: When light passes at an angle from one material to another where it travels at a different speed, it changes direction. Entering a slower material, it bends towards the normal; leaving into a faster one, it bends away.
refractive index n = speed in vacuum ÷ speed in material
The marching analogy
Imagine soldiers marching diagonally from tarmac onto sand. The first to reach the sand slow down first, so the whole row swings round. Light waves behave the same way at a boundary.
Pools look shallow
Light from the bottom of a pool bends away from the normal as it leaves the water. Your brain assumes light travels straight, so it traces the rays back to a point higher than the real bottom.

x: Pool 2 m deep, seen from straight above
Apparent depth ≈ real depth ÷ 1.33
Looks about 1.5 m deep

items: Straws look bent in a glass
Sun visible just after it sets

deep.x: Atmospheric refraction

Air bends light a little too. Near the horizon it lifts the setting Sun's image by about its own width, so you see the Sun for a couple of minutes after it has geometrically set. Hot air over a road bends skylight upwards, creating the "wet road" mirage.

deep.w: Light bends because it hits the surface
deep.r: It bends because it changes speed; light hitting straight on slows but doesn't bend

deep.x: Light bends when it changes speed crossing from one material into another.

cards.title: Reflexão interna total

steps: Bate na parede num ângulo rasante

cards.text: Dentro do vidro, a luz que bate na superfície com um ângulo suficientemente rasante é totalmente refletida. As fibras óticas prendem a luz desta forma e levam dados da internet através dos oceanos.

deep.x: When light travels from a slow material like glass into a faster one like air, it bends away from the normal. Make the angle shallower and shallower, and at the **critical angle** the light skims along the surface. Beyond that, none escapes: all of it reflects back inside.
Optical fibres

An optical fibre is a glass strand thinner than a hair, with a core surrounded by cladding of slightly lower refractive index. Light zigzags along the core, reflecting completely at every bounce, even round gentle bends.
The internet runs on light

Undersea fibre cables carry the vast majority of data between continents. Portugal is an important landing point: the EllaLink cable, opened in 2021, links Sines directly to Brazil. Signals are boosted by amplifiers every 50–100 km or so.
Other uses

x: Endoscopes let doctors see inside the body through a flexible tube
Diamonds sparkle because their small critical angle traps and bounces light inside before it escapes
Binoculars use prisms that reflect light totally, better than mirrors

deep.x: Charles Kao shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics for showing in the 1960s that ultra-pure glass could carry light over long distances.
Light hitting a surface beyond the critical angle can't escape, so glass fibres can trap it for thousands of kilometres.

cards.title: Lentes
cards.text: As lentes convexas desviam a luz para dentro, até um foco: lupas, câmaras, o olho. As lentes côncavas espalham-na, e usam-se para corrigir a miopia.

deep.x: A lens uses refraction at two curved surfaces to bend rays in a controlled way. Its strength is described by its focal length: the distance from the lens to the point where parallel rays meet.
Dioptres
Opticians measure lens power in dioptres: one divided by the focal length in metres. Positive numbers are converging lenses, negative are diverging.
power (dioptres) = 1 ÷ focal length (m)

x: Reading glasses of +2.5 dioptres
Focal length = 1 ÷ 2.5
= 0.4 m, or 40 cm

deep.x: Real and virtual images
A short history

Eyeglasses for reading appeared in Italy around 1286. Spectacle makers in the Netherlands built the first telescopes around 1608, and Galileo turned one to the sky in 1609, discovering Jupiter's moons. Microscopes followed soon after, revealing cells and bacteria.

deep.w: A magnifying glass makes things bigger
deep.r: It makes rays enter your eye as if from a larger, virtual object

deep.x: Convex lenses bring light together to a focus; concave lenses spread it apart.

cards.title: O olho
cards.text: A córnea e o cristalino focam a luz na retina, onde os bastonetes (luz fraca, sem cor) e os cones (cor) a transformam em sinais nervosos. O cérebro endireita a imagem invertida.

deep.x: The eye is a living camera. About two-thirds of its focusing is done by the curved, clear **cornea** at the front. The **lens** behind it fine-tunes focus by changing shape, pulled by tiny muscles.
The retina

The cones are packed into a small central spot, the fovea, which gives sharp, coloured vision where you look directly. Where the optic nerve leaves the eye there are no receptors at all: a blind spot that your brain fills in.
The image is upside down

Like a camera, the eye projects an inverted image on the retina. Your brain interprets it so the world appears the right way up. Experiments with image-flipping goggles show people can adapt to an upside-down view within days.
Adapting to light

x: The pupil changes from about 2 mm in sunshine to about 8 mm in the dark
Full dark adaptation, as rods become more sensitive, takes 20–30 minutes
That's why astronomers use dim red torches: red light barely disturbs the rods

deep.x: Underwater, everything looks blurry because the cornea loses most of its focusing power when water, not air, touches it; goggles restore an air gap.

deep.w: Carrots give you night vision
deep.r: Vitamin A is needed for healthy eyes, but extra carrots won't improve normal vision

deep.x: The cornea and lens focus an upside-down image on the retina, and the brain does the rest.

cards.title: Miopia e hipermetropia

items.b: óculos de leitura com a idade

cards.text: Os olhos míopes focam os objetos distantes à frente da retina; as lentes côncavas resolvem isso. Os olhos hipermetropes focam atrás dela; as lentes convexas resolvem isso.

deep.x: For sharp vision, light must focus exactly on the retina. Often the eyeball is a little too long or too short, or the cornea too curved or too flat, and the focus lands in the wrong place.
Reading a prescription

Glasses prescriptions are in dioptres. A minus number, such as −2.00, means myopia; a plus number means long sight. A separate "cylinder" value corrects **astigmatism**, where the cornea is curved more in one direction than another.
A growing epidemic

Myopia is becoming far more common. Roughly a third of the world's people are short-sighted, and some projections suggest half will be by 2050. In some East Asian cities over 80% of young adults are myopic.
Strong evidence shows that children who spend more time outdoors are less likely to become short-sighted, probably because of bright daylight and looking at distant things.
After 40

In middle age the eye's lens stiffens and can't change shape enough to focus up close. This is **presbyopia**, and it's why most people need reading glasses in their forties, even with otherwise perfect eyesight.
Short-sighted eyes focus too early and need diverging lenses; long-sighted eyes focus too late and need converging ones.

cards.title: Câmaras
cards.text: Uma câmara funciona como um olho: uma lente foca a luz num sensor com milhões de píxeis. A abertura controla quanta luz entra; a velocidade do obturador controla durante quanto tempo.

deep.x: Like the eye, a camera uses a lens to form an image on a light-sensitive surface. Instead of rods and cones, a digital sensor has millions of tiny light detectors called pixels, each recording how much light falls on it.

items.b: hole size: light, depth of field

deep.x: f-numbers
Aperture is given as an f-number: the focal length divided by the hole's diameter. Smaller numbers mean wider holes. Each standard "stop" (f/2.8, f/4, f/5.6, f/8) halves the light.

x: 50 mm lens at f/2
Aperture diameter = 50 ÷ 2 = 25 mm
At f/4 it's 12.5 mm, letting in a quarter of the light

deep.x: Freezing motion
A shutter speed of 1/1000 s freezes a running dog. Half a second lets moving water blur into silk. Too long a handheld exposure and the whole picture blurs from camera shake.
Phone cameras

Phone sensors are small, so each pixel gathers little light. Phones make up for it with computing: they capture several frames in a burst and merge them, reducing noise and balancing bright and dark areas.
The first surviving photograph, taken by Nicéphore Niépce in France around 1826–27, needed an exposure of many hours, possibly days.
A camera balances aperture, shutter speed and sensitivity to collect just the right amount of light.

cards.title: Arco-íris

steps: A luz do sol entra numa gota

cards.text: A luz do sol que entra nas gotas de chuva é refratada, refletida no interior e novamente refratada à saída. Cada cor desvia-se de forma ligeiramente diferente, espalhando a luz branca num espetro.

deep.x: Each raindrop acts like a tiny prism with a mirror at the back. Sunlight refracts as it enters, reflects off the back of the drop, and refracts again leaving. Violet bends a little more than red, so the colours fan out.
Where to look

The rainbow is a circle centred on the point directly opposite the Sun, the shadow of your head. Red light comes out at about 42° from that point, violet at about 40°. So you need the Sun behind you and fairly low, which is why rainbows appear mostly in the morning and late afternoon.
Your own private rainbow

Each person sees light from a different set of drops, so no two people see exactly the same rainbow. You can never reach the end of one; it moves as you move. From a plane, you can sometimes see the full circle.
Who explained it
René Descartes worked out the 42° angle in 1637 by tracing rays through a glass globe of water. Newton later explained the colours, showing that white light is a mix that refraction separates.

deep.w: A rainbow has seven distinct colours
deep.r: The spectrum is continuous; Newton chose seven names, partly to match the seven notes of a musical scale

deep.x: Raindrops refract, reflect and refract sunlight, sending each colour back at a slightly different angle.
The sky between a primary and secondary rainbow is noticeably darker; it's called Alexander's dark band.

cards.title: Lasers
cards.text: Um laser produz luz de uma só cor, em fase e num feixe estreito. Usa-se em leitores de códigos de barras, fibra ótica, cirurgia, corte de metal e medição de distâncias (lidar).

deep.x: "Laser" stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. Einstein described stimulated emission in 1917: a photon passing an excited atom can trigger it to release an identical photon. Theodore Maiman built the first working laser, using a ruby crystal, in 1960.
What makes laser light special
Laser light in your life

x: Barcode scanners at the supermarket
Fibre-optic internet and many printers
Eye surgery that reshapes the cornea
Lidar, measuring distance by timing reflected pulses, used in surveying and self-driving cars
CD (infrared), DVD (red) and Blu-ray (blue-violet) players

deep.x: Measuring with light

x: Lidar pulse returns after 200 ns

deep.x: Even a laser beam spreads a little. Shone at the Moon, a tight beam has widened to a few kilometres by the time it arrives, yet observatories still detect the few photons that return from Apollo reflectors.

deep.w: Lasers are dangerous because they're very powerful
deep.r: Many are weak, but the concentrated beam can damage eyes; never point one at people or aircraft

deep.x: A laser makes light of one colour with all its waves in step, packed into a narrow beam.

quiz.q: Porque é que uma palhinha parece torta dentro de água?
options: A luz refrata-se ao passar entre a água e o ar
quiz.explain: A luz muda de velocidade e de direção.

quiz.q: O que transporta dados da internet através dos oceanos usando luz?
options: Fibras óticas, por reflexão interna total
quiz.explain: A luz fica presa no vidro.

quiz.q: A miopia corrige-se com…
quiz.explain: As lentes côncavas espalham a luz para que foque mais atrás.

lessons.title: Cor
lessons.summary: Porque é que o céu é azul e as folhas são verdes.

cards.title: A luz branca é uma mistura
cards.text: Newton mostrou com um prisma que a luz branca contém todas as cores. Cada cor é luz com um comprimento de onda diferente, do vermelho (cerca de 700 nm) ao violeta (cerca de 400 nm).

deep.x: In 1666, the young Isaac Newton darkened his room, let a thin beam of sunlight through a hole in the shutter and passed it through a glass prism. A band of colours appeared on the far wall. Many people thought the glass was somehow adding the colour. Newton's key step was to pass one colour through a second prism: it stayed the same colour. Then he recombined the whole band and got white again.
Why a prism splits light

Light slows down in glass, and the slowdown bends it, an effect called **refraction**. Short wavelengths such as violet slow slightly more than long ones such as red, so they bend more. The colours fan out by wavelength. Raindrops do the same thing, which is how rainbows form, each at about 42° from the point opposite the Sun.
How small are these waves?
A nanometre (nm) is a millionth of a millimetre. Visible light spans about 380 to 750 nm, so roughly 2,000 waves of green light would fit across one millimetre.
speed of light = frequency × wavelength

x: Green light, 530 nm
≈ 570 trillion waves per second

deep.x: Newton named seven colours, including indigo, partly to match the seven notes of a musical scale; most people today can't pick out indigo as a separate band.
White light isn't pure: it's a blend of every visible wavelength, and a prism simply sorts them.

cards.title: Os objetos absorvem e refletem
cards.text: Uma folha parece verde porque a clorofila absorve a luz vermelha e azul e reflete a verde. Uma camisola preta absorve a maior parte da luz (e aquece ao sol); uma branca reflete a maior parte.

deep.x: An object has no colour of its own in the dark. Its colour is the light it sends back to your eyes. Molecules in the surface absorb some wavelengths, turning their energy into heat, and reflect or scatter the rest.
Leaves and chlorophyll

**Chlorophyll** uses red and blue light to power photosynthesis, and reflects much of the green, which is less useful to it. In autumn, deciduous trees break down their chlorophyll and recycle its nutrients. The yellow and orange pigments that were there all along, called carotenoids, show through.
Black, white and heat
This is why houses in the Alentejo and Algarve are traditionally whitewashed: a white wall can reflect over 80% of sunlight, keeping the rooms inside cooler.
Colour depends on the light

x: A red car under the yellow light of an old sodium street lamp looks dark brown or grey: there is little red light to reflect
A strawberry lit only with blue light looks almost black
Clothes that match in a shop can clash in daylight, because each light source contains a different mix of wavelengths

deep.w: An object "is" red
deep.r: It reflects red light; change the lighting and its colour changes too

deep.x: The colour you see is the light an object doesn't absorb.

cards.title: Misturar luz vs misturar tinta
cards.text: A luz mistura-se de forma aditiva: vermelho + verde + azul dão branco (ecrãs). A tinta mistura-se de forma subtrativa: cada pigmento absorve algumas cores, por isso misturar muitos dá uma cor escura e lamacenta (as impressoras usam ciano, magenta, amarelo e preto).

deep.x: There are two completely different ways of mixing colour. Light sources **add** wavelengths together. Paints, inks and dyes **subtract** wavelengths, because each pigment absorbs part of the light that falls on it.
Additive mixing
Shine red, green and blue spotlights onto a white wall, overlapping:

x: Red + green = yellow
Green + blue = cyan
Blue + red = magenta
All three = white

deep.x: Subtractive mixing

Cyan ink absorbs red, magenta absorbs green and yellow absorbs blue. Overlap cyan and yellow and only green survives both, so you see green. Mix all three and almost nothing is reflected. In practice that gives a muddy dark brown, which is why printers add a separate black ink, the K in **CMYK**. Black ink is also cheaper and prints sharper text.

x: Cyan ink removes red
Yellow ink removes blue
Only green is left: cyan + yellow = green

deep.x: What about red, yellow and blue?

Painters have used red, yellow and blue as primaries for centuries, and they work reasonably well. But cyan, magenta and yellow can mix a wider range of colours, which is why modern printing uses them.
Brown doesn't appear in the rainbow: it's really dark orange, seen next to brighter colours.
Light adds colours towards white; pigments take colours away towards black.

cards.title: Porque é que o céu é azul

steps: A luz do sol entra na atmosfera
O azul vem de todo o céu

cards.text: As moléculas do ar dispersam os comprimentos de onda curtos, azuis, muito mais do que os vermelhos (dispersão de Rayleigh). A luz azul dispersa chega aos teus olhos vinda de todas as direções do céu.

deep.x: Sunlight passing through the atmosphere hits nitrogen and oxygen molecules, which are far smaller than the wavelength of light. They make the light's electric field jiggle their electrons, which then re-radiate light in all directions. This is **Rayleigh scattering**, named after Lord Rayleigh, who worked out the maths in 1871.
Strongly favouring blue
Scattering by tiny particles depends on the fourth power of wavelength: halve the wavelength and the scattering rises 16 times.
scattering ∝ 1 ÷ wavelength⁴

x: Red 700 nm, blue 450 nm
Blue scattered about 6 times more

deep.x: Why not violet?

Violet is scattered even more, but sunlight contains less violet than blue, some is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are much less sensitive to it. The mix of scattered colours that reaches us looks sky blue.
Clouds and space

Water droplets in clouds are much bigger than the wavelength of light, so they scatter all colours equally and look white or grey. On the Moon there's no air to scatter light, so the sky is black even in daylight.
On Mars the daytime sky is butterscotch-coloured because of fine dust, while sunsets there look bluish.
The sky is blue because air molecules scatter blue sunlight across the whole sky far more than red.

cards.title: Pores do sol vermelhos
cards.text: Ao pôr do sol, a luz atravessa muito mais atmosfera. A maior parte do azul é dispersa antes de chegar até ti, e ficam os vermelhos e os laranjas.

deep.x: When the Sun is overhead, its light crosses roughly 10 km of dense air. When it sits on the horizon, the light travels a slanting path through air equivalent to almost 40 times as much. Along that long path, blue and green are scattered out to the sides, lighting up skies elsewhere, and mainly red and orange get through.
Dust, smoke and volcanoes
Particles in the air can make sunsets more vivid or turn the Sun deep red in the middle of the day.

x: Saharan dust blown over Portugal and Spain can turn skies orange and leave dust on cars
Wildfire smoke can make the Sun look like a red disc you can almost look at (never stare at it)
After the 1883 Krakatoa eruption, brilliant red sunsets were seen around the world for months

deep.x: More sunset tricks

The air also bends sunlight, so you see the Sun for a couple of minutes after it has actually dropped below the horizon. The bending is stronger near the ground, which squashes the Sun into an oval. In very clear air, the last sliver can flash green for a second, the famous **green flash**, best seen over a sea horizon such as Portugal's west coast.

deep.w: Sunsets are red because the Sun cools in the evening
deep.r: The Sun doesn't change; its light just crosses far more air

deep.x: Sunsets are red because the blue has been scattered away along the long path through the air.

cards.title: Ver a cor
cards.text: O teu olho tem três tipos de cones, mais sensíveis a luz aproximadamente vermelha, verde e azul. Cada cor que vês é o teu cérebro a comparar os seus sinais.

deep.x: Your retina holds about 120 million **rods** and about 6 million **cones**. Rods are very sensitive but can't tell colours apart, which is why everything looks grey in moonlight. Cones work in brighter light and come in three types.
The brain compares

Each cone type responds to a wide band of wavelengths, overlapping a lot. A single cone can't tell colour; it only signals how much light it absorbs. Your brain compares the signals from the three types. Strong L and M signals with little from S feel like yellow, even though there is no "yellow cone".
Colours that aren't in the rainbow

Magenta stimulates L and S cones but not M. No single wavelength does that, so magenta isn't in the spectrum; your brain invents it. Brown, pink and grey are also mixtures your brain labels, not single wavelengths.

x: Most mammals, including dogs, have only two cone types
Many birds, reptiles and fish have four, including one for ultraviolet
Humans can tell apart roughly a million different shades

deep.w: The mantis shrimp sees far more colours than us
deep.r: It has 12 or more receptor types but, in tests, is worse than humans at telling similar colours apart

deep.x: Colour isn't in the light itself; it's your brain's comparison of three cone signals.

cards.title: Daltonismo
cards.text: Cerca de 8% dos homens e 0,5% das mulheres de ascendência norte-europeia têm alguma deficiência na visão das cores vermelho–verde, normalmente hereditária. Um bom design nunca depende só da cor.

deep.x: Most red–green colour vision deficiency is inherited. The genes for the M and L cone pigments sit on the X chromosome. Men have only one X, so one faulty copy is enough. Women have two, so they need faulty copies on both, which is much rarer.
The main types

x: Deuteranomaly: green-sensitive cones shifted towards red; the most common form, about 5% of men
Protan types: weak or missing red-sensitive cones; reds look darker
Tritan types: blue–yellow problems, very rare
Complete colour blindness, seeing only shades of grey, is extremely rare

deep.x: Daltonism

The chemist John Dalton described his own colour vision in 1794, after noticing that a flower looked different to him than to others. Colour blindness is still called **daltonismo** in Portuguese. Screening often uses the Ishihara test, plates of coloured dots hiding numbers, first published in 1917.
Designing for everyone

Good design adds labels, patterns, shapes or position, so meaning never depends on colour alone. Traffic lights use a fixed order. The Portuguese designer Miguel Neiva created **ColorADD**, a code of simple symbols for colours, now used on school materials, transport maps and products in Portugal and abroad.
In a typical school class of 30 with 15 boys, chances are at least one boy has a red–green deficiency.
About one man in twelve sees colours differently, so colour should never be the only clue.

cards.title: Infravermelho e ultravioleta
cards.text: Para lá do vermelho está o infravermelho, que sentimos como calor e que as câmaras noturnas veem. Para lá do violeta está o ultravioleta, que causa queimaduras solares e faz alguns materiais brilhar.

deep.x: Visible light is a narrow slice of the **electromagnetic spectrum**. Just beyond each end of the rainbow lie wavelengths our eyes can't detect, but many animals and instruments can.
Discovering them

In 1800 William Herschel placed thermometers in the colours of a spectrum. The temperature rose towards red, and was highest just beyond the red end, where there was no visible light: he had found **infrared**. A year later Johann Ritter found that something beyond violet darkened silver chloride: ultraviolet.
Infrared around you

x: Your body glows in infrared at about 10 µm; thermal cameras turn this into images
TV remotes flash infrared at about 940 nm; many phone cameras can see the flashes
Night-vision cameras light scenes with infrared lamps

deep.x: Ultraviolet

UV-A (315–400 nm) ages skin and passes through window glass. UV-B (280–315 nm) causes sunburn and drives skin cancer risk. UV-C is the most energetic but is blocked by the ozone layer. In Portugal the summer UV index often reaches 8–10, rated very high.
Glowing in UV

**Fluorescent** materials absorb UV and re-emit visible light. Tonic water glows blue because of its quinine, white shirts glow because of brighteners in washing powder, and euro banknotes show hidden glowing marks under UV lamps.
Bees see ultraviolet, and many flowers have UV "landing strip" patterns that are invisible to us.
Infrared and ultraviolet are just light our eyes can't see: one we feel as warmth, the other we feel as sunburn.

cards.title: Temperatura de cor
cards.text: As lâmpadas descrevem-se em kelvin: branco quente cerca de 2700 K (amarelado), luz do dia cerca de 5000–6500 K (azulado). A luz quente parece mais acolhedora à noite.

deep.x: Heat anything enough and it glows. A stove ring glows dull red, a filament yellow-white, and the hottest stars blue-white. The colour of this glow depends only on temperature. **Colour temperature** describes a light source by comparing it with an ideal glowing object, measured in kelvin (K). 0 K is absolute zero, −273 °C.
The "warm" paradox

Artists call red and orange "warm" and blue "cool". But in physics, bluer light comes from hotter sources. A "cool" daylight bulb at 6,500 K matches a hotter glowing body than a "warm" 2,700 K bulb. LED bulbs don't actually get that hot; they are designed to produce the same mix of colours.
Peak colour and temperature
Hotter objects emit most strongly at shorter wavelengths, a rule called **Wien's law**.
peak wavelength ≈ 2,900,000 nm·K ÷ temperature

x: Sun's surface ≈ 5,800 K
Peak ≈ 500 nm, blue-green

deep.x: In daily life

x: Cameras and phones adjust white balance so white paper looks white under any light
Evening light rich in blue can make it harder for some people to feel sleepy
Stars show it too: Betelgeuse is reddish at about 3,500 K, Rigel blue-white at about 12,000 K

deep.x: The Sun's light peaks in blue-green, yet it looks white because it contains a balanced mix of all visible colours.
In physics, hotter means bluer: "warm" light actually comes from cooler sources.

cards.title: Ecrãs
cards.text: Cada píxel de um ecrã tem subpíxeis vermelho, verde e azul. Variar o seu brilho cria milhões de cores. Aproxima uma lupa de um ecrã e consegues vê-los.

deep.x: Look closely at a screen with a magnifying glass, or a drop of water on a phone, and you'll see tiny red, green and blue elements. From normal viewing distance they're too small to see apart, so your eye blends them and you see one mixed colour.
How many colours?
Most screens control each sub-pixel in 256 steps, from 0 to 255, called 8-bit colour.

x: = 16,777,216 combinations
About 16.7 million colours

deep.x: HDR screens often use 10 bits per channel: 1,024 steps each, over a billion colours.
LCD versus OLED

An LCD shines a backlight through liquid crystals that act as tiny shutters, and colour filters. Because the backlight never fully switches off, blacks look slightly grey. In an OLED screen each sub-pixel makes its own light, so black pixels are simply off, which also saves power with dark themes.

deep.w: A screen showing yellow emits yellow light
deep.r: It emits only red and green; your cones respond just as they would to yellow

deep.x: A screen fools your eyes: three tiny colours, mixed by your brain, make millions.

lessons.title: Som
lessons.summary: Volume, altura e como ouvimos.

cards.title: O que é o som
cards.text: O som é uma onda de pressão: um objeto a vibrar empurra e puxa o ar, criando compressões e rarefações que viajam até ao teu ouvido.

deep.x: When a guitar string or loudspeaker cone moves outwards, it pushes air molecules together, making a **compression**. When it moves back, it leaves a region of lower pressure, a **rarefaction**. These regions travel outwards as a wave. The air itself doesn't travel; each molecule just jiggles back and forth and passes the push on.
A longitudinal wave

In sound, air moves back and forth in the same direction as the wave travels, so it's called a **longitudinal** wave. Push a Slinky spring along its length and you'll see pulses of bunched-up coils travel along it in the same way. Waves on water or a shaken rope are transverse: they move up and down across the direction of travel.
Tiny pressure changes

Your ears are astonishingly sensitive. Ordinary conversation changes air pressure by only about 0.02 pascals, against atmospheric pressure of about 101,000 Pa. The quietest sound you can hear is a change of just 0.00002 Pa.

x: Speed of sound 343 m/s, note of 343 Hz
wavelength = 343 ÷ 343
= 1 metre between compressions

deep.x: wavelength = speed ÷ frequency
The quietest sound a young ear can detect moves the eardrum by less than the width of an atom.
Sound is a travelling pattern of squeezes and stretches in the air, not air flowing towards you.

cards.title: Altura e frequência
cards.text: A altura é o quão agudo ou grave é um som, e é definida pela frequência. Os humanos ouvem mais ou menos de 20 Hz a 20 000 Hz; o limite superior desce com a idade.

deep.x: **Frequency** is how many vibrations happen each second, measured in hertz (Hz). A high frequency sounds high-pitched; a low frequency sounds low. Doubling the frequency raises the pitch by exactly one octave, which is why notes an octave apart sound so alike.
Familiar frequencies

x: Orchestras tune to the A above middle C at 440 Hz, an international standard
Adult male speaking voices mostly vibrate around 85–180 Hz, female voices around 165–255 Hz
A piano spans about 27.5 Hz to 4,186 Hz, but its overtones go much higher

deep.x: Hearing range and age

Babies can hear up to about 20,000 Hz. The hair cells that detect the highest frequencies are the most easily worn out, so the top limit falls with age. Many adults over 50 can't hear above about 12,000–14,000 Hz. This is called **presbycusis**.
The Doppler effect
When an ambulance races towards you, the waves in front are squashed together and the siren sounds higher. As it passes and moves away, they stretch out and the pitch drops.
Some shops have used high-pitched "mosquito" alarms at around 17,000 Hz to discourage teenagers from loitering, because most adults can't hear them.
Pitch is frequency: double the vibrations per second and the note goes up an octave.

cards.title: Volume e decibéis
cards.text: O volume mede-se em decibéis, uma escala logarítmica: cada +10 dB é dez vezes a intensidade do som e parece mais ou menos duas vezes mais alto.

deep.x: The ear can handle an enormous range of sound intensities: the loudest bearable sound carries about a million million times more energy per second than the faintest you can hear. A linear scale would be useless, so we use **decibels** (dB), a logarithmic scale where 0 dB is the threshold of hearing.
Everyday levels
Working with decibels
Because the scale is logarithmic, decibels don't add up the normal way. Two identical sound sources together are only 3 dB louder than one, not twice the decibels.

x: Conversation 60 dB to busy street 90 dB
1,000 × the intensity, about 8 × as loud

deep.x: Weighted for human ears

Our ears are most sensitive around 2,000–5,000 Hz and much less to very low or very high sounds. Noise meters usually use an **A-weighting**, written dB(A), that mimics this, so a deep rumble counts for less than a shrill whine of the same energy.

x: The "bel" is named after Alexander Graham Bell; a decibel is a tenth of a bel
Sound above about 120–130 dB becomes painful

deep.w: 80 dB is twice as loud as 40 dB
deep.r: 80 dB has 10,000 times the intensity and sounds about 16 times as loud

deep.x: Every 10 dB means ten times the sound energy, so small numbers on the scale hide huge differences.

cards.title: Lesões auditivas
cards.text: A exposição prolongada acima de cerca de 85 dB pode danificar para sempre as minúsculas células ciliadas do ouvido interno. Concertos e ferramentas elétricas pedem tampões.

deep.x: Deep in the inner ear, each cochlea has about 15,000 **hair cells** topped with tiny bundles of stiff hairs. Loud sound bends them too far, damaging or killing them. In humans, they don't grow back, so the loss is permanent. It often starts at high frequencies, around 4,000 Hz.
Dose: level × time
Damage depends on both loudness and duration. A common rule is that 85 dB is safe for up to 8 hours a day, and every extra 3 dB, a doubling of energy, halves the safe time.

x: 85 dB: 8 hours
100 dB: only about 15 minutes

deep.x: Warning signs

x: Ringing or buzzing in the ears afterwards, called **tinnitus**
Sounds seeming muffled after a concert or nightclub
Having to raise your voice to talk to someone 1 m away means it's probably over 85 dB

deep.x: Protecting your ears

Foam earplugs cut about 20–30 dB. Musicians' earplugs reduce all frequencies evenly, so music still sounds natural. EU rules require employers to provide hearing protection when workplace noise exceeds 80 dB(A). With headphones, keep the volume below about 60% and take breaks; noise-cancelling headphones help you avoid turning it up.
The World Health Organization estimates that over a billion young people are at risk of hearing loss from unsafe listening habits.
Hearing loss from noise is gradual, painless and permanent, so protect your ears before it happens.

cards.title: Velocidade do som
cards.text: O som viaja a cerca de 343 m/s no ar, cerca de 1500 m/s na água e à volta de 5000 m/s no aço. O som precisa de um meio: no espaço, ninguém te ouve.

deep.x: Sound travels by molecules bumping into their neighbours, so its speed depends on the medium. In stiffer materials, where particles are tightly linked, the push passes on much faster. That's why sound travels faster in water and much faster in steel than in air.
Warmer air, faster sound

In air at 0 °C, sound travels at about 331 m/s. It goes about 0.6 m/s faster for every degree warmer, reaching 343 m/s at 20 °C. High up, where the air is cold, it's slower: about 295 m/s at airliner cruising height.
speed ≈ 331 + 0.6 × temperature (°C) m/s
Counting thunder
Light arrives almost instantly, but sound takes about 3 seconds to travel 1 km.

x: Flash, then thunder after 9 seconds
Lightning about 3 km away

deep.x: Breaking the sound barrier

An aircraft flying at the speed of sound is at **Mach 1**. Chuck Yeager first flew faster than sound in level flight in 1947. A supersonic aircraft drags a cone of compressed air behind it that sweeps the ground as a sonic boom.
No air, no sound
In space there are almost no molecules to carry vibrations, so explosions are silent. Astronauts talk by radio, which uses electromagnetic waves.

deep.w: Helium makes your vocal cords vibrate faster
deep.r: Your cords vibrate the same; sound moves faster in helium, shifting the throat's resonances and changing the tone

deep.x: Sound needs something to travel through, and the stiffer the medium, the faster it goes.

cards.title: Timbre
cards.text: Um violino e uma flauta a tocar a mesma nota soam diferentes porque cada um produz uma mistura diferente de harmónicos por cima da frequência principal.

deep.x: **Timbre**, pronounced "tam-ber", is the quality that lets you tell a violin from a flute, or a friend's voice from a stranger's, even on the same note at the same loudness. It comes mainly from the mix of **overtones**.
The harmonic series

A vibrating string doesn't just vibrate as a whole. It also vibrates in halves, thirds, quarters and so on, all at once. These make extra frequencies at whole-number multiples of the main one, called **harmonics**.

x: Fundamental 220 Hz
Harmonics at 2 ×, 3 ×, 4 ×
440, 660, 880 Hz all sounding together

deep.x: Every instrument's recipe
The 12 steel strings of the Portuguese guitar, played in pairs, give the bright, ringing sound so typical of fado.
More than overtones

x: The attack, how a note starts, matters a lot: a piano recording played backwards sounds more like an organ
Vibrato and noise, such as a flute's breathiness, add character
Your mouth shapes overtones into vowels: "ee" and "ah" on the same note differ only in timbre

deep.x: In 1822 the mathematician Joseph Fourier showed that any repeating wave can be built by adding simple sine waves. Sound software uses this idea to analyse and recreate timbre.
A tuning fork produces an almost pure tone with hardly any overtones, which is why it sounds plain.
Two instruments playing the same note differ in their overtone recipe, and that recipe is timbre.

cards.title: Acústica das salas
cards.text: As superfícies duras refletem o som e fazem as salas ecoar; os estofos, as cortinas e os painéis acústicos absorvem-no. As salas de concertos são concebidas para ter a reverberação certa.

deep.x: In a room, you hear sound directly from the source and then as many reflections from walls, floor and ceiling. Reflections that arrive within about 50 milliseconds blend in and make sound fuller. Later, stronger ones are heard as a separate **echo**. The gradual fading of all the reflections is called **reverberation**.
Reverberation time

Acousticians measure **reverberation time**: how long a sound takes to fade by 60 dB, to one millionth of its intensity. Around 1900, the American physicist Wallace Sabine found it depends on the room's volume and how much its surfaces absorb.
Matching the room to its use

x: Speech needs short reverberation, so words don't blur together
Orchestral music sounds best with about 2 seconds, which feels rich and enveloping
Gregorian chant was suited to long, slow cathedral echoes

deep.x: Concert halls

Many of the best halls, like Vienna's Musikverein, are long "shoebox" shapes, sending plenty of reflections from the sides. Porto's Casa da Música, opened in 2005, has a shoebox-shaped main hall with corrugated glass walls at each end, shaped to help the sound.
In an anechoic chamber, where foam wedges absorb almost all sound, the silence is so deep that visitors can hear their own heartbeat.
Good acoustics means the right amount of reverberation for the job: short for speech, longer for music.

cards.title: Ultrassons
cards.text: As frequências acima da audição humana usam-se em imagiologia médica, banhos de limpeza, sensores de distância, e pelos morcegos e golfinhos para se orientarem.

deep.x: **Ultrasound** is sound above about 20,000 Hz, too high for humans to hear. Its short wavelengths can reveal small details, and it reflects off boundaries between different materials, which makes it ideal for "seeing" with echoes.
Medical imaging

A medical scanner uses 2–18 million Hz. A probe made of **piezoelectric** crystals, which vibrate when a voltage is applied, sends pulses into the body and listens for echoes. A computer turns echo times into a picture. It uses no ionising radiation, so it's used routinely in pregnancy; Ian Donald in Glasgow pioneered this in the late 1950s.

x: Echo returns after 0.1 ms, sound in tissue ≈ 1,540 m/s
1,540 × 0.0001 = 0.154 m there and back
Organ boundary ≈ 7.7 cm deep

deep.x: distance = speed × time ÷ 2
Other uses

x: Car parking sensors at around 40 kHz
Cleaning baths, where bubbles form and collapse to scrub jewellery and tools
Sonar on ships, first developed during the First World War to detect submarines
Breaking up kidney stones and some cataract surgery

deep.x: Echolocation
Bats emit rapid high-pitched calls and listen to the echoes, building a detailed sound map. They can catch insects in total darkness. Dolphins use clicks in the same way to find fish buried in sand.

deep.w: Bats are blind
deep.r: All bats can see; many also use echolocation to hunt at night

deep.x: Ultrasound lets machines and animals see with echoes, timing how long sound takes to bounce back.

cards.title: Infrassons
cards.text: As frequências muito baixas, abaixo dos 20 Hz, percorrem distâncias enormes. Os elefantes comunicam com elas; vulcões, sismos e testes nucleares são detetados por estações de monitorização de infrassons.

deep.x: **Infrasound** is sound below about 20 Hz, too low for humans to hear as a tone, though very strong infrasound can be felt as pressure or vibration. Its long wavelengths, from about 17 metres to many kilometres, lose very little energy in air, so it can travel hundreds or thousands of kilometres.
Animal messages

x: Elephants make deep rumbles, some below 20 Hz, that other elephants can detect several kilometres away, partly through their feet
Blue and fin whales call at about 10–40 Hz, and their calls can cross ocean basins
Some birds may use infrasound from ocean waves to navigate

deep.x: Listening to the planet

The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty set up a global network of about 60 infrasound stations, one of them in the Azores, to detect secret nuclear explosions. The same stations hear volcanoes, meteors, storms and avalanches.
Global pressure waves
In January 2022 the Hunga Tonga undersea volcano exploded. Its pressure wave was recorded by barometers all over the world and circled the planet several times.
The 1883 Krakatoa eruption's pressure wave was detected by barometers worldwide as it circled Earth about seven times.
The lowest sounds travel the furthest, letting elephants, whales and scientists listen across great distances.

cards.title: Como ouvimos
cards.text: O tímpano vibra, três ossinhos amplificam o movimento e, na cóclea em forma de caracol, milhares de células ciliadas transformam vibrações de diferentes frequências em sinais nervosos.

deep.x: Hearing turns tiny pressure waves into nerve signals in three stages: the outer ear collects sound, the middle ear amplifies it, and the inner ear analyses it.
The middle ear

The eardrum passes vibrations to three tiny bones, the **malleus** (hammer), **incus** (anvil) and **stapes** (stirrup). The stapes, about 3 mm long, is the smallest bone in your body. Sound must pass from air into fluid in the inner ear, which would normally reflect most of it. The bones solve this.

x: Eardrum area ≈ 55 mm², oval window ≈ 3.2 mm²
Area ratio ≈ 17 ×
With lever action, pressure boosted about 20 ×

deep.x: The cochlea sorts frequencies

The cochlea is a fluid-filled tube about 35 mm long, coiled like a snail. Running along it is the **basilar membrane**. Near the entrance it is narrow and stiff and vibrates to high frequencies; at the far end it is wide and floppy and responds to low ones. Each spot has its own hair cells, so position tells your brain the pitch.
Where sound comes from

Your brain compares the two ears. A sound on your left reaches your left ear up to about 0.6 milliseconds earlier and slightly louder. The shape of your outer ear also colours sounds differently from above, below, front or back.

x: Georg von Békésy won the 1961 Nobel Prize for showing how the cochlea sorts frequencies
Cochlear implants bypass damaged hair cells by stimulating the nerve directly with electrodes

deep.x: Your ear canal, about 2.5 cm long, resonates around 3,000 Hz, which helps make you most sensitive to frequencies in human speech.
Your ear is a mechanical amplifier and frequency analyser, turning air vibrations into a map of pitch for the brain.

quiz.explain: Os decibéis são logarítmicos.

quiz.q: O som viaja mais depressa no…
quiz.explain: Materiais mais rígidos transmitem o som mais depressa.
