lessons.title: Átomos
lessons.summary: De que é feito tudo o que existe.

cards.title: Minúsculo e quase vazio
cards.text: Um átomo tem um núcleo minúsculo e denso de protões e neutrões, rodeado por uma nuvem de eletrões. Se o núcleo fosse um berlinde no centro de um estádio de futebol, os eletrões estariam nas bancadas exteriores.

deep.x: An atom is about a tenth of a billionth of a metre across (0.1 nanometres). Its nucleus is roughly 100,000 times smaller again. Yet the nucleus holds more than 99.9% of the atom's mass, so nearly all of the weight sits in a speck at the centre.
How we found out

In 1909 Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, working for Ernest Rutherford in Manchester, fired alpha particles at gold foil a few hundred atoms thick. Most went straight through. About 1 in 8,000 bounced back sharply. Rutherford said it was like firing a shell at tissue paper and having it come back. In 1911 he concluded that the positive charge and mass were packed into a tiny core.
Why things still feel solid

If atoms are mostly empty, why doesn't your hand pass through a table? The electrons of neighbouring atoms repel each other electrically, and quantum rules stop electrons crowding into the same state. What you feel as "touch" is that push, not hard balls meeting.

If you removed the empty space from every atom in every human on Earth, all eight billion of us would squeeze into something about the size of a sugar cube, though that cube would weigh hundreds of millions of tonnes.

deep.w: Electrons orbit the nucleus like tiny planets
deep.r: Electrons form fuzzy clouds of probability; the planet picture is a useful early model, not reality

deep.x: Matter is almost entirely empty space, held in shape by electric forces between electrons.

cards.title: Protões, neutrões, eletrões
cards.text: Os protões são positivos, os eletrões negativos e os neutrões neutros. Os protões e os neutrões pesam mais ou menos o mesmo; um eletrão pesa cerca de 1/1836 disso.

deep.x: Three particles build every ordinary atom. Their discovery took 35 years: J. J. Thomson found the electron in 1897, Rutherford identified the proton around 1919, and James Chadwick found the neutron in 1932.
Charge and mass

x: Proton: charge +1, mass about 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg
Neutron: no charge, about 0.1% heavier than a proton
Electron: charge −1, about 1/1,836 of a proton's mass

deep.x: An atom has as many electrons as protons, so the charges cancel and it is neutral overall. Lose or gain an electron and it becomes an **ion**, which is how salt dissolves in water and how nerves send signals.
What holds the nucleus together

Protons repel each other, and squeezed this close the push is enormous. The **strong nuclear force** wins at very short range, binding protons and neutrons together. Neutrons add "glue" without adding repulsion, which is why heavy nuclei need more neutrons than protons.
Protons and neutrons are not fundamental: each is made of three quarks. A proton is two "up" quarks and one "down"; a neutron is one up and two down.
An atom's identity comes from its protons, its mass from protons and neutrons, and its chemistry from its electrons.

cards.title: Elementos
cards.text: O número de protões decide o elemento: 1 é hidrogénio, 6 carbono, 8 oxigénio, 26 ferro, 79 ouro. Conhecem-se 118 elementos.

deep.x: An element is a substance made of atoms that all have the same number of protons, called the **atomic number**. Change the proton count and you change the element. That is why medieval alchemists could never turn lead (82 protons) into gold (79): chemistry only moves electrons around, and the nucleus stays untouched.
Natural and made

About 90 elements occur naturally on Earth. The rest have been made in laboratories and reactors, often only a few atoms at a time, and many last less than a second. The four newest names, nihonium, moscovium, tennessine and oganesson, were approved in 2016, completing the table's seventh row at element 118.
What your body is made of
Just six elements (oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, calcium, phosphorus) make up about 99% of you. Most of the oxygen and hydrogen are in water.

deep.w: Modern alchemy is impossible
deep.r: Physicists have turned other elements into gold in particle accelerators, but it costs vastly more than the gold is worth

deep.x: Element names honour places, people and myths. Polonium is named after Poland, curium after the Curies, and helium after the Greek word for the Sun, where it was spotted in 1868 before it was found on Earth.
The number of protons is an element's fingerprint: one more or one fewer and you have a different substance.

cards.title: Isótopos
cards.text: Átomos do mesmo elemento podem ter números diferentes de neutrões: são isótopos. O carbono-12 e o carbono-14 são ambos carbono; o carbono-14 é radioativo e usa-se para datar restos antigos.

deep.x: Isotopes are versions of an element with different numbers of neutrons. They behave almost identically in chemistry, because chemistry depends on electrons, but their masses differ and some have unstable nuclei. The word was coined in 1913 by Frederick Soddy, from Greek for "same place", since isotopes share one spot in the periodic table.
Hydrogen's three faces
Water made with deuterium is "heavy water", about 11% denser than normal water. An ice cube of heavy water sinks in ordinary water.
Carbon's isotopes

x: Carbon-12: about 98.9% of all carbon, stable
Carbon-13: about 1.1%, stable
Carbon-14: about one atom per trillion, radioactive

deep.x: Why isotopes matter

Medicine uses radioactive isotopes to see inside the body and treat cancer. Nuclear power depends on uranium-235, only 0.7% of natural uranium, which must be concentrated or "enriched". Climate scientists read the ratio of oxygen-18 to oxygen-16 in ice cores to work out temperatures hundreds of thousands of years ago.
Most elements have several stable isotopes. Tin has ten, more than any other element.
Isotopes are the same element with different weights; most are stable, some decay.

cards.title: A tabela periódica
cards.text: Em 1869, Mendeleev organizou os elementos por massa e propriedades, deixando espaços para elementos ainda por descobrir, e previu as suas propriedades. As colunas agrupam elementos que se comportam de forma semelhante.

deep.x: In 1869 the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev wrote the 63 known elements on cards and arranged them by atomic mass, grouping those that behaved alike. Where the pattern broke, he left gaps and boldly predicted that new elements would fill them.
Predictions that came true

He predicted germanium's density at about 5.5 g/cm³; the measured value turned out to be 5.35. Successes like this convinced chemists the table reflected something real. In 1913 Henry Moseley showed the true order is by atomic number, not mass, which fixed a few awkward swaps.
Reading the table

x: Rows (periods): each new row starts filling a new electron shell
Columns (groups): elements with the same number of outer electrons
Left side: reactive metals; right side: non-metals and noble gases

deep.x: The modern table has 18 columns and 7 rows. Sodium and potassium both fizz in water because each has a single outer electron to give away.
Mendeleev was not alone: Lothar Meyer in Germany built a similar table at the same time, but Mendeleev's predictions won him the credit.

deep.w: Mendeleev invented the periodic table out of nowhere
deep.r: Earlier chemists had noticed patterns; Mendeleev's bold predictions made his version stick

deep.x: The periodic table works because an element's place reveals its electron pattern, and electrons decide chemistry.

cards.title: Camadas eletrónicas
cards.text: Os eletrões ocupam níveis de energia ou camadas. A química tem sobretudo a ver com os eletrões exteriores: os átomos partilham-nos, cedem-nos ou recebem-nos para formar ligações e completar a camada exterior.

deep.x: Electrons can't have just any energy inside an atom. They occupy fixed energy levels, often pictured as shells around the nucleus. Niels Bohr proposed this in 1913. The first shell holds up to 2 electrons, the second up to 8, and the third holds 8 in the simple picture used for light elements.
Why atoms bond
Atoms are most stable with a full outer shell, like the noble gases neon and argon. Others get there in two main ways:

x: **Ionic bonds**: one atom hands electrons to another. Sodium (2, 8, 1) gives its lone outer electron to chlorine (2, 8, 7), making table salt
**Covalent bonds**: atoms share pairs of electrons, as in water and methane
**Metallic bonds**: outer electrons roam freely, which is why metals conduct electricity

deep.x: Light from jumps

When an electron drops from a higher shell to a lower one, it gives out light of a precise colour. Each element has its own set of colours, like a barcode. Sodium street lamps glow orange for this reason, and fireworks get red from strontium and green from barium.
Astronomers identify elements in stars billions of kilometres away by these colour barcodes in starlight.
Chemistry is the story of atoms trying to complete their outer shell of electrons.

cards.title: Moléculas
cards.text: Os átomos juntam-se em moléculas: dois hidrogénios e um oxigénio formam água (H₂O); um carbono e dois oxigénios formam dióxido de carbono (CO₂).

deep.x: A molecule is two or more atoms held together by shared electrons. Some are tiny, like oxygen gas (O₂). Others are huge: a single human DNA molecule in one chromosome contains billions of atoms and would stretch several centimetres if unwound.
Shape matters

Water is bent, with an angle of about 104.5° between its two hydrogens. Oxygen pulls the shared electrons towards itself, making one end slightly negative and the other slightly positive. That lopsidedness lets water dissolve salt and sugar, gives it surface tension, and makes it boil at 100 °C rather than about −80 °C as a molecule its size otherwise would.
Counting molecules

x: A glass holds 250 g of water
One mole of water is 18 g
14 × 6 × 10²³ ≈ 8 × 10²⁴ molecules

deep.x: That is about eight million billion billion molecules in one glass, far more than there are glasses of water in all the oceans.
Same atoms, different molecules
How atoms are arranged can matter as much as which atoms there are. Ethanol (in wine) and dimethyl ether (a gas) have the same atoms in different layouts.

deep.w: Molecules are always made of different elements
deep.r: O₂ and N₂ are molecules of one element; together they make up about 99% of dry air

deep.x: A molecule's properties come from both its atoms and the shape they take.

cards.title: Estados da matéria
cards.text: Os sólidos mantêm a forma, os líquidos tomam a forma do recipiente e os gases enchem-no. Aquecer dá às partículas mais energia para se libertarem. O plasma, um gás quente ionizado, é um quarto estado, presente nas estrelas e nos relâmpagos.

deep.x: Whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas depends on a tug-of-war between particle motion and the attractions holding particles together. Heat adds energy and motion; cooling lets attractions win.
Changing state

x: Melting and freezing: solid ↔ liquid (water at 0 °C)
Boiling and condensing: liquid ↔ gas (water at 100 °C at sea level)
Sublimation: solid straight to gas, as with dry ice at about −78 °C

deep.x: While ice melts, its temperature stays at 0 °C: the heat goes into breaking bonds, not warming. Pressure matters too. At the top of Serra da Estrela, about 2,000 m up, water boils at roughly 93 °C, so pasta cooks more slowly.
Water is odd
Most substances shrink as they freeze. Water expands by about 9%, so ice floats. That's why lakes freeze from the top down and fish survive winter underneath, and why frozen pipes burst.
Plasma is the most common state of visible matter in the universe, because stars are made of it. On Earth you see it in lightning, neon signs and auroras.
States of matter are a balance between how fast particles move and how strongly they attract.

cards.title: Ver átomos
cards.text: Os átomos são demasiado pequenos para os microscópios óticos, mas os microscópios de efeito túnel, inventados em 1981, conseguem obter imagens deles e até mover átomos individuais. Em 1989, a IBM escreveu o seu logótipo com 35 átomos de xénon.

deep.x: Light can't show atoms because its waves are thousands of times wider than an atom. In 1981 Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer at IBM's Zurich lab got round this with the **scanning tunnelling microscope** (STM). It won them the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics.
How an STM works

The tip ends in a single atom. Electrons "tunnel" across the gap, a quantum effect. The current changes about tenfold if the gap changes by just a tenth of a nanometre, so the tip can feel each atom's bump as it scans.
Moving atoms

In 1989 Don Eigler at IBM used an STM to push 35 xenon atoms on a nickel surface into the letters "IBM". The work was done at about −269 °C so the atoms would stay put. In 2013 IBM made a short stop-motion film, "A Boy and His Atom", by moving carbon monoxide molecules frame by frame.
Other ways to see small

x: Atomic force microscopes "feel" surfaces with a tiny cantilever and work on non-conductors
Electron microscopes use electrons, whose wavelengths are far shorter than light's
X-ray crystallography reveals atom positions in crystals, including DNA's double helix in 1953

deep.w: An STM takes a photograph of atoms
deep.r: It builds a map of electric current point by point; the colours are added by computer

deep.x: We can't see atoms with light, but we can feel them with a tip one atom sharp.

cards.title: De onde vêm os átomos
cards.text: O hidrogénio e o hélio formaram-se no Big Bang. Os elementos mais pesados foram forjados no interior das estrelas e em explosões estelares. O carbono do teu corpo e o ferro do teu sangue foram feitos em estrelas.

deep.x: Almost every atom in you is billions of years old. They were made in three great forges: the Big Bang, the hearts of stars, and violent stellar deaths.
The first minutes

In the first 20 minutes after the Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years ago, the universe was hot enough to fuse protons. It ended up roughly 75% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass, with a trace of lithium. The hydrogen in your body's water dates from then.
Star forges

Stars fuse hydrogen into helium, then, if massive enough, helium into carbon and oxygen, and onwards up to iron. Fusion stops at iron because making heavier nuclei costs energy instead of releasing it. When massive stars explode as supernovae, they scatter these elements and make some heavier ones.

steps: Up to iron in big stars

deep.x: Gold from collisions

Much of the gold and platinum in the universe is thought to come from colliding neutron stars. In 2017 astronomers detected such a merger through gravitational waves and saw the glow of freshly made heavy elements.
The Sun and Earth formed 4.6 billion years ago from a cloud already enriched by earlier generations of stars. Your atoms have been through several stars before you.
You are made of stardust: the carbon in your cells and the iron in your blood were forged in stars.

quiz.q: O que decide qual é o elemento de um átomo?
quiz.explain: O número de protões define o elemento.

quiz.q: O carbono-12 e o carbono-14 são…
quiz.explain: Os mesmos protões, neutrões diferentes.

quiz.q: Onde foi produzida a maioria dos elementos pesados, como o ferro do teu sangue?
options: No interior das estrelas e em explosões estelares
quiz.explain: As estrelas forjam os elementos mais pesados.

lessons.title: Radioatividade
lessons.summary: Núcleos instáveis, radiação e semividas.

cards.title: Núcleos instáveis
cards.text: Alguns núcleos têm uma combinação instável de protões e neutrões. Libertam energia e partículas para se tornarem mais estáveis: é o decaimento radioativo.

deep.x: A nucleus is a balance between the strong force, which binds protons and neutrons, and electric repulsion between protons. Only certain mixes are stable. Too many neutrons, too many protons, or simply too big, and the nucleus will eventually rearrange itself and release energy.
Three ways to fix an imbalance
Each decay can change the element. Uranium-238 passes through 14 steps, including radium and radon, before ending as stable lead-206.
Random but predictable

You can never say when one particular nucleus will decay. It's like popcorn: you can't tell which kernel pops next, but you can predict roughly how long the bag takes. Temperature, pressure and chemistry make essentially no difference to the rate.
Discovery
In 1896 Henri Becquerel left uranium salts on a wrapped photographic plate in a drawer and found the plate fogged, with no sunlight involved. The rays came from the uranium itself.
Every element heavier than lead is radioactive. Two lighter ones, technetium (43) and promethium (61), have no stable isotopes at all.
A radioactive nucleus is one with the wrong mix of particles, and decay is its way to a more stable state.

cards.title: Três tipos de radiação
cards.text: As partículas alfa (2 protões + 2 neutrões) são travadas pelo papel. As partículas beta (eletrões), por alguns mm de alumínio. Os raios gama (luz muito energética) exigem chumbo ou betão espessos.

deep.x: The three classic types were named alpha, beta and gamma, the first letters of the Greek alphabet, by Rutherford (1899) and Paul Villard (1900), before anyone knew what they were. They differ in what they are, how much damage they do and how far they get.

items: Alpha: stopped by paper or skin
Beta: stopped by mm of aluminium

deep.x: What each one is

x: **Alpha**: a helium nucleus, heavy and doubly charged. Travels only a few cm in air
**Beta**: a fast electron (or positron). Travels about a metre in air
**Gamma**: high-energy light, no mass or charge. Weakened by matter but never fully stopped

deep.x: Outside vs inside

Alpha particles dump all their energy in a short distance, so swallowed or inhaled alpha emitters are especially harmful. That is why radon, an alpha emitter breathed into the lungs, is a health concern. Gamma rays pass through you, so they are dangerous from outside but are also useful for imaging and therapy.
Ionising radiation

All three are "ionising": they knock electrons off atoms, which can break chemical bonds, including in DNA. Neutrons, released in reactors, are a fourth important type that needs water or concrete to stop.

deep.w: Radiation makes things radioactive
deep.r: Alpha, beta and gamma do not make objects radioactive; contamination means radioactive material itself has landed somewhere

deep.x: The more easily a radiation type is stopped, the more damage it does over a short distance.

cards.title: Semivida
cards.text: Cada isótopo radioativo tem uma semivida: o tempo que demora metade de uma amostra a decair. Ao fim de duas semividas resta um quarto; ao fim de dez, menos de 0,1%.

deep.x: A half-life is the time it takes for half the nuclei in a sample to decay. It's a statistical property: each nucleus has the same chance of decaying in any given time, regardless of its age. So the amount left keeps halving, never quite reaching zero.
Working it out

x: Iodine-131 half-life is 8 days
After 8 days: 1/2 left
After 80 days (10 half-lives): 1/1,024, under 0.1%

deep.x: Iodine-131 is used to treat thyroid conditions, and was released at Chernobyl. Its short half-life means it was a serious risk for weeks but faded within months.
amount left = start × (1/2)^(time ÷ half-life)
Short vs long

A short half-life means intense radiation that disappears quickly. A long half-life means weaker radiation lasting a long time. A rough rule: after 10 half-lives, a source has dropped to about a thousandth.

deep.w: After two half-lives everything has decayed
deep.r: After two half-lives a quarter remains; the amount halves again each time

deep.x: Radioactivity fades by halving: the same fraction disappears in each half-life, however much is left.

cards.title: As semividas variam imenso
cards.text: Alguns isótopos decaem em segundos, outros ao longo de milhares de milhões de anos.

deep.x: Half-lives range across more than 40 powers of ten, from a tiny fraction of a second to far longer than the age of the universe. The value depends on how unstable the nucleus is and which decay route it takes.
Why the range matters

x: **Medicine** wants short half-lives: technetium-99m (6 hours) lights up scans then fades within a day
**Dating** needs half-lives matched to the age being measured: carbon-14 for thousands of years, uranium for billions
**Waste** problems come from middle and long half-lives: caesium-137 and strontium-90 (about 30 years) dominate the first centuries

deep.x: Earth's inner heat

Long-lived uranium-238, thorium-232 and potassium-40 have been decaying inside Earth since it formed. Their heat helps keep the mantle churning, which drives plate tectonics and volcanoes, including the Azores.
Tellurium-128 has the longest half-life ever measured, about 2 × 10²⁴ years, over 100 trillion times the age of the universe.
Short half-lives burn bright and fade fast; long ones whisper for ages.

cards.title: Datação por carbono

steps: Medir o que resta: a idade

cards.text: Os seres vivos absorvem carbono-14 constantemente. Quando morrem, este decai com uma semivida de 5730 anos. Medir o que resta permite datar restos orgânicos com até cerca de 50 000 anos.

deep.x: Cosmic rays hit nitrogen atoms high in the atmosphere and turn some into carbon-14. This joins carbon dioxide, plants absorb it, and animals eat the plants. So every living thing carries the same tiny proportion of carbon-14 as the air, about one atom per trillion carbon atoms.
The clock starts at death
Once an organism dies, it stops taking in carbon. The carbon-14 decays with a half-life of 5,730 years, while carbon-12 stays put. Measuring the ratio tells you how long ago it died.

x: Bone has 25% of living C-14 level
Two half-lives

deep.x: Limits and corrections

x: After about 50,000 years (nearly 9 half-lives) too little is left to measure
Only works on once-living material: wood, bone, charcoal, cloth, shell
Atmospheric C-14 has varied, so dates are calibrated with tree rings and other records
Nuclear tests in the 1950s–60s almost doubled atmospheric C-14, the "bomb pulse"

deep.x: Modern accelerator mass spectrometry counts carbon-14 atoms directly and needs only milligrams of sample.

deep.w: Carbon dating can date dinosaurs
deep.r: Dinosaurs died 66 million years ago; their age comes from dating volcanic rock with longer-lived isotopes

deep.x: Living things share the air's carbon-14; after death, its steady decay becomes a clock.

cards.title: Radiação de fundo
cards.text: Estamos sempre expostos a uma radiação natural baixa vinda de rochas, solo, raios cósmicos e do nosso próprio corpo. O gás radão das rochas graníticas é a maior fonte natural, e é importante no norte de Portugal.

deep.x: Radiation is everywhere, and always has been. Worldwide, a person receives about 2.4 mSv a year from natural sources on average, though this varies widely with geology and altitude.
Where it comes from

x: **Radon**: a gas from uranium in rocks and soil, about half the natural dose
**Ground**: uranium, thorium and potassium in rocks and building materials
**Cosmic rays**: higher at altitude and on flights
**Your own body**: potassium-40 and carbon-14 in your tissues

deep.x: Your radioactive body
An adult body contains about 140 g of potassium, of which a tiny fraction is radioactive potassium-40. Together with carbon-14, around 8,000 atoms decay inside you every second.
Portugal's granite

Much of northern and central Portugal sits on granite, which contains more uranium than most rocks. Districts such as Guarda, Viseu, Vila Real and Braga have some of the highest indoor radon levels in Europe, so the natural dose there can be several times the world average.
Places such as Ramsar in Iran and Kerala in India have natural doses many times the world average, and people have lived there for generations.
Natural radiation is a constant background to life; radon from the ground is the biggest part of it.

cards.title: Radão em casa

items: Medir com um detetor durante 2–3 meses
Extração sob o pavimento se for alto

cards.text: O granito do norte de Portugal liberta radão, que se pode acumular em caves e rés-do-chão. Ventilar e selar os pavimentos reduz o radão; detetores baratos medem-no ao longo de meses.

deep.x: Radon-222 forms when radium in rocks decays. It is a colourless, odourless gas that seeps out of soil and through cracks, pipes and gaps in floors. Outdoors it dilutes harmlessly; indoors it can build up, especially in cellars and ground floors in winter when windows stay shut.
Why it matters

Radon itself is breathed in and out, but its decay products are solid alpha emitters that lodge in the lungs. The World Health Organization calls radon the second biggest cause of lung cancer after smoking, and the risk multiplies for smokers.
Limits and testing

Under EU rules, Portugal set a reference level of 300 becquerels per cubic metre (Bq/m³) for homes and workplaces in 2018. The WHO suggests aiming for 100 where possible. Levels swing with weather and season, so a reliable test uses a passive detector left for at least three months, ideally over winter. Detectors are cheap and posted to a lab for analysis.
Reducing it

x: Ventilate ground floors and cellars; open windows on opposite sides
Seal cracks in floors and gaps around pipes
Fit a sump with a small fan under the floor to draw radon out (often cuts levels by 80–90%)
In new builds, lay a radon-proof membrane

deep.w: Radon is only a problem in old stone houses
deep.r: Any building on uranium-bearing ground can collect radon, including new concrete ones

deep.x: Radon is invisible but easy to measure and usually cheap to reduce, so testing is worth it in granite areas.

cards.title: Medir a dose
cards.text: A dose de radiação nas pessoas mede-se em sieverts (Sv), normalmente milisieverts (mSv). Um raio X ao tórax são cerca de 0,02 mSv; uma TAC, vários mSv; um voo Lisboa–Nova Iorque, cerca de 0,04 mSv.

deep.x: Two different units matter. The **becquerel** (Bq) counts how many nuclei decay per second in a source. The **sievert** (Sv) estimates the biological effect on a person, weighting for the type of radiation and the organs hit. Doses to the public are usually in millisieverts (mSv), thousandths of a sievert.
Putting doses in context

x: Dental X-ray: about 0.005 mSv
Eating a banana: about 0.0001 mSv
Public limit from artificial sources (excluding medicine): 1 mSv a year
Radiation workers in the EU: up to 20 mSv a year
1,000 mSv (1 Sv) at once: radiation sickness likely
CT scan 8 mSv
Natural background 2.4 mSv a year
About three years of background in one scan

deep.x: Dose vs risk

Large doses damage cells fast and cause burns and sickness. Small doses are thought to add a small extra cancer risk roughly in proportion to dose. Medical scans are used when the diagnostic benefit clearly outweighs that small risk.
The unit is named after Rolf Sievert, a Swedish physicist who pioneered radiation protection in the early 20th century.
Becquerels describe the source; sieverts describe what it does to you.

cards.title: Usos da radiação
cards.text: A radiação salva vidas na medicina (raios X, tratamento do cancro, esterilização de equipamento), verifica soldaduras na indústria, alimenta naves espaciais e deteta fumo nos alarmes.

deep.x: The same properties that make radiation dangerous make it useful: it penetrates matter, can be detected in tiny amounts and can kill cells.
Medicine

x: **Diagnosis**: technetium-99m is used in tens of millions of scans a year; PET scans use fluorine-18, half-life about 110 minutes
**Radiotherapy**: about half of all cancer patients receive it, aiming beams to destroy tumour cells
**Sterilising**: gamma rays from cobalt-60 sterilise syringes, gloves and implants sealed in their packaging

deep.x: Industry and home

x: Gamma radiography checks welds in pipelines and aircraft parts
Smoke alarms use a speck of americium-241: its alpha particles let a tiny current flow, and smoke interrupts it
Food irradiation kills bacteria and delays sprouting without making food radioactive

deep.x: Power far from the Sun

Radioisotope generators use heat from plutonium-238 decay to make electricity. They have powered the Voyager probes since 1977, now beyond the Solar System, and the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers on Mars.

deep.w: Irradiated food is radioactive
deep.r: Food irradiation uses gamma rays or electrons that pass through; the food does not become radioactive

deep.x: Radiation is a tool: controlled and shielded, it diagnoses, heals, sterilises and powers.

cards.title: Marie Curie

events.l: Os Curie descobrem o polónio e o rádio

cards.text: Marie Curie descobriu o polónio e o rádio com Pierre Curie, criou a palavra "radioatividade" e ganhou dois Prémios Nobel, em física (1903) e química (1911), tendo sido a primeira pessoa a ganhar em duas ciências.

deep.x: Born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw in 1867, she moved to Paris in 1891 because women could not attend university in Russian-ruled Poland. She studied physics and maths at the Sorbonne, often living on very little, and married the physicist Pierre Curie in 1895.
The discoveries

Following Becquerel's uranium rays, she found the pitchblende ore was more active than its uranium could explain. She and Pierre processed tonnes of it in a leaky shed to isolate two new elements: polonium, named after her homeland, and radium, which glows in the dark. She realised radioactivity was a property of atoms themselves, a key step toward nuclear physics.
Firsts

x: First woman to win a Nobel Prize
First person to win two, and still the only one in two different sciences
First woman professor at the Sorbonne, in 1906, after Pierre's death in a street accident

deep.x: War and legacy

In the First World War she equipped about 20 mobile X-ray vans, the "petites Curies", and trained women to operate them, helping treat over a million soldiers. Her daughter Irène Joliot-Curie won the 1935 Nobel in Chemistry. Long exposure to radiation, unknown then as a danger, led to her death from aplastic anaemia in 1934.
Her laboratory notebooks are still radioactive more than a century later and are kept in lead-lined boxes in Paris; readers must sign a waiver.
Marie Curie showed that radioactivity comes from inside the atom, and opened the nuclear age.

quiz.q: Que radiação é travada por uma folha de papel?
quiz.explain: As partículas alfa são grandes e pesadas.

quiz.q: Ao fim de 3 semividas, quanto resta de uma amostra?
Qual é, para muitas pessoas, a maior fonte natural de radiação?
quiz.explain: O radão vem de rochas como o granito.

lessons.title: Energia nuclear
lessons.summary: Fissão, fusão e como funcionam os reatores.

cards.title: E = mc²
cards.text: Einstein mostrou que a massa e a energia são equivalentes. Uma quantidade minúscula de massa converte-se numa quantidade enorme de energia, porque c², a velocidade da luz ao quadrado, é gigantesco.

deep.x: Einstein published the idea in 1905, as a short follow-up to his paper on special relativity. It says mass is a very concentrated form of energy. The conversion factor is the speed of light squared, and since light travels about 300,000 km per second, that factor is enormous.
How much energy?

x: m = 1 gram = 0.001 kg
c² = 9 × 10¹⁶ m²/s²
About 25 million kWh, roughly the Hiroshima bomb

deep.x: Converting a single kilogram fully would give about 25 billion kWh, around half of Portugal's yearly electricity use. In practice, no everyday process converts more than a small fraction of mass.
What fraction gets converted?
That is why nuclear reactions release millions of times more energy per kilogram than chemical ones such as burning coal or petrol.

deep.w: E = mc² was what made the atomic bomb possible
deep.r: The bomb depended on discovering fission in 1938; E = mc² just accounts for where the energy comes from

deep.x: The first direct test came in 1932, when John Cockcroft and Ernest Walton split lithium nuclei in Cambridge and found the fragments' energy matched the missing mass.
A little mass is a huge amount of energy, because c² is a gigantic number.

cards.title: Fissão
cards.text: Um núcleo pesado como o urânio-235 absorve um neutrão e divide-se em dois núcleos mais pequenos, libertando energia e mais dois ou três neutrões, que podem dividir outros núcleos: uma reação em cadeia.

deep.x: Fission was discovered in Berlin in December 1938 by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann, who found barium, a much lighter element, after bombarding uranium with neutrons. Lise Meitner, who had fled Nazi Germany, and her nephew Otto Frisch explained it weeks later: the nucleus had split in two, and they named the process after cell division.
The chain reaction

Each split releases about 200 million electronvolts, roughly 50 million times the energy from burning one carbon atom. If at least one of the new neutrons splits another nucleus, the reaction keeps itself going.
Why uranium-235?

Natural uranium is 99.3% uranium-238, which rarely splits. Only 0.7% is uranium-235, which splits easily, especially with slow neutrons. Reactors use a **moderator**, usually water, to slow neutrons down. Plutonium-239, made inside reactors from uranium-238, also splits well.
First chain reaction
On 2 December 1942, Enrico Fermi's team started the first controlled chain reaction in Chicago Pile-1, a stack of graphite and uranium under a sports stand. It produced about half a watt.
Nature beat us to it. About 2 billion years ago, uranium deposits at Oklo in Gabon ran as natural fission reactors, on and off, for hundreds of thousands of years.
Fission splits heavy nuclei; the spare neutrons can split more, making a self-sustaining chain.

cards.title: Dentro de um reator
cards.text: As barras de combustível aquecem a água; o calor produz vapor, que faz girar uma turbina e um gerador, tal como numa central a carvão, mas sem combustão. As barras de controlo absorvem neutrões para manter a reação em cadeia estável.

deep.x: Most of the world's roughly 400 power reactors are **pressurised water reactors**. Their core holds tens of thousands of fuel rods filled with uranium oxide pellets, each the size of a fingertip. Water around them slows neutrons and carries heat away.
Keeping it steady

x: **Control rods** of boron or cadmium soak up neutrons; pushing them in slows the reaction
If cooling water heats up and expands, it slows fewer neutrons, so power falls by itself
Emergency systems drop all rods in about two seconds, a "scram"

deep.x: Heat after shutdown

Even after the chain reaction stops, the radioactive fission products keep releasing heat, about 6–7% of full power at first, falling over days. That is why cooling must never fail, as Fukushima showed.
Efficiency
A typical reactor turns about a third of its heat into electricity; the rest leaves through cooling towers or into a river or sea. A 1,000 MW electric plant runs at around 3,000 MW of heat.

deep.w: The clouds above nuclear cooling towers are pollution
deep.r: They are water vapour, the same as from any steam power station

deep.x: Spain's Almaraz plant, on the Tagus about 100 km from the Portuguese border, has supplied Iberian electricity since the early 1980s.
A reactor is a kettle with a nuclear heat source: fission boils water, steam turns a turbine.

cards.title: Densidade energética

items.l: por kg de urânio natural num reator típico

cards.text: Um quilograma de combustível de urânio pode produzir tanta energia como milhares de toneladas de carvão. A energia nuclear ocupa muito pouco terreno e quase não emite CO₂ durante o funcionamento.

deep.x: Nuclear fuel packs extraordinary energy into a small mass, because nuclear forces are millions of times stronger than the chemical bonds broken in burning.

x: 1 kg of U-235 fully split ≈ 8 × 10¹³ J
1 kg of coal ≈ 3 × 10⁷ J
Ratio ≈ 2.7 million
1 kg U-235 ≈ 2,700 tonnes of coal

deep.x: Real reactor fuel is only 3–5% uranium-235 and is not fully used, so a kilogram of fuel replaces roughly 100–150 tonnes of coal. Still, a 1,000 MW plant needs only about 25 tonnes of fresh fuel a year, a few lorry loads, where a coal plant burns millions of tonnes.
Climate and land
Over their whole life cycle, including mining and construction, nuclear plants emit about 12 g of CO₂ per kWh, similar to wind and far below gas or coal.

v.unit: g CO₂ per kWh, life cycle (IPCC)

deep.x: The catch

High energy density doesn't automatically mean cheap. Recent European projects, such as Flamanville 3 in France and Olkiluoto 3 in Finland, ran over a decade late and cost several times their budgets.
A person's entire lifetime of electricity from nuclear power would produce spent fuel about the size of a drinks can.
Nuclear fuel is a million times denser in energy than fossil fuel, which is both its strength and why its waste is so compact.

cards.title: Resíduos nucleares
cards.text: O combustível usado é altamente radioativo durante milhares de anos. Ocupa pouco volume e é guardado em piscinas de arrefecimento e depois em contentores secos. O Onkalo, na Finlândia, é o primeiro repositório geológico profundo a ser preparado para armazenamento definitivo.

deep.x: Spent fuel is about 95% uranium, 1% plutonium and 4% fission products. Those fission products make it intensely radioactive and hot when it leaves the reactor, so it must be cooled and shielded.
How long?

Radioactivity falls fast at first: after 40 years it is about a thousandth of the level at removal. But long-lived elements such as plutonium mean it takes very roughly 100,000 years to drop to the level of the uranium ore it came from. Reprocessing, as France does, recovers uranium and plutonium and cuts the volume of high-level waste.
Onkalo

Finland is building the world's first permanent repository at Olkiluoto. Fuel goes into copper canisters, packed in bentonite clay, placed about 430 m deep in 1.9-billion-year-old granite. The idea is several barriers, so no single failure matters. A full trial run began in 2024; Sweden began building a similar site at Forsmark in 2025.
Volume

deep.w: Nuclear waste is glowing green goo
deep.r: Spent fuel is solid ceramic pellets in metal rods; the blue glow in pools is Cherenkov light in water

deep.x: Nuclear waste is small in volume but long-lived, so the plan is to isolate it deep in stable rock.

cards.title: Acidentes
cards.text: Os piores acidentes foram Chernobyl (1986), um reator mal concebido e um teste inseguro, e Fukushima (2011), onde um tsunami deitou abaixo o arrefecimento. Moldaram regras de segurança rigorosas em todo o mundo.

deep.x: The International Nuclear Event Scale runs from 1 to 7. Only two accidents have reached level 7.
Chernobyl, 26 April 1986

During a badly run safety test at night, reactor 4 surged out of control. The Soviet RBMK design had a dangerous flaw: as water boiled, power rose instead of fell. A steam explosion blew off the reactor's massive steel lid and the graphite burned for days, with no strong containment building. About 30 workers and firefighters died within months. Thousands of thyroid cancers followed in children who drank contaminated milk, most treated successfully. Estimates of long-term deaths are disputed. A 30 km exclusion zone remains.
Fukushima, 11 March 2011

A magnitude-9 earthquake shut the reactors down safely, but a tsunami about 14 m high flooded the backup generators. Without cooling, three cores melted and hydrogen explosions wrecked buildings. Around 150,000 people were evacuated. The tsunami itself killed about 18,000 people; one later worker death has been attributed to radiation, while the stress of evacuation contributed to many deaths among the elderly.
Lessons
After 2011, EU reactors went through stress tests, adding backup power and flood defences. Germany chose to phase out nuclear power, closing its last plants in 2023.
Wildlife has flourished in the Chernobyl exclusion zone without people; wolves, lynx and Przewalski's horses roam there.
The worst nuclear accidents came from design flaws and losing cooling, and each one rewrote safety rules worldwide.

cards.title: Portugal e o nuclear

events.l: fecham as últimas minas de urânio

cards.text: Portugal nunca teve uma central nuclear. Um plano dos anos 1970 para uma central em Ferrel, perto de Peniche, foi abandonado depois de protestos locais. O país explorou minas de urânio até 2001, na Urgeiriça e noutros locais.

deep.x: Portugal is one of several EU countries never to have generated nuclear power. Yet nuclear history runs through its geology, its science and its politics.
Ferrel

In the 1970s the government chose Ferrel, near Peniche, for a nuclear plant. In March 1976 local farmers and fishermen occupied the site and protested, and the plan was shelved. Later energy plans mentioned nuclear but never went ahead, and Portugal chose hydro, wind and later solar instead.
Uranium country

The granite of the Beiras is rich in uranium. Mining began for radium early in the 20th century at Urgeiriça, near Nelas, and later supplied uranium. Around 60 old mines remain, and many have been cleaned up by the state company EDM to deal with tailings and radon.
Science

Portugal ran a small research reactor at Sacavém/Bobadela, near Lisbon, from 1961 to 2016 for materials research and isotopes. Portuguese physicists also take part in CERN and in European fusion research.

deep.w: Portugal uses no nuclear electricity
deep.r: Portugal trades power with Spain, which gets about a fifth of its electricity from nuclear

deep.x: Portugal never built a nuclear plant, but it mined uranium for decades and remains part of a nuclear-powered Iberian grid.

cards.title: Fusão
cards.text: A fusão junta núcleos leves, como isótopos do hidrogénio, em hélio, libertando ainda mais energia por quilo do que a fissão. É o que alimenta o Sol. Fazê-la na Terra exige temperaturas acima dos 100 milhões de °C.

deep.x: Fusion is the opposite of fission: light nuclei join to make a heavier one. The product weighs slightly less than the parts, and the missing mass becomes energy. Per kilogram, the deuterium–tritium reaction releases about four times as much energy as fission.
Why so hot?

Nuclei are positively charged and repel each other strongly. To make them touch, they must hit at huge speed. The Sun manages at 15 million °C thanks to crushing pressure, gravity and quantum tunnelling. On Earth we can't match that pressure, so we use temperatures of 100–150 million °C, about ten times the Sun's core.
Fuel

x: Deuterium is in all water: about 1 hydrogen atom in 6,400 in seawater
Tritium is rare and radioactive, so reactors must breed it from lithium
The waste is helium, and fusion produces no long-lived high-level waste, though the reactor walls become radioactive

deep.x: The hard part
Fusion is not a chain reaction. If anything goes wrong, the plasma cools and stops in seconds. The challenge is the opposite of fission: keeping it going at all.
The deuterium in about 45 litres of water, fused with tritium bred from the lithium in one laptop battery, could supply about 200,000 kWh: roughly 30 years of one EU citizen's electricity.
Fusion releases energy by joining light nuclei, but only at temperatures hotter than the Sun's core.

cards.title: Reatores de fusão
cards.text: Os tokamaks, como o ITER, em construção em França, confinam plasma quente com ímanes potentes. Em 2022, a National Ignition Facility dos EUA conseguiu uma reação de fusão que libertou mais energia do que a que os seus lasers forneceram ao alvo.

deep.x: There are two main approaches. **Magnetic confinement** holds a hot plasma for a long time in a magnetic cage. **Inertial confinement** crushes a tiny fuel pellet with lasers for a few billionths of a second.
ITER

ITER, in Cadarache in southern France, is a collaboration of the EU, China, India, Japan, Korea, Russia and the US. Its goal is to produce 500 MW of fusion power from 50 MW of heating, a gain of ten. It has faced long delays: the current plan targets first research operations in 2034 and full deuterium–tritium fuel in 2039. It will not make electricity; it is an experiment.
NIF's milestone

On 5 December 2022, the US National Ignition Facility fired 2.05 MJ of laser light at a target and got 3.15 MJ of fusion energy out. Later shots did better. But the lasers drew around 300 MJ from the grid, so the whole facility is far from a net gain.
Portugal's part

Lisbon's Instituto Superior Técnico runs a fusion research institute, operated a small tokamak (ISTTOK) and contributes to ITER and the European EUROfusion programme. Private companies worldwide are also racing to build compact machines.

deep.w: Fusion is always 30 years away and never progresses
deep.r: Fusion performance has improved by many orders of magnitude since the 1970s; the step to cheap, practical power is still unproven

deep.x: Fusion has proved it can release more energy than goes into the fuel; turning that into practical power is the next challenge.

cards.title: Pequenos reatores modulares
cards.text: Os SMR são reatores mais pequenos construídos em fábrica e transportados para o local, com o objetivo de reduzir custos e prazos de construção. Há vários modelos em desenvolvimento e licenciamento em todo o mundo.

deep.x: Small modular reactors (SMRs) produce up to about 300 MW of electricity, compared with 1,000–1,600 MW for large plants. "Modular" means building standard parts in a factory and assembling them on site, like aircraft, instead of building each plant as a unique giant project.
The promise

x: Lower up-front cost, so smaller utilities and countries can afford one
Passive safety: many designs cool themselves by natural circulation, without pumps or power
Can replace old coal plants and reuse their grid connections
Can supply heat for industry or hydrogen as well as electricity

deep.x: Where things stand
The doubts

Cheaper per plant is not the same as cheaper per kWh: large reactors benefit from scale. A flagship US project by NuScale was cancelled in 2023 when costs rose. Mass production only pays off once many units are ordered, and the first few are always the most expensive.
Nuclear-powered submarines and aircraft carriers have run on small reactors since the USS Nautilus in 1954, so the idea of compact reactors is not new.
SMRs bet on factory production and smaller size to make nuclear power faster and cheaper to build; the bet is still being tested.

lessons.title: Relatividade
lessons.summary: As ideias de Einstein sobre o espaço, o tempo e a gravidade.

cards.title: A velocidade da luz é igual para todos

steps: Luz com velocidade fixa para todos

cards.text: O ponto de partida de Einstein, em 1905: a velocidade da luz no vácuo é a mesma para todos os observadores, seja qual for a sua velocidade. Esta regra simples obriga o espaço e o tempo a esticar.

deep.x: Throw a ball forward from a moving train and its speed adds to the train's. Common sense says light should behave the same way. It doesn't. In 1887 Albert Michelson and Edward Morley tried to detect Earth's motion through a supposed "ether" by timing light in different directions, and found no difference at all.
Einstein's two rules (1905)

x: The laws of physics are the same for everyone moving at a steady speed
Light in a vacuum always travels at the same speed, about 300,000 km/s, whoever measures it

deep.x: Something has to give

Speed is distance divided by time. If light's speed can't change, then distance and time must differ between observers. Moving rulers shrink along their direction of motion and moving clocks run slow, by exactly the amounts needed to keep light's speed fixed.
A fixed number
Since 1983 the speed of light has been defined as exactly 299,792,458 m/s, and the metre is defined from it: the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
Einstein was 26 and working as a patent clerk in Bern when he published special relativity, along with three other landmark papers in 1905, his "miracle year".
Light's speed is the one thing everyone agrees on; space and time adjust to keep it that way.

cards.title: Dilatação do tempo
cards.text: Os relógios em movimento andam mais devagar. Às velocidades do dia a dia o efeito é minúsculo, mas a 87% da velocidade da luz o tempo passa a metade do ritmo.

deep.x: The slowing of moving clocks is set by the **Lorentz factor**, γ (gamma). It is almost exactly 1 at everyday speeds and climbs steeply close to light speed.

x: γ ≈ 2: one hour on board = two hours outside

deep.x: Proof from the sky

Cosmic rays striking the upper atmosphere, about 15 km up, create particles called **muons**. Muons live only about 2 millionths of a second, long enough to travel about 600 m. Yet many reach the ground. Travelling at over 99% of light speed, their clocks run slow enough to make the trip.
Nobody feels it
Each observer sees their own clock ticking normally. Only when comparing with someone moving relative to them do they see the difference.
Astronauts who spend a year on the International Space Station come back a few thousandths of a second younger than if they had stayed on Earth.
Time is not universal: the faster you move relative to someone, the slower your clock runs in their eyes.

cards.title: O paradoxo dos gémeos
cards.text: Se uma gémea viajar até uma estrela distante perto da velocidade da luz e regressar, estará mais nova do que a irmã que ficou na Terra. Experiências com partículas rápidas e relógios atómicos em aviões confirmam-no.

deep.x: Imagine twins, Ana and Rita. Ana boards a ship to a star 10 light-years away, travelling at 87% of the speed of light, then comes straight back. Rita stays in Viana do Castelo.

x: Distance there and back: 20 light-years
Rita's time: 20 ÷ 0.87 ≈ 23 years
Ana's clock runs at half rate
Ana ages about 11.5 years

deep.x: Why it's not really a paradox

From Ana's ship, Earth moves away, so shouldn't Rita's clock run slow? The answer is that the situation isn't symmetrical. Ana has to accelerate, turn round and decelerate, switching between moving frames. Rita stays in one. When the full calculation includes the turnaround, both agree Ana is younger.
Tested for real
In 1971 Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating flew caesium atomic clocks round the world on airliners, eastward and westward, and compared them with clocks left in Washington.

The results matched relativity's predictions, combining speed effects and gravity effects, within the experimental error. Particle accelerators confirm the effect every day with unstable particles that live many times longer when moving fast.

deep.w: The traveller just feels younger
deep.r: Her body really has aged less: fewer heartbeats, fewer cell divisions, less time

deep.x: Travel fast enough and you return to a future where more time has passed for everyone else.

cards.title: Nada mais rápido do que a luz
cards.text: À medida que um objeto acelera, é preciso cada vez mais energia para o acelerar ainda mais. Atingir a velocidade da luz exigiria energia infinita, por isso nada com massa o consegue.

deep.x: Pushing an object closer to light speed takes ever more energy for ever smaller gains in speed. Its energy grows by the Lorentz factor, which shoots towards infinity as speed approaches c.
Fastest things we've made

x: Protons in CERN's Large Hadron Collider reach 99.999999% of light speed, yet never c
The Parker Solar Probe, the fastest spacecraft, reached about 190 km/s in 2024, under 0.1% of c
Voyager 1, launched 1977, takes about 23 hours for its radio signals to reach us

deep.x: Why it matters

If information could travel faster than light, some observers would see an effect before its cause. Relativity's speed limit protects cause and effect. Light itself goes at c only because photons have no mass.
Faster than light in water
Light slows to about 75% of c in water. Particles from a reactor core can outrun it there, producing an eerie blue glow called **Cherenkov radiation**, an optical version of a sonic boom.

deep.w: Nothing at all can move faster than light
deep.r: Nothing with mass can reach c in a vacuum, but light can be beaten in water, and distant galaxies recede faster than c because space itself expands

deep.x: Reaching light speed would need infinite energy, so it is a limit, not a target.

cards.title: Relatividade geral
cards.text: Em 1915, Einstein descreveu a gravidade não como uma força, mas como espaço-tempo curvo: a massa curva o espaço-tempo e os objetos seguem as curvas. A imagem habitual é a de uma bola pesada num trampolim.

deep.x: In 1907 Einstein had what he called his "happiest thought": a person falling freely doesn't feel their own weight. Gravity and acceleration feel the same. Eight years of hard maths later, in November 1915, he published general relativity.
The idea

Mass and energy curve space-time, the four-dimensional fabric of space and time together. Objects move along the straightest possible paths through this curved fabric. As the physicist John Wheeler summed it up: matter tells space-time how to curve; space-time tells matter how to move.
Its first triumph

For decades Mercury's orbit had puzzled astronomers. Its closest point to the Sun shifts by an extra 43 arcseconds per century that Newton's theory couldn't explain. Einstein's equations gave exactly 43. He said the result gave him heart palpitations.
Gravitational waves

Accelerating masses send ripples through space-time. On 14 September 2015, the LIGO detectors in the US caught waves from two black holes merging 1.3 billion light-years away. The signal stretched their 4 km arms by less than a thousandth of a proton's width. The discovery won the 2017 Nobel Prize.

deep.w: The trampoline picture shows how gravity works
deep.r: It's a helpful analogy for space curving, but it uses gravity to explain gravity, and real curvature also involves time

deep.x: Gravity isn't a pull across space; it's the shape of space-time guiding how things move.

cards.title: A gravidade atrasa o tempo
cards.text: Os relógios andam mais devagar onde a gravidade é mais forte. Um relógio ao nível do mar anda ligeiramente mais devagar do que um no alto de uma montanha. O efeito é minúsculo, mas mensurável.

deep.x: General relativity predicts that clocks deeper in a gravitational field tick more slowly. Light climbing out of gravity loses energy and shifts towards red, which is the same effect seen another way.
Measuring it

In 1959 Robert Pound and Glen Rebka at Harvard sent gamma rays 22.5 m up a tower and measured a tiny change in their frequency, matching the prediction. In 2010 optical atomic clocks at the US standards lab detected the difference from raising one clock just 33 cm.

x: Height difference: 1,000 m
Rate change ≈ g × h ÷ c² ≈ 1 part in 10¹³
About 9 nanoseconds a day
Over 80 years: about 0.3 milliseconds

deep.x: Practical uses

Clocks are now so precise that they act as altimeters: comparing two clocks can reveal a centimetre of height difference. Scientists plan to use networks of clocks to measure Earth's shape and sea level and to detect underground mass, such as magma.
Because of gravity, Earth's core is estimated to be about two and a half years younger than its surface, after 4.5 billion years.

deep.w: Time slows because gravity affects the clock's mechanism
deep.r: All processes slow equally, from atoms to heartbeats; it's time itself

deep.x: The stronger the gravity, the slower time flows, and modern clocks can measure it over the height of a table.

cards.title: O GPS precisa da relatividade

items.l: erro diário de posição sem correção

cards.text: No total, os relógios dos satélites GPS adiantam-se cerca de 38 microssegundos por dia (a gravidade acelera-os, a velocidade orbital atrasa-os). Sem correção, as posições desviar-se-iam cerca de 10 km por dia.

deep.x: GPS, and Europe's Galileo system, work by timing. Your phone receives signals from at least four satellites, each saying when it was sent. Since radio waves travel at light speed, each microsecond of delay means about 300 m. So the clocks must agree to within billionths of a second.
Two effects, opposite directions

GPS satellites orbit about 20,200 km up at about 14,000 km/h. Their speed slows their clocks by about 7 microseconds a day. Being higher in Earth's gravity makes them tick faster by about 45. The net result: +38 microseconds a day.

x: Error per day: 38 µs
Light travels 0.3 km per µs
Positions drift about 10 km a day

deep.x: The fix
Engineers set the satellite clocks to run slightly slow before launch, at 10.22999999543 MHz instead of 10.23 MHz, so they tick at the right rate in orbit.

In 2014 two Galileo satellites were launched into the wrong, elliptical orbits. Scientists turned the mistake into an experiment, using their changing altitude to confirm the gravity effect on time more precisely than ever before.
Your phone's map works only because engineers account for both of Einstein's theories every day.

cards.title: A luz curva-se

steps: A luz da estrela passa pelo Sol

cards.text: A gravidade curva a luz. Em 1919, durante um eclipse solar, os astrónomos viram estrelas perto do Sol deslocadas exatamente como Einstein previra, o que o tornou famoso em todo o mundo. Parte da observação foi feita na ilha do Príncipe.

deep.x: If space-time is curved, light passing a heavy object should bend. Einstein predicted that starlight grazing the Sun would be deflected by 1.75 arcseconds, twice the value from Newton's theory. The only chance to see stars close to the Sun is during a total solar eclipse.
The 1919 expeditions

On 29 May 1919, British teams photographed the eclipse from two places: Arthur Eddington on Príncipe island in the Gulf of Guinea, then a Portuguese colony, and another team at Sobral in Brazil. Clouds almost ruined Eddington's view, but the measurements favoured Einstein. In November the results were announced in London and newspapers made Einstein a global celebrity overnight.
Gravitational lenses

Whole galaxies and clusters bend light from objects far behind them. This produces arcs, multiple images, and even complete circles called Einstein rings. Astronomers use these natural lenses as telescopes to see galaxies too faint to observe otherwise, and to map invisible dark matter.
There's a plaque at the Roça Sundy plantation on Príncipe marking where Eddington set up his telescope; a centenary celebration was held there in 2019.
Mass bends light's path, and the 1919 eclipse, partly seen from Príncipe, turned this into a world headline.

cards.title: Buracos negros

events.l: deteção da fusão de buracos negros

cards.text: Se se comprimir massa suficiente num espaço pequeno, a sua gravidade torna-se tão forte que nem a luz escapa. A fronteira é o horizonte de acontecimentos. A primeira imagem de um buraco negro foi publicada em 2019.

deep.x: In 1916, months after Einstein's theory appeared, Karl Schwarzschild found a solution describing a point mass. It contained a radius at which escape speed equals light speed. Squeeze any mass inside that radius and it becomes a black hole.
How they form

Most stellar black holes form when a star more than about 20 times the Sun's mass runs out of fuel and its core collapses. Supermassive black holes, millions to billions of solar masses, sit at the centres of most galaxies; how they grew so big so early is an open question.
Seeing the unseeable

The Event Horizon Telescope linked radio dishes across the planet into a virtual telescope the size of Earth. In April 2019 it published an image of the black hole in galaxy M87: a dark shadow inside a ring of glowing gas, 6.5 billion solar masses, 55 million light-years away. In 2022 it imaged Sagittarius A*, the 4-million-solar-mass black hole at our galaxy's centre.
Near the edge

Near a small black hole, the pull on your feet would be far stronger than on your head, stretching you thin, called "spaghettification". Stephen Hawking showed in 1974 that quantum effects should make black holes slowly leak radiation and evaporate.

deep.w: Black holes suck in everything around them
deep.r: From a distance, a black hole pulls like any object of the same mass; if the Sun became one, Earth's orbit wouldn't change

deep.x: A black hole is mass squeezed so tightly that its event horizon hides everything inside from the rest of the universe.

cards.title: Energia e massa
cards.text: A relatividade restrita também deu origem a E = mc². Numa reação nuclear, os produtos pesam ligeiramente menos do que o material inicial; a massa em falta transformou-se em energia.

deep.x: E = mc² means every form of energy has mass, and mass is a form of energy. Most of the time the effect is far too small to notice. In nuclear reactions it becomes obvious.
The missing mass in fusion

x: 4 hydrogen atoms: 4.0313 mass units
1 helium-4 atom: 4.0026 mass units
Difference: 0.0287, about 0.7%
That 0.7% becomes the Sun's energy

deep.x: Binding energy

The energy holding a nucleus together shows up as missing mass. Iron and nickel nuclei are the most tightly bound, which is why light nuclei release energy by fusing towards iron and heavy nuclei by splitting towards it.
Everyday mass changes

x: A hot cup of coffee weighs slightly more than when it's cold
A wound-up spring weighs slightly more than an unwound one
Burning petrol: the exhaust weighs about one part in ten billion less than fuel plus oxygen

deep.x: All true, but far too small for any scale to detect.
Most of your body's mass doesn't come from the mass of quarks at all. Over 98% of a proton's mass is the energy of the quarks and the gluon fields binding them.
Mass is stored energy: in nuclear reactions the products weigh less, and the difference is the energy released.

quiz.q: O que se mantém igual para todos os observadores na relatividade?
options: A velocidade da luz no vácuo
quiz.explain: Tudo o resto se ajusta à volta dela.
