quiz.explain: Sem correção, os erros crescem ~10 km por dia.

quiz.q: Segundo a relatividade geral, a gravidade é…
options: A curvatura do espaço-tempo causada pela massa
quiz.explain: A massa curva o espaço-tempo.

lessons.title: O mundo quântico
lessons.summary: Como as coisas minúsculas se comportam de forma muito estranha.

cards.title: A energia vem em pacotes
cards.text: A escalas pequenas, a energia não é contínua: vem em pacotes chamados quanta. A luz é feita de fotões, cada um com uma energia definida pela sua frequência. Os fotões azuis transportam mais energia do que os vermelhos.

deep.x: In 1900 Max Planck was trying to explain the colours of light given off by hot objects, such as a glowing iron bar. The classical theory predicted absurd results: infinite energy at ultraviolet wavelengths. Planck fixed the maths by assuming energy could only be emitted in chunks, which he called quanta. He thought it was a trick; it turned out to be how nature works.
E = h × f
Colour sets the packet size

Higher frequency means more energetic photons. That is why ultraviolet light can damage skin cells and cause sunburn while a much brighter red lamp cannot: each UV photon carries enough energy to break chemical bonds in DNA.

x: Red light: f ≈ 4.3 × 10¹⁴ Hz
About 1.8 electronvolts per photon

deep.x: Why we don't notice
Each photon is tiny. A small 5 milliwatt laser pointer sends out roughly 15 million billion photons every second, so the light looks perfectly smooth.
Photographers' darkrooms used red safelights because red photons don't carry enough energy to trigger the chemistry in photographic paper.

deep.w: Brighter light means more energetic photons
deep.r: Brightness is the number of photons; colour (frequency) sets the energy of each one

deep.x: Light is delivered in packets, and its colour decides how much energy each packet carries.

cards.title: O efeito fotoelétrico
cards.text: Ilumina um metal e a luz pode arrancar-lhe eletrões, mas só se cada fotão tiver energia suficiente. Uma luz azul fraca funciona; uma luz vermelha intensa pode não funcionar. Einstein explicou isto em 1905, o que lhe valeu o Prémio Nobel.

deep.x: Heinrich Hertz noticed in 1887 that ultraviolet light helped sparks jump between metal electrodes. Later experiments showed the light was knocking electrons out of the metal, and the details made no sense if light were just a wave.
The puzzle
Einstein's answer (1905)

Light arrives as photons. One photon gives all its energy to one electron. If that energy is less than the metal's "work function", the energy needed to escape, no electron leaves however many photons arrive. Brighter light means more photons, so more electrons, but not faster ones.
electron energy = photon energy − work function
Recognition

Robert Millikan spent ten years testing Einstein's equation, half expecting to disprove it, and instead confirmed it in 1916. Einstein's Nobel Prize, for 1921, was awarded for this work, not for relativity, which was still considered controversial.
Everywhere today

x: Solar panels turn photons into electric current (a close cousin, the photovoltaic effect)
Camera sensors in phones count photons pixel by pixel
Night-vision devices and photomultipliers amplify single photons

deep.x: Caesium releases electrons with visible light because its work function is only about 2 eV; zinc needs ultraviolet, over 4 eV.
One photon frees one electron, but only if that single photon has enough energy.

cards.title: Dualidade onda–partícula
cards.text: A luz e os eletrões comportam-se umas vezes como partículas e outras como ondas. Dispara eletrões um a um através de duas fendas e, mesmo assim, formam um padrão de interferência de ondas.

deep.x: In 1801 Thomas Young shone light through two narrow slits and saw stripes of light and dark on a screen. That is **interference**, waves adding where crests meet and cancelling where crest meets trough. It seemed to prove light was a wave, until Einstein's photons.
Matter waves

In 1924 Louis de Broglie proposed that particles also behave as waves, with a wavelength that shrinks as momentum grows. In 1927 electrons fired at a nickel crystal were found to diffract exactly like waves.
wavelength = h ÷ momentum
One at a time

In 1989 Akira Tonomura's team at Hitachi sent electrons through a double-slit device so slowly that only one was in the apparatus at a time. Each arrived as a single dot. But over thousands of arrivals, the dots built up interference stripes. Each electron behaved as a wave passing through both slits, then landed as a particle.
Look and it changes
If you add a detector to see which slit each electron uses, the stripes vanish and you get two plain bands. Gaining "which-path" information destroys the interference.
Interference has been shown with molecules of up to about 2,000 atoms. Electron microscopes rely on electrons' tiny wavelength to see details far smaller than light allows.
Everything small travels like a wave and arrives like a particle.

cards.title: Incerteza
cards.text: Heisenberg mostrou que não é possível conhecer ao mesmo tempo a posição exata e o momento exato de uma partícula. Quanto mais rigor tens num, mais difuso fica o outro.

deep.x: In 1927 Werner Heisenberg, aged 25, showed that a particle's position and momentum can't both have exact values at the same time. This isn't about clumsy instruments; it follows from particles being waves. A wave spread over a small region contains a wide mix of wavelengths, so its momentum is blurry, and vice versa.
Δx × Δp ≥ h ÷ 4π
Why atoms don't collapse

x: Electron confined to an atom, Δx ≈ 0.1 nm
Δp ≥ about 5 × 10⁻²⁵ kg·m/s
Divide by electron mass
Speed spread ≈ 600 km/s

deep.x: Squeeze an electron closer to the nucleus and its momentum spread, and so its energy, shoots up. This is why electrons don't spiral into the nucleus and why atoms have the size they do.
Why footballs are unaffected
Planck's constant is so tiny that for anything you can see, the uncertainty is far below anything measurable.
Because of uncertainty, particles can never be completely still. That "zero-point" jiggling is why helium stays liquid even at absolute zero unless squeezed.

deep.w: Uncertainty means measuring disturbs the particle
deep.r: Measurement can disturb things, but the principle is deeper: a particle doesn't have both exact values to begin with

deep.x: The more sharply a particle's position is defined, the more spread out its momentum must be.

cards.title: Sobreposição
cards.text: Um sistema quântico pode estar numa combinação de estados até ser medido. O spin de um eletrão pode estar "para cima e para baixo" ao mesmo tempo; medi-lo dá uma resposta definida, com probabilidades determinadas pelo estado.

deep.x: In quantum theory a system's state can be a blend of possibilities. An electron's spin, a kind of built-in magnetism, can be "up", "down", or a superposition of both. The state assigns each outcome a weight; squaring it gives the probability. This rule was set out by Max Born in 1926.
What measuring does

Measure, and you always get one definite result. Repeat the experiment with identically prepared electrons and the results follow the probabilities. Before measurement, the electron isn't secretly up or down; experiments rule out that kind of hidden answer in many situations.
Schrödinger's cat

In 1935 Erwin Schrödinger imagined a cat in a box whose fate depends on a single decaying atom. If the atom is in superposition, is the cat both alive and dead? He meant it as a criticism, to show how strange the theory sounds when scaled up.
Why we don't see it

Large objects constantly interact with air molecules and light, which effectively measures them. This process, **decoherence**, destroys superpositions almost instantly. Keeping superpositions alive is the main challenge in building quantum computers.

deep.w: The cat really is half alive
deep.r: Schrödinger used the cat to mock a naive reading; a cat is constantly decohered by its surroundings

deep.x: A quantum system holds several possibilities at once until an interaction forces one outcome.

cards.title: Entrelaçamento

items.a: mensagens mais rápidas que a luz

cards.text: Duas partículas podem ficar ligadas de modo que medir uma te diz instantaneamente algo sobre a outra, por mais longe que estejam. Einstein chamou-lhe "ação fantasmagórica à distância". Não permite enviar mensagens mais depressa do que a luz.

deep.x: When two particles interact in certain ways, they can share a single quantum state. Measure one and you instantly know what the matching measurement on the other will show, even if it's on the other side of the planet.
Einstein's objection

In 1935 Einstein, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen argued this meant quantum theory was incomplete: the particles must carry hidden instructions from the start. In 1964 John Bell found a way to test that idea. If hidden instructions were real, certain correlations could never exceed a limit.
The verdict

Experiments by John Clauser, Alain Aspect and Anton Zeilinger broke Bell's limit again and again, in line with quantum theory. They shared the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics. Nature is not "locally" pre-programmed in the way Einstein hoped.
No faster-than-light messages

Each side's results, on their own, look completely random. Only when the two lists are compared, using an ordinary signal, does the correlation appear. So entanglement can't send information faster than light.
In 2017 China's Micius satellite sent entangled photons to ground stations about 1,200 km apart. The EU's EuroQCI project, which includes Portugal, is building quantum-secured communication links.
Entangled particles share one state: their results match across any distance, yet no message can ride on them.

cards.title: Efeito túnel
cards.text: Às vezes, as partículas conseguem atravessar barreiras que, pela física clássica, não conseguiriam ultrapassar. O efeito túnel está por trás da fusão no Sol, das memórias flash e dos microscópios de efeito túnel.

deep.x: Roll a ball at a hill without enough speed and it rolls back. A quantum particle is a wave, and part of the wave leaks into the barrier and out the other side. So there's a chance the particle simply appears beyond it, even without enough energy to climb over.
Thin barriers only
The chance falls off steeply with the barrier's width and height. For an electron, a barrier a few atoms thick is passable; for anything you can see, the odds are effectively zero.
Where it matters

x: **The Sun**: protons in the core don't have enough energy to touch. Tunnelling lets a few fuse, enough to power the Sun for 10 billion years
**Alpha decay**: George Gamow explained in 1928 how alpha particles escape nuclei by tunnelling, which accounts for the huge range of half-lives
**Flash memory**: in USB sticks and phones, electrons tunnel through a thin insulating layer to store bits
**Microscopes**: the scanning tunnelling microscope images individual atoms

deep.x: A limit for chips
As transistors shrink to a few nanometres, electrons tunnel through barriers meant to stop them, leaking current and wasting power. Chipmakers redesign transistors partly to fight this.
Without tunnelling, the Sun's core would need to be roughly a thousand times hotter for fusion to proceed at its actual rate. Life on Earth depends on a quantum leak.
Particles can cross barriers they lack the energy to climb, and that leak powers the stars.

cards.title: O quântico no teu bolso
cards.text: A física quântica não é exótica: transístores, lasers, LED, células solares, aparelhos de ressonância magnética e os relógios atómicos do GPS dependem todos dela.

deep.x: Quantum physics can sound remote, but it's built into most of the technology you use. Understanding how electrons behave in solids led to the electronics revolution.
The transistor

Silicon conducts in a controlled way because of how quantum rules arrange electron energies into "bands". The transistor, invented at Bell Labs in 1947, uses this to switch current on and off. A modern phone chip holds around 15–20 billion of them, each a few tens of atoms across in key dimensions.
Light and medicine

x: **Lasers** read barcodes, carry internet data along fibres and perform eye surgery
**LEDs** emit a colour set by their band gap; the blue LED, which made white LED lighting possible, won the 2014 Nobel Prize
**MRI scanners** flip the spins of hydrogen nuclei in your body and listen to the radio signals they give back

deep.x: Timekeeping
Since 1967 the second has been defined by the frequency of a quantum jump in caesium atoms. Atomic clocks keep GPS and Galileo working, and timestamp phone networks and financial trades.
Solar panels, digital cameras, smoke detectors, fibre-optic internet and the hard drive in a data centre all depend on quantum effects.
Quantum physics isn't exotic: it's the hidden engine of almost every electronic device.

cards.title: Computadores quânticos
cards.text: Os computadores quânticos usam qubits, que podem estar em sobreposição e entrelaçados. Para certos problemas, como simular moléculas ou quebrar alguma encriptação, poderiam superar em muito os computadores normais, mas construir computadores grandes e fiáveis é muito difícil.

deep.x: A normal bit is 0 or 1. A **qubit** can be in a superposition of both, and many qubits can be entangled. A quantum computer manipulates these combined states so that wrong answers cancel out through interference and right ones are reinforced.
Describing 300 qubits exactly would take more numbers than there are atoms in the observable universe (about 10⁸⁰).
What they'd be good at

x: Simulating molecules and materials, for drugs, batteries and fertilisers
Breaking widely used public-key encryption, using Shor's algorithm (1994)
Some optimisation and search problems, though the speed-ups are often modest

deep.x: Why it's hard

Qubits are fragile: heat, vibration and stray signals cause errors. Superconducting qubits are cooled to about −273 °C, colder than outer space. Error correction combines many physical qubits into one reliable "logical" qubit. In 2024 Google's Willow chip showed errors falling as more qubits were added, a key milestone.
Preparing now

Because encrypted data stolen today could be decrypted later, governments are moving to "post-quantum" encryption. The US standards body published the first such standards in 2024, and the EU wants critical systems switched by the early 2030s.

deep.w: Quantum computers try every answer at once
deep.r: They can't simply read out all answers; algorithms must use interference cleverly, so they help only for specific problems

deep.x: Quantum computers won't replace laptops, but for a few important problems they could do what no normal machine can.

cards.title: Os fundadores da teoria quântica
cards.text: Planck (1900), Einstein (1905), Bohr (1913), Heisenberg e Schrödinger (1925–26) construíram a mecânica quântica em cerca de 25 anos. É a teoria testada com mais precisão em toda a ciência.

deep.x: Quantum mechanics was built in a burst, mostly by young physicists in Europe. Heisenberg was 23 when he made his breakthrough, and Paul Dirac 26 when he wrote his equation. Older colleagues nicknamed it "Knabenphysik", boys' physics.
Other key builders

x: **Louis de Broglie** (1924): matter waves
**Wolfgang Pauli** (1925): no two electrons in the same state, which explains the periodic table
**Max Born** (1926): the wave tells you probabilities
**Paul Dirac** (1928): merged quantum theory with special relativity and predicted antimatter, found in 1932

deep.x: Arguments that shaped it

At the 1927 Solvay Conference in Brussels, Einstein and Bohr began a famous, friendly debate. Einstein, uneasy with chance at the heart of physics, said God does not play dice; Bohr defended the new theory. Of the 29 people in the conference photograph, 17 were or later became Nobel laureates.
How precise?
Quantum electrodynamics predicts the electron's magnetism and it matches experiment to about one part in a trillion, the most precise agreement in science.

deep.w: Quantum theory is just a speculative idea
deep.r: It is the best-tested theory in physics and underpins chemistry, electronics and lasers

deep.x: A generation of physicists rewrote the rules of nature in 25 years, and every test since has backed them.

quiz.q: Porque é que uma luz azul fraca consegue arrancar eletrões e uma luz vermelha intensa não?
options: Cada fotão azul transporta mais energia
A luz vermelha é mais lenta
quiz.explain: A energia do fotão depende da frequência.

quiz.q: O que acontece quando medes uma partícula em sobreposição?
quiz.explain: A medição dá um único resultado.

quiz.q: Que tecnologia do dia a dia depende da física quântica?
quiz.explain: Os semicondutores são dispositivos quânticos.

lessons.title: O Sistema Solar
lessons.summary: O nosso Sol, oito planetas e muito mais.

cards.title: O Sol
cards.text: O Sol é uma estrela comum, com 109 vezes o diâmetro da Terra, e concentra 99,8% da massa do Sistema Solar. Funde cerca de 600 milhões de toneladas de hidrogénio em hélio a cada segundo.

deep.x: The Sun holds about 99.8% of all the mass in the Solar System, roughly 333,000 times Earth's. Everything else, from Jupiter to the smallest grain of dust, is a crumb by comparison.
Layers of the Sun

Energy made in the core takes a very long time to stagger out through the dense radiative zone, then rises by convection. The visible surface, the photosphere, looks granular, like boiling rice, with cells about the size of Portugal.
The surprising corona

Strangely, the thin outer atmosphere, the corona, is hundreds of times hotter than the surface. Magnetic fields are thought to carry energy up and release it, and missions like NASA's Parker Solar Probe and ESA's Solar Orbiter are investigating exactly how.
An active star

x: Sunspots are cooler, darker regions where magnetic fields poke through
Their number rises and falls over an 11-year cycle; the latest peak came around 2024–25
Flares and coronal mass ejections fling charged particles into space

deep.x: In May 2024 the strongest geomagnetic storm in two decades produced auroras visible as far south as Portugal and Spain, a rare sight at these latitudes.

deep.w: The Sun is on fire
deep.r: There is no burning; it shines by nuclear fusion, which needs no oxygen

deep.x: The Sun dominates the Solar System by mass and energy, and its magnetic moods reach all the way to Earth.

cards.title: Oito planetas
cards.text: Quatro pequenos planetas rochosos (Mercúrio, Vénus, Terra, Marte) e quatro gigantes (Júpiter e Saturno, de gás; Úrano e Neptuno, de gelo). Plutão foi reclassificado como planeta anão em 2006.

deep.x: The planets formed from a disc of gas and dust around the young Sun. Close in, it was too hot for ice, so only rock and metal could clump together, giving small rocky planets. Beyond the "frost line", between Mars and Jupiter, ice was plentiful, cores grew big enough to grab huge amounts of gas, and giants formed.
Sizes compared
What happened to Pluto?

In 2005 astronomers found Eris, beyond Pluto and about as large. Either the Solar System had many more planets, or the definition needed tightening. In 2006 the International Astronomical Union in Prague agreed a planet must:

x: orbit the Sun
be massive enough to be pulled into a round shape
have cleared its orbital neighbourhood of other bodies

deep.x: Pluto fails the third test, since it shares its zone with many Kuiper Belt objects. It became a **dwarf planet**, alongside Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.
In 2015 NASA's New Horizons flew past Pluto and found mountains of water ice, nitrogen glaciers and a heart-shaped plain, a far livelier world than expected.
Rocky worlds formed near the hot Sun, giants formed out where ice could survive, and Pluto belongs to a crowd of icy dwarfs.

cards.title: Distâncias
cards.text: As distâncias medem-se em unidades astronómicas (UA): 1 UA é a distância Terra–Sol, cerca de 150 milhões de km. Neptuno está a cerca de 30 UA; a luz demora mais de 4 horas a lá chegar.

deep.x: Space distances are so big that kilometres become unwieldy. The **astronomical unit** (AU), the average Earth–Sun distance, is fixed at exactly 149,597,870.7 km, about 150 million km.
Travelling at light speed
A model you can walk

x: Shrink the Sun to a football 22 cm wide
Earth becomes a 2 mm peppercorn 24 m away
Neptune: a 8 mm bead 700 m away
Nearest star: another football 6,400 km away

deep.x: On that scale, the nearest star would be further away than Lisbon is from New York. The Solar System is almost entirely empty space.
Talking to spacecraft

Mission controllers must plan around these delays. A command to a Mars rover takes between 3 and 22 minutes to arrive, depending on where the planets are. Voyager 1, more than 160 AU away, waits nearly a day for each message.
The planets in pictures are always drawn close together. In reality, all eight would fit in the gap between Earth and the Moon, with room to spare.
The Solar System is vast and mostly empty: light from the Sun takes hours to reach its outer planets.

cards.title: Vénus: a estufa
cards.text: Vénus tem um tamanho mais próximo do da Terra, mas uma atmosfera espessa de CO₂ com uma pressão esmagadora de 90 bar e temperaturas à superfície de cerca de 465 °C, mais quente do que Mercúrio.

deep.x: Venus is Earth's near twin in size, about 95% of its diameter, and formed from similar material. Yet its surface is the most hostile in the Solar System for a landing probe.
A runaway greenhouse

Venus probably once had more water. Being closer to the Sun, it warmed, water evaporated, and water vapour, itself a greenhouse gas, trapped more heat. Eventually the oceans boiled away, and with no liquid water to lock carbon into rocks, CO₂ built up into a crushing atmosphere. Today its thick clouds of sulphuric acid reflect most sunlight, yet the trapped heat keeps the surface hot enough to melt lead.
Strange rotation
Venus spins backwards compared with most planets, and very slowly: one rotation takes 243 Earth days, longer than its 225-day year.
Visiting Venus
Soviet Venera probes landed in the 1970s and 80s. The longest survived about two hours before heat and pressure destroyed it. New missions are planned for the 2030s, including ESA's EnVision.
The pressure on Venus's surface equals being about 900 m deep in Earth's ocean.

deep.w: Mercury is hottest because it's closest to the Sun
deep.r: Venus is hotter, day and night, because its thick CO₂ atmosphere traps heat

deep.x: Venus shows what a runaway greenhouse effect can do to an Earth-sized planet.

cards.title: Marte
cards.text: Marte é um deserto frio com uma atmosfera fina de CO₂, o maior vulcão do Sistema Solar (Olympus Mons) e indícios de rios e lagos antigos. Robôs como o Perseverance procuram sinais de vida passada.

deep.x: Mars is about half Earth's width and has 38% of its gravity, so you would weigh about a third as much there. Its red colour comes from iron oxide, rust, in its dust. Its air is about 1% as dense as Earth's, and mostly CO₂.
Giant landscapes

x: **Olympus Mons** is about 22 km high, two and a half times Everest, and around 600 km wide, about the length of mainland Portugal
**Valles Marineris** is a canyon system some 4,000 km long, which would stretch across Europe
Polar caps of water ice and frozen CO₂ grow and shrink with the seasons

deep.x: A wetter past

Dried riverbeds, deltas and minerals that form only in water show that Mars had lakes and rivers over 3 billion years ago. It lost much of its atmosphere, likely because its magnetic field died and the solar wind stripped gas away, and its surface water froze or escaped.
Searching for life

Perseverance landed in Jezero crater in 2021, an ancient lake with a river delta. It has been collecting rock samples in sealed tubes. In 2025 NASA reported one rock's chemical patterns as possible signs of past microbial life, but such features can also form without life, and confirming it would need the samples back on Earth.
Perseverance carried a small helicopter, Ingenuity, which made 72 flights, the first powered flights on another world.
Mars was once warm and wet enough for rivers; whether life ever began there is one of science's biggest questions.

cards.title: Júpiter e Saturno

items.b: anéis de gelo, menos denso que a água

cards.text: Júpiter é tão grande que todos os outros planetas caberiam lá dentro. A sua Grande Mancha Vermelha é uma tempestade maior do que a Terra. Os anéis de Saturno são feitos de pedaços de gelo, e Saturno flutuaria numa banheira gigante: a sua densidade média é inferior à da água.

deep.x: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets put together. About 1,300 Earths would fit inside it. It spins in under 10 hours, the fastest of any planet, which flattens it visibly at the poles.
The Great Red Spot

This storm has raged for at least 190 years, and possibly since the 1600s. Its winds blow at hundreds of km/h. It has been shrinking: once wide enough for three Earths, it's now a little larger than one.
Saturn's rings

The rings span about 280,000 km but are typically only about 10 m thick, thinner, relative to their width, than a sheet of paper. They are mostly chunks of water ice, from dust grains to house-sized boulders. Their age is debated; some evidence suggests they could be far younger than Saturn.
Would Saturn really float?

x: Water density: 1.0 g/cm³
Saturn's average density: 0.69 g/cm³
In a big enough bathtub, it would float

deep.x: Galileo first saw Saturn's rings in 1610 through his small telescope but couldn't make them out, describing Saturn as having "ears".

deep.w: Gas giants are just big balls of gas
deep.r: Deep down, the gas is squeezed into liquid, and Jupiter's interior holds metallic hydrogen that generates a powerful magnetic field

deep.x: Jupiter dominates the planets by mass, while Saturn, lighter than water on average, wears the Solar System's finest rings.

cards.title: Luas

steps: Corpo do tamanho de Marte atinge a Terra

cards.text: O Sistema Solar tem centenas de luas conhecidas. A nossa Lua formou-se provavelmente quando um corpo do tamanho de Marte chocou com a Terra jovem, há cerca de 4,5 mil milhões de anos.

deep.x: Mercury and Venus have no moons; Earth has one; Mars has two tiny ones. The giants have dozens each: Saturn has over 270 known and Jupiter close to 100, most of them small captured rocks a few kilometres wide.
How our Moon formed

Evidence for this giant impact: Moon rocks brought back by Apollo have almost the same oxygen isotope mix as Earth's mantle, the Moon has only a small iron core, and its surface was once a global ocean of magma.
The Moon is leaving

Lasers bounced off mirrors left by Apollo astronauts show the Moon drifting away by about 3.8 cm a year. Tides slow Earth's spin, and the Moon gains that energy. Days are lengthening by about 2 milliseconds per century.
Worlds in their own right

Europa and Saturn's Enceladus hide salty oceans beneath their ice, among the best places to look for life. NASA's Europa Clipper (launched 2024) and ESA's JUICE (launched 2023) are on their way to Jupiter's moons.
The Moon is about 400 times smaller than the Sun but also about 400 times closer, which is why it can just cover the Sun in a total eclipse, like the one crossing northern Spain in August 2026.
Our Moon was probably born in a giant collision, and moons elsewhere include some of the Solar System's most promising places for life.

cards.title: Asteroides e cometas
cards.text: A cintura de asteroides entre Marte e Júpiter guarda restos rochosos. Os cometas são corpos gelados do Sistema Solar exterior que ganham caudas brilhantes quando se aproximam do Sol.

deep.x: Asteroids and comets are leftover building blocks from 4.6 billion years ago. Asteroids are rocky or metallic and mostly orbit between Mars and Jupiter, where Jupiter's gravity stopped them forming a planet. Comets are icy and come from far out.
The belt is empty

Films show asteroids packed close together, but the main belt is mostly empty. Its total mass is only about 3% of the Moon's, and a third of that is the dwarf planet Ceres. Spacecraft pass through without dodging.
Comet tails

As a comet nears the Sun, ice turns straight to gas, releasing dust. It forms two tails, both pointing away from the Sun: a curved dust tail and a straight blue tail of charged gas blown by the solar wind.
Planetary defence

On 26 September 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into the small asteroid Dimorphos and shortened its orbit around its partner by about 32 minutes: the first test of nudging an asteroid. ESA's Hera mission is following up.
Meteor showers, like the Perseids peaking around 12 August, happen when Earth passes through dust left by comets. Each "shooting star" is a grain often smaller than a grain of sand.
Asteroids and comets are the Solar System's leftover scraps, and we can now nudge one off course.

cards.title: Estações noutros planetas
cards.text: Os planetas com eixos inclinados têm estações. Úrano está deitado de lado, por isso cada polo tem cerca de 42 anos de luz solar contínua seguidos de 42 anos de escuridão.

deep.x: Seasons come from a planet's tilt, not its distance from the Sun. When your hemisphere tilts towards the Sun, sunlight arrives more directly and days are longer. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of the northern winter.
Uranus on its side
Uranus is tilted 98°, probably knocked over by an ancient collision. During its 84-year orbit, each pole points almost straight at the Sun for part of the year, then away.

x: Uranus year: 84 Earth years
Each pole: half the orbit in light
84 ÷ 2 = 42 years
Then 42 years of darkness

deep.x: Elsewhere

x: **Mars** has a similar tilt to Earth, so similar seasons, but each lasts about twice as long; its elongated orbit makes southern summers hotter
**Saturn** and **Neptune** have seasons lasting 7 and about 40 years
**Jupiter**, barely tilted, has almost no seasons
**Mercury**, with almost no tilt, has craters at its poles never touched by sunlight, holding ice despite being closest to the Sun

deep.w: Summer happens when Earth is closest to the Sun
deep.r: Earth is closest in January; seasons come from the tilt, which is why hemispheres have opposite seasons

deep.x: Tilt, not distance, makes seasons, and a planet tipped on its side gets decades-long days and nights.

cards.title: Idade
cards.text: O Sistema Solar formou-se há cerca de 4,6 mil milhões de anos a partir de uma nuvem de gás e poeira em colapso. Os meteoritos dão as datas mais precisas.

deep.x: The Solar System is about 4.57 billion years old. The most precise date comes from tiny white grains in meteorites called calcium-aluminium-rich inclusions, the first solids to condense from the cloud around the newborn Sun.
How do we date it?

Radioactive uranium decays into lead at known rates. Measuring the ratio of uranium to lead isotopes in meteorite grains gives their age. In 1956 Clair Patterson used lead in a meteorite to calculate Earth's age at about 4.55 billion years, a figure that has barely changed since.
Clues from the beginning

x: Meteorites are unchanged leftovers, unlike Earth's constantly recycled crust
The oldest Earth crystals, zircons from western Australia, are about 4.4 billion years old
Traces of short-lived isotopes in meteorites suggest a nearby exploding star may have helped trigger the cloud's collapse

deep.x: Watching it happen elsewhere
Radio telescopes such as ALMA in Chile have imaged young stars surrounded by dusty discs with gaps, where planets are being born right now, as our own system once was.
While measuring lead, Patterson discovered how much lead pollution from petrol was everywhere, and his campaign helped get leaded petrol banned; the EU phased it out by 2000.
Meteorites are time capsules from the Solar System's birth, and their radioactive clocks give its age: about 4.57 billion years.

quiz.q: Qual é o planeta mais quente?
quiz.explain: A sua espessa atmosfera de CO₂ retém o calor.

quiz.q: Quanto é 1 UA?
quiz.explain: A distância média Terra–Sol.

quiz.q: Porque é que Plutão foi reclassificado em 2006?
options: Passou a ser considerado um planeta anão
quiz.explain: Não limpa a sua órbita de outros corpos.

lessons.title: Estrelas e galáxias
lessons.summary: Como as estrelas vivem e morrem, e qual é o tamanho do universo.

cards.title: O que é uma estrela
cards.text: Uma estrela é uma bola gigante de gás quente mantida pela sua própria gravidade, que brilha porque a fusão nuclear no seu núcleo converte hidrogénio em hélio.

deep.x: Stars are born inside cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae. A denser clump starts to collapse under its own gravity, heating up as it shrinks. When the core reaches about 10 million °C, hydrogen nuclei slam together hard enough to fuse, and a star switches on.
A balancing act

For most of its life a star is stable because two forces cancel. Gravity pulls every layer inwards; the pressure of hot gas, fed by fusion, pushes outwards. If fusion speeds up, the star swells and cools slightly, and fusion slows again. Astronomers call this **hydrostatic equilibrium**.
How small, how big

x: The lightest stars have about 8% of the Sun's mass, roughly 80 Jupiters. Below that, the core never gets hot enough: you get a failed star, a **brown dwarf**.
The heaviest known stars have over 100 times the Sun's mass.
Most stars are small, dim **red dwarfs**, about three in four. Not one is visible to the naked eye.

deep.w: Stars are giant fires
deep.r: Fire is chemistry that needs oxygen; stars shine by fusing atomic nuclei, millions of times more energy per kilo

deep.x: Many stars are not alone: a large share of Sun-like stars have a companion star, orbiting together as a pair.
A star is a long tug-of-war between gravity squeezing in and fusion pushing out.

cards.title: Anos-luz
cards.text: Um ano-luz é a distância que a luz percorre num ano: cerca de 9,5 biliões de km. A estrela mais próxima depois do Sol, Próxima do Centauro, está a 4,2 anos-luz.

deep.x: Despite the name, a light-year measures distance, not time. Light crosses about 300,000 km every second, the fastest anything can travel, and a year contains about 31.6 million seconds.

x: 300,000 km/s × 31.6 million s
1 light-year ≈ 9.5 trillion km

deep.x: A ladder of light-times
The same idea works for shorter hops, and it gives a feel for the emptiness of space.
Our nearest neighbour

Proxima Centauri is a small red dwarf, too faint to see without a telescope. It belongs to a triple system with Alpha Centauri A and B, which together look like one bright star from the southern sky. That gap of 4.2 light-years is about 40 trillion km.

x: Voyager 1 travels at about 17 km/s
40 trillion km ÷ 17 km/s ≈ 2.4 trillion s
About 75,000 years to reach Proxima

deep.x: Professional astronomers often use the **parsec** instead, about 3.26 light-years, which comes from how far a star seems to shift as Earth orbits the Sun.

deep.w: A light-year is a long time
deep.r: It is a distance: how far light goes in a year

deep.x: A light-year is a distance so large that our fastest spacecraft would need tens of thousands of years to cross one to the nearest star.

cards.title: As cores das estrelas
cards.text: A cor de uma estrela revela a sua temperatura: as estrelas vermelhas são mais frias (cerca de 3000 °C), o nosso Sol amarelo tem cerca de 5500 °C e as estrelas azuis mais de 20 000 °C.

deep.x: Heat anything enough and it glows. An electric hob ring glows dull red; a filament bulb is hotter and glows yellow-white. Stars follow the same physics: the hotter the surface, the more the light shifts towards blue. This is **Wien's law**: peak wavelength shrinks as temperature rises.
The star alphabet
Astronomers sort stars into classes by their spectra, from hottest to coolest: O, B, A, F, G, K, M. Generations of students have learnt it as "Oh Be A Fine Girl/Guy, Kiss Me". The Sun is a G star.

items: K, M: orange to red, cool

deep.x: See it yourself

On a winter night, find Orion. Betelgeuse at the top left shines orange-red; Rigel at the bottom right is blue-white. The difference is easy to see without a telescope, and it is a difference of thousands of degrees.

deep.w: Red means hot
deep.r: On taps red means hot, but among stars red is the coolest and blue the hottest

deep.x: There are no green stars. A star hot enough to peak in green also gives out plenty of red and blue, and the mix looks white to us. The Sun's light actually peaks in the green.
A star's colour is a thermometer you can read from trillions of kilometres away.

cards.title: A vida de uma estrela como o Sol
cards.text: Uma estrela como o Sol queima hidrogénio durante cerca de 10 mil milhões de anos, incha até se tornar uma gigante vermelha, liberta as camadas exteriores e acaba como anã branca. O Sol vai mais ou menos a meio.

deep.x: The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago and is roughly halfway through its hydrogen-burning life. It isn't static, though: it grows about 10% brighter every billion years as helium builds up in its core.
Running out of fuel

When the core hydrogen is used up, the core shrinks and heats while the outer layers swell enormously. The Sun will become a **red giant** perhaps 200 times its current width, swallowing Mercury and Venus. Whether Earth is engulfed is still uncertain. Later the core fuses helium into carbon and oxygen.
The quiet end

The outer layers are puffed away into a glowing shell called a **planetary nebula**. The name is a historical mistake: through 18th-century telescopes they looked like round planets. What is left is a white dwarf, a carbon-oxygen core about the size of Earth.

x: A white dwarf has about half the Sun's mass
Squeezed into an Earth-sized ball
A teaspoon would weigh several tonnes

deep.x: With no fusion, a white dwarf just slowly cools. It takes so long to fade to a cold "black dwarf" that the universe isn't yet old enough for any to exist.
The Sun will die gently, not with a bang: a swollen red giant, then a fading white ember the size of Earth.

cards.title: As estrelas massivas explodem

steps: Estrela de neutrões ou buraco negro

cards.text: As estrelas com muitas vezes a massa do Sol queimam depressa e depois colapsam e explodem como supernovas, deixando estrelas de neutrões ou buracos negros. As explosões espalham elementos pesados pelo espaço.

deep.x: Big stars live fast. Their huge weight makes the core hotter and denser, so fusion runs far faster. A star of 20 solar masses burns through its fuel in about 10 million years, a thousandth of the Sun's lifespan.
An onion of elements

As each fuel runs out, the core fuses heavier elements: helium, then carbon, neon, oxygen and silicon. The star ends up layered like an onion. The process stops at **iron**, because fusing iron absorbs energy instead of releasing it.
Collapse and rebound

Once the iron core passes about 1.4 solar masses, nothing can hold it up. It collapses in under a second, the infalling layers bounce off the ultra-dense centre, and a flood of neutrinos helps blast the star apart. For a few weeks, a single supernova can outshine its whole galaxy.

The 1054 explosion was recorded by Chinese astronomers and was visible in daylight for weeks. Its remains are the Crab Nebula. In 1987, detectors in Japan and the USA caught about two dozen neutrinos from a supernova in a neighbouring galaxy, hours before its light was seen.

deep.w: Betelgeuse is about to explode
deep.r: It will go supernova, but "soon" for astronomers means sometime in the next 100,000 years or so

deep.x: Much of the iron in your blood and the oxygen you breathe was forged in stars and scattered by these explosions.
Massive stars build the heavy elements, then explode and seed space with the raw material for planets and people.

cards.title: Estrelas de neutrões
cards.text: Uma estrela de neutrões concentra mais do que a massa do Sol numa bola com cerca de 20 km de diâmetro. Uma colher de chá dela pesaria cerca de mil milhões de toneladas na Terra. Algumas rodam centenas de vezes por segundo, como pulsares.

deep.x: When a massive star's core collapses, electrons are forced into protons, turning them into neutrons. The result is a ball of almost pure neutrons, as dense as an atomic nucleus.

x: Density ≈ 200 million million kg per m³
A teaspoon is about 5 millilitres
≈ 1,000 billion kg = 1 billion tonnes

deep.x: Cosmic lighthouses
A collapsing core spins up like a skater pulling in her arms. Its magnetic field shoots beams from the magnetic poles; if a beam sweeps past Earth, we see regular pulses. That is a **pulsar**.
Discovery

In 1967 Jocelyn Bell, a PhD student at Cambridge, noticed a signal repeating every 1.3 seconds. It was so regular the team half-jokingly labelled it "LGM-1", for Little Green Men. The 1974 Nobel Prize went to her supervisor, Antony Hewish, and not to her, a decision still widely criticised.

x: Surface gravity is about 100 billion times Earth's
Magnetars have the strongest magnetic fields known
The fastest pulsar known spins 716 times a second

deep.x: In 2017 detectors saw gravitational waves from two neutron stars colliding. The blast made heavy elements such as gold and platinum, several Earth masses' worth.
A neutron star is the crushed core of a dead star: a city-sized atomic nucleus spinning like a top.

cards.title: A Via Láctea
cards.text: A nossa galáxia é uma espiral barrada com talvez 100–400 mil milhões de estrelas e cerca de 100 000 anos-luz de diâmetro. O Sol fica num braço exterior e demora cerca de 230 milhões de anos a dar a volta ao centro.

deep.x: From inside, our galaxy is a faint band of light across the sky. The ancient Greeks called it a river of milk, which gives us "galaxy" (from *gala*, milk) and the Portuguese **Via Láctea**. Galileo's telescope showed in 1610 that it is made of countless stars.
Its shape

Seen from outside, it would look like a flat disc with a central bar and spiral arms, only about 1,000 light-years thick. The Sun sits about 26,000 light-years from the centre, in a minor arm called the Orion Arm.
The heart

At the centre lies **Sagittarius A***, a black hole of about 4 million solar masses. Its existence was proved by tracking stars orbiting it, work that won the 2020 Nobel Prize, and it was imaged in 2022.

x: Sun's orbit ≈ 2 × π × 26,000 light-years
≈ 160,000 light-years round
At 230 km/s ≈ 230 million years per lap

deep.x: The last time the Sun was at this point in its orbit, the first dinosaurs were only just appearing.
Portugal's Alqueva region became the world's first certified "Starlight Tourism Destination" in 2011, one of the best places in Europe to see the Milky Way.
We live in the suburbs of a spinning spiral of hundreds of billions of stars, and we are carried around it at 230 km per second.

cards.title: Galáxias por todo o lado
cards.text: O universo observável contém entre centenas de milhares de milhões e cerca de dois biliões de galáxias. A galáxia de Andrómeda, a 2,5 milhões de anos-luz, vê-se a olho nu em noites escuras e vai fundir-se com a nossa daqui a cerca de 4–5 mil milhões de anos.

deep.x: A century ago, many astronomers thought the Milky Way was the whole universe and the fuzzy "spiral nebulae" were clouds inside it. In 1923–24 Edwin Hubble found a pulsating star in Andromeda whose brightness revealed its distance: far beyond our galaxy. Andromeda was a galaxy in its own right.
Shapes of galaxies
Counting them

In 1995 the Hubble Space Telescope stared for ten days at a patch of sky as small as a grain of sand at arm's length. It found about 3,000 galaxies. Scaled up across the whole sky, that suggests hundreds of billions; models of faint, unseen galaxies push estimates higher.
The coming merger

Andromeda is approaching at about 110 km/s. A head-on merger has long been predicted in 4–5 billion years, though a 2025 study using newer data put the odds of a merger in the next 10 billion years at only about one in two. Even if they merge, individual stars would almost never collide: the gaps between them are vast.

The two Magellanic Clouds, small galaxies visible from the southern hemisphere, are named after the Portuguese navigator Fernão de Magalhães, whose crew described them on the first voyage around the world.
The Milky Way is just one galaxy among hundreds of billions, each with its own hundreds of billions of stars.

cards.title: Olhar para o passado
cards.text: A luz demora tempo a viajar, por isso vemos os objetos distantes como eram. Vemos o Sol como era há 8 minutos e Andrómeda como era há 2,5 milhões de anos.

deep.x: Light is fast but not instant. Every time you look at something, you see it as it was when the light left it. Nearby, the delay is negligible. Across space, it becomes enormous.

x: Sun to Earth ≈ 150 million km
≈ 500 s ≈ 8.3 minutes

deep.x: A time machine for free

Astronomers use this delay. To study young galaxies, they look very far away, because that light set out when the universe was young. The farthest light of all, the cosmic microwave background, shows the universe about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
Nothing is "now"

Even on Earth there is a delay: you see a friend across the room as they were about ten billionths of a second ago. In space there is no single shared "now" you can observe; there is only the latest news to arrive.

deep.w: Many stars we see are already dead
deep.r: Almost every naked-eye star is within a few thousand light-years, so nearly all of them still shine

deep.x: When Andromeda's light now reaching your eye set off, our ancestors were early members of the human family in Africa, long before *Homo sapiens*.
The farther you look, the further back in time you see.

cards.title: Exoplanetas

steps: O planeta passa à frente da estrela
O brilho da estrela baixa um pouco

cards.text: Desde o primeiro confirmado, em 1995, à volta de uma estrela como o Sol, já se encontraram mais de 5000 planetas à volta de outras estrelas, sobretudo pelas minúsculas quebras de brilho quando passam à frente delas.

deep.x: For centuries, planets around other stars were pure speculation. The first confirmed ones, in 1992, orbit a pulsar. Then in 1995, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz in Geneva found 51 Pegasi b around a Sun-like star: a gas giant orbiting so close its "year" lasts just over four days. They shared the 2019 Nobel Prize.
How we find them
Planets are tiny and faint next to their stars, so most are detected indirectly.
The transit method
When a planet crosses its star, it blocks a fraction of the light equal to the ratio of their areas. NASA's Kepler (2009–2018) and TESS (from 2018) found thousands this way.

x: Jupiter is about 1/10 the Sun's width
Area ratio (1/10)² = 1/100
Starlight dims by about 1%

deep.x: Where things stand

The count passed 6,000 confirmed planets in 2025. Proxima b orbits our nearest star; TRAPPIST-1 has seven Earth-sized worlds. The James Webb telescope now reads some planets' atmospheres, and ESA's PLATO mission is being prepared to hunt Earth-like planets around Sun-like stars.
Portuguese astronomers in Porto and Lisbon helped build ESPRESSO, an instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope in Chile that detects stellar wobbles of a few tens of centimetres per second.
Planets are the rule, not the exception: most stars in the sky probably have at least one.

quiz.q: Um ano-luz mede…
quiz.explain: A distância que a luz percorre num ano.

quiz.q: Em que se vai tornar o Sol, um dia?
quiz.explain: Não tem massa suficiente para explodir.

quiz.q: Quando vemos Andrómeda, vemo-la como era…
options: Há cerca de 2,5 milhões de anos
quiz.explain: A sua luz demorou esse tempo a chegar.

lessons.title: O universo
lessons.summary: O Big Bang, a expansão e o que ainda não sabemos.

cards.title: Um universo em expansão
cards.text: Em 1929, Edwin Hubble descobriu que as galáxias distantes se estão a afastar de nós, tanto mais depressa quanto mais longe estão. O próprio espaço está a expandir-se, como pontos num balão a encher.

deep.x: From about 1912, Vesto Slipher measured the light of spiral nebulae and found most of it shifted towards red: they were moving away. In 1927 Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, showed expansion followed from Einstein's equations. In 1929 Edwin Hubble added distances and saw the pattern clearly.

x: Galaxy at 100 megaparsecs (326 million light-years)
Moving away at about 7,000 km/s

deep.x: Redshift: stretched light
As light travels through expanding space, its waves are stretched to longer, redder wavelengths. The amount of stretching tells astronomers how much the universe has grown since the light set out.
No centre
On a balloon covered in dots, every dot sees all the others moving away, with farther ones receding faster. No dot is the centre. The same is true of galaxies.

x: Things held together by gravity or electric forces don't expand: not you, not Earth, not the Milky Way
Nearby Andromeda is actually approaching us, because local gravity wins

deep.w: We are at the centre of the expansion
deep.r: Every galaxy sees the same pattern; there is no centre

deep.x: Since 2018 the rule is officially called the **Hubble–Lemaître law**, recognising Lemaître's earlier work.
Galaxies aren't flying through space away from us; space between them is growing.

cards.title: O Big Bang
cards.text: Andando com a expansão para trás, o universo foi em tempos extremamente quente e denso, há cerca de 13,8 mil milhões de anos. O Big Bang não foi uma explosão no espaço, mas a expansão do próprio espaço.

deep.x: If galaxies are rushing apart, they were once closer together. Run the film backwards and everything converges on a hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago. Lemaître called it the "primeval atom". The name "Big Bang" was coined by Fred Hoyle in a 1949 BBC radio talk; he favoured a rival "steady state" theory.
Not an explosion
An explosion happens at a point and throws debris into surrounding space. The Big Bang happened everywhere at once: all of space was hot and dense, and all of it has been expanding since.
Why we believe it

x: Galaxies are receding, as expansion predicts
The cosmic microwave background, leftover heat from the early universe
The amounts of hydrogen, helium and lithium match predictions
Distant galaxies look younger and different from nearby ones

deep.x: What it doesn't say
The theory describes how the universe evolved from a very early moment. It does not explain what, if anything, came "before", or why there was a universe at all.

deep.w: The Big Bang was a bomb going off in empty space
deep.r: There was no outside; space itself was expanding everywhere

deep.x: The Big Bang is not the explosion of a thing in space, but the expansion of space itself from a hot, dense past.

cards.title: A radiação cósmica de fundo
cards.text: Quando o universo arrefeceu o suficiente para se formarem átomos, a luz pôde viajar livremente. Essa luz, esticada até às micro-ondas, ainda enche o céu a 2,7 K. Foi descoberta por acaso em 1965.

deep.x: For its first 380,000 years the universe was a glowing fog of charged particles. Light couldn't travel far before bouncing off free electrons. When things cooled to about 3,000 °C, electrons joined nuclei to make neutral atoms, and the fog cleared. That light has been travelling ever since.
Stretched to microwaves
Since then the universe has grown about 1,100 times larger, and the light's wavelength with it. What was orange-yellow glow is now faint microwaves.

x: Released at about 3,000 K
Stretched about 1,100 times

deep.x: Found by accident

In 1965 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson at Bell Labs in the USA were troubled by a hiss in their radio antenna that came from every direction. They even cleaned out pigeon droppings. Nearby physicists had just realised what it must be. The pair won the 1978 Nobel Prize.
Ripples that became galaxies

The glow is uniform to about one part in 100,000. Those tiny ripples mark slightly denser regions which gravity later pulled into galaxies and clusters. ESA's Planck satellite mapped them in exquisite detail.
On an old analogue TV tuned between channels, about 1% of the "snow" was this leftover glow from the Big Bang.
The cosmic microwave background is the oldest light in the universe: a baby photo taken 380,000 years after the Big Bang.

cards.title: Matéria escura
cards.text: As galáxias rodam demasiado depressa para que a matéria visível as mantenha unidas. Algo invisível acrescenta gravidade extra: a matéria escura. Ninguém sabe ainda o que é.

deep.x: In 1933 Fritz Zwicky noticed galaxies in the Coma cluster moving so fast the cluster should fly apart. He proposed unseen "dark matter". In the 1970s Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured how fast stars orbit in spiral galaxies, and the evidence became hard to ignore.
The rotation puzzle
In the Solar System, outer planets orbit more slowly, because most mass is in the Sun. Galaxies should behave the same way. They don't: stars far out orbit as fast as those further in.
More evidence

In the Bullet Cluster, two clusters collided. The hot gas, most of the ordinary matter, slowed and piled up in the middle, but the gravity, mapped by how it bends background light, passed straight through. Something with mass but no light went its own way.
What could it be?

Leading ideas are new particles, such as WIMPs or axions. Sensitive detectors deep underground have searched for decades and found nothing yet. A minority of physicists think gravity itself may need modifying instead. ESA's Euclid telescope, launched in 2023, is mapping dark matter across a third of the sky.

deep.w: Dark matter is just dark gas and dust
deep.r: Ordinary gas absorbs or glows in some kind of light; dark matter doesn't interact with light at all

deep.x: There seems to be about five times more invisible matter than ordinary matter, and we only know it's there by its gravity.

cards.title: Energia escura
cards.text: Em 1998, os astrónomos descobriram que a expansão está a acelerar. Aquilo que a impulsiona chama-se energia escura. Constitui a maior parte do conteúdo energético do universo.

deep.x: In the 1990s two teams set out to measure how fast the expansion was slowing. They used a type of supernova that always peaks at about the same brightness, so how bright it looks reveals its distance. In 1998 they found the distant ones were too faint: farther away than expected. The expansion is speeding up.
Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess shared the 2011 Nobel Prize for the discovery.
What it might be

The simplest explanation is energy belonging to empty space itself, Einstein's **cosmological constant**. As space grows, there is more of it, so its push grows too. Gravity dominated until roughly 5 billion years ago; since then dark energy has taken over.
Thin but everywhere
Its density is tiny: equivalent to the mass of a few hydrogen atoms per cubic metre. But it fills all of space, so it adds up to most of the cosmos.
Still changing?
Results from the DESI survey in 2024–25 hinted that dark energy may be weakening over time. If confirmed, the cosmological constant would not be constant at all. The evidence is not yet conclusive.

deep.w: Everything we see makes up the universe
deep.r: Atoms, stars, planets and people are only about 5% of its energy content

deep.x: Most of the universe is a mysterious energy of empty space that is pushing galaxies apart ever faster.

cards.title: Que tamanho tem?
cards.text: O universo observável tem cerca de 93 mil milhões de anos-luz de diâmetro, mais do que 13,8 mil milhões × 2, porque o espaço se expandiu enquanto a luz viajava. Para lá dele, o universo pode ser infinito.

deep.x: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, so you might think we can see 13.8 billion light-years in every direction. But while the light was travelling, space kept expanding, carrying its source farther away.

x: Oldest light set off when its source was ~42 million ly away
Space then grew about 1,100 times
That source is now about 46 billion light-years away

items.l: radius of what we can see

deep.x: Faster than light?

Nothing can move through space faster than light. But space itself can expand faster, and over large distances it does. Galaxies beyond about 14 billion light-years are already receding faster than light, and we still see light they sent long ago.

items.w: Nothing can recede faster than light
items.r: Space can grow faster than light

deep.x: Beyond the edge

The "edge" is only the limit of our view, like the horizon at sea. Measurements show space is very nearly flat, so the whole universe is at least much larger than the part we see, and may be infinite.

x: Because of dark energy, light emitted today by galaxies over about 16 billion light-years away will never reach us
Every observer has their own observable universe, centred on them

deep.x: Over trillions of years, all galaxies outside our local group will slip beyond view. Astronomers then would see only one merged galaxy in an empty sky.
The observable universe is a bubble 93 billion light-years across, and the whole universe is at least far larger.

cards.title: Telescópios como máquinas do tempo
cards.text: O Telescópio Espacial James Webb, lançado em 2021, vê a luz infravermelha de galáxias formadas apenas algumas centenas de milhões de anos depois do Big Bang.

deep.x: The James Webb Space Telescope lifted off on 25 December 2021 on a European Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou, in French Guiana. It is a joint mission of NASA, ESA and the Canadian Space Agency. It orbits about 1.5 million km from Earth, hidden behind a sunshield the size of a tennis court.
Why infrared?

The first galaxies gave out ultraviolet and visible light. Over 13 billion years, expansion has stretched it deep into the infrared. Webb's mirror is coated in gold, which reflects infrared well, and it is kept below about −230 °C so its own warmth doesn't swamp the faint signals.
What it found

Webb has seen galaxies from about 300 million years after the Big Bang, and they are brighter and more mature than many models expected. That puzzle is reshaping ideas about how fast the first stars and galaxies formed.

x: Infrared also passes through dust, revealing stars being born inside clouds
Webb studies the atmospheres of planets around other stars

deep.x: Portugal is a member of ESO, the European Southern Observatory, which is building the Extremely Large Telescope in Chile's Atacama Desert.
To see the first galaxies you must look far away, and to catch their stretched light you need a cold infrared telescope.

cards.title: Elementos do universo primitivo
cards.text: O Big Bang produziu sobretudo hidrogénio e hélio, com vestígios de lítio. Tudo o que é mais pesado veio depois, das estrelas, por isso o universo ainda é cerca de 74% hidrogénio e 24% hélio em massa.

deep.x: For about the first 20 minutes, the whole universe was a nuclear reactor. Protons and neutrons fused into helium and a few other light nuclei. Then expansion cooled everything too much for fusion to continue. This is called **Big Bang nucleosynthesis**.

x: About 1 neutron for every 7 protons
16 particles: 2 neutrons + 14 protons
2n + 2p make one helium (mass 4)
Helium ≈ 4 ÷ 16 = 25% by mass

v.unit: share of ordinary matter by mass, %

deep.x: A strong test

The theory predicts the amounts of helium, deuterium (heavy hydrogen) and lithium from first principles. Helium and deuterium match observations well. Lithium doesn't quite: old stars have about three times less than predicted, the unsolved "lithium problem".
Where the rest came from
A classic 1948 paper by Alpher and Gamow added Hans Bethe as co-author largely as a pun, so the authors read "Alpher, Bethe, Gamow", like alpha, beta, gamma.
The hydrogen atoms in the water you drink were made in the first minutes of the universe, 13.8 billion years ago.
The Big Bang supplied the hydrogen and helium; nearly every other element in you was cooked later inside stars.

cards.title: Perguntas em aberto

items: O que é a matéria escura?
O que é a energia escura?

cards.text: Os físicos ainda não sabem o que são a matéria escura e a energia escura, porque há mais matéria do que antimatéria, nem como juntar a mecânica quântica com a gravidade.

deep.x: Cosmology can describe the universe with remarkable precision, yet some of its biggest ingredients remain unidentified. The open problems are not gaps at the edges: they sit at the centre of the picture.
The missing antimatter
The Big Bang should have made matter and antimatter in equal amounts, and they annihilate on contact. Yet some matter survived. Physics has found tiny asymmetries, but far too small to explain it.

x: For every billion antiparticles
there were about a billion and one particles
Everything we see is that "one" left over

deep.x: Quantum gravity

Quantum mechanics rules atoms; general relativity rules gravity and space. Both work superbly, but they clash inside black holes and at the Big Bang itself. String theory and loop quantum gravity are candidate fixes, untested so far.
The Hubble tension

Measured from the cosmic microwave background, the expansion rate is about 67 km/s per megaparsec; from nearby stars and supernovae, about 73. The gap has survived years of checks. It could be an error, or a sign of new physics.
Portugal has been a member of CERN in Geneva since 1985. Experiments there make and trap antimatter to test whether it behaves exactly like matter.
About 95% of the universe is made of things we can name but cannot yet explain.

cards.title: O nosso endereço cósmico
cards.text: Terra, Sistema Solar, Braço de Orionte, Via Láctea, Grupo Local, Superenxame de Virgem, Superenxame Laniakea, universo observável.

deep.x: Like a postal address, from house to country, our place in the universe can be written as a series of nested regions, each vastly larger than the one before.
The scale jumps
Our neighbourhoods

x: The **Local Group** contains the Milky Way, Andromeda, Triangulum and dozens of small dwarf galaxies
The **Virgo Supercluster** is centred on the Virgo Cluster, over 1,000 galaxies about 54 million light-years away
**Laniakea**, Hawaiian for "immense heaven", was mapped in 2014 by tracking how about 100,000 galaxies flow

deep.x: Moving through it all

Nothing on this list is still. Earth orbits the Sun at about 30 km/s; the Sun circles the galaxy at about 230 km/s; and the Local Group moves at about 600 km/s relative to the cosmic microwave background.
Beyond Laniakea lie even larger structures: walls and filaments of galaxies separated by vast, nearly empty voids, like the threads of a cosmic web.
Your full address ends not with a country but with a supercluster in a universe of uncountable galaxies.

quiz.q: Que idade tem o universo?
options: Cerca de 13,8 mil milhões de anos
quiz.explain: Medida a partir da expansão e da radiação cósmica de fundo.

quiz.q: Qual é a maior parte do conteúdo do universo?
quiz.explain: Cerca de 68%.

quiz.q: Em 1929, Hubble descobriu que…
options: As galáxias distantes se afastam, por isso o espaço está a expandir-se
quiz.explain: A expansão do universo.

lessons.title: A física do tempo
lessons.summary: Vento, nuvens, chuva e tempestades.

cards.title: O Sol comanda o tempo

steps: Ar quente sobe, ar frio desce

cards.text: O Sol aquece mais o equador do que os polos, e mais a terra do que o mar. A atmosfera e os oceanos estão sempre a deslocar calor para equilibrar isso, e esse movimento é o tempo meteorológico.

deep.x: Sunlight arrives at the top of the atmosphere at about 1,360 watts per square metre. Near the equator it strikes almost head-on; near the poles it arrives at a low angle, spread over a much larger area, and passes through more air. Over a year, the tropics receive more than twice as much solar energy per square metre as the poles.

v.unit: yearly average sunshine at top of air, W/m² (about)

deep.x: Land versus sea

Water needs about four to five times more energy than dry soil to warm by the same amount, and sunlight mixes deep into it. So land heats and cools fast while the sea changes slowly. That's why Bragança has hot summers and cold winters, while coastal Viana do Castelo stays milder all year.
Heat on the move

Warm air rises at the equator, flows towards the poles high up, sinks around 30° latitude and returns along the surface. This loop, the **Hadley cell**, creates the tropical rains and the desert belt, and feeds the Azores High that shapes Portugal's summers. Ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream do the rest, keeping western Europe far milder than eastern Canada at the same latitude.

deep.w: Summer is when Earth is closest to the Sun
deep.r: Earth is closest in early January; seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis

deep.x: Weather is the atmosphere and oceans endlessly trying, and failing, to spread the Sun's uneven heat evenly.

cards.title: Vento
cards.text: O ar flui das altas para as baixas pressões. A rotação da Terra desvia-o (o efeito de Coriolis), por isso os ventos rodam em espiral à volta das depressões: no sentido contrário aos ponteiros do relógio no hemisfério norte.

deep.x: Air pressure is the weight of the air above you, about 1,013 hectopascals at sea level. Where air is warmer or rising, pressure falls; where it is cooler or sinking, pressure rises. Air pushes from high to low, and the steeper the difference, the stronger the wind. On weather maps, closely packed isobars mean a windy day.
The Coriolis twist

Earth spins underneath moving air. Seen from the ground, air heading north or south seems to swerve: to the right in the northern hemisphere, to the left in the southern. Air rushing towards a low never reaches it directly; it swirls around it instead.

x: Northern hemisphere: anticlockwise around lows, clockwise around highs
Southern hemisphere: the reverse
Near the equator the effect vanishes, which is why hurricanes never cross it

deep.x: A handy rule
Stand with your back to the wind in the northern hemisphere and the low pressure is on your left. This is **Buys Ballot's law**, from 1857.

deep.w: The Coriolis effect makes sinks drain the other way round
deep.r: It is far too weak over a basin; the shape of the sink and how the water was poured decide

deep.x: The Beaufort scale was devised in 1805 by a British naval officer, describing wind by its effect on a ship's sails; it was later adapted to effects on land and sea.
Wind is air sliding from high to low pressure, bent into great spirals by the turning Earth.

cards.title: Nuvens
cards.text: O ar que sobe expande-se e arrefece. Quando arrefece até ao ponto de orvalho, o vapor de água condensa em gotículas à volta de poeiras: uma nuvem. Cada tipo de nuvem diz-te algo sobre o ar.

deep.x: As air rises, the pressure around it drops, so it expands. Expanding takes energy, and the air cools: about 10 °C per kilometre while dry. Once it cools to its **dew point**, vapour condenses onto tiny specks of dust, sea salt or smoke called condensation nuclei. Without them, clouds would struggle to form at all.
Finding the cloud base

x: Ground temperature 25 °C, dew point 13 °C
Gap = 12 °C
Flat cloud bases at about 1,500 m

deep.x: Reading the sky

In 1802–03, Luke Howard, an English pharmacist, gave clouds Latin names that are still used: cumulus (heap), stratus (layer), cirrus (curl of hair) and nimbus (rain). Today there are ten main types, grouped by height.

x: Cirrus thickening from the west often means a front within a day
Puffy cumulus on a summer afternoon shows the ground heating the air
Grey stratus means a shallow layer of stable, moist air

deep.x: A modest cumulus cloud about 1 km across holds roughly 500 tonnes of water, but the droplets are so small they float on gentle updrafts.
A cloud is the visible sign that air has risen and cooled to its dew point.

cards.title: Chuva

items: Cristais de gelo crescem em nuvens frias
Ou chegam como neve ou granizo

cards.text: As gotículas das nuvens são minúsculas. A chuva forma-se quando as gotículas colidem e se juntam, ou quando cristais de gelo crescem em nuvens frias e derretem ao cair. Uma gota de chuva contém cerca de um milhão de gotículas de nuvem.

deep.x: Cloud droplets are about 0.02 mm across, so light that they fall at around a centimetre per second and are held up by the gentlest updraft. To make rain, about a million of them must combine.

x: Raindrop ≈ 2 mm, droplet ≈ 0.02 mm
100 times wider
≈ 1 million droplets per raindrop

deep.x: Two routes to rain

In warm clouds, bigger droplets fall faster and sweep up smaller ones. In clouds colder than 0 °C, water often stays liquid, "supercooled", alongside ice crystals. Vapour moves from the droplets to the ice, which grows into snowflakes. These fall and usually melt into rain on the way down. Most rain in Europe begins this way, as snow.
The rainy northwest

Moist Atlantic air forced up over the mountains of the Minho and Peneda-Gerês dumps heavy rain: over 3,000 mm a year in the wettest places, among the highest in Europe. Lisbon gets around 700 mm, and parts of the Alentejo less than 600.

deep.w: Raindrops are teardrop-shaped
deep.r: Small drops are spheres; bigger ones flatten like burger buns, and drops over about 5 mm break apart

deep.x: Rain is a million cloud droplets joined into one, usually after starting life as ice.

cards.title: Humidade e orvalho

viz.unit: g de água por m³ de ar (máx., aprox.)

cards.text: O ar quente contém mais vapor de água do que o ar frio. À noite, o ar arrefece até não conseguir reter o vapor, que condensa em orvalho ou nevoeiro. A humidade relativa compara o vapor existente com o máximo possível.

deep.x: Faster-moving water molecules escape into the air more easily, so warm air can hold far more vapour before it saturates. The maximum roughly doubles with every 10 °C rise. That is why a summer storm can drop so much water.

v.unit: max water vapour, g per m³ of air

deep.x: Relative humidity
relative humidity = vapour present ÷ maximum possible × 100%

x: Evening at 20 °C, air holds 8.7 g/m³
Overnight it cools to about 9 °C
Now saturated: dew forms

deep.x: Why clear nights are wet

Ground loses heat by radiating it to the sky. Clouds act like a blanket and send some back; on clear, calm nights the ground and the air touching it cool quickly. Grass and car roofs, which lose heat especially fast, reach the dew point first.
Fog
Fog is a cloud at ground level. Cool, damp air settles into valleys overnight, which is why the Douro and Lima valleys often wake up under fog that burns off by mid-morning.

deep.w: 100% humidity means it is raining
deep.r: It means the air is saturated; you get fog or dew, but rain needs droplets to grow and fall

deep.x: Muggy days feel hotter because sweat evaporates slowly when the air is already near saturation, so your body loses less heat.
Cool air down far enough and it must give up its water as dew, fog or frost.

cards.title: Frentes
cards.text: Onde massas de ar quente e frio se encontram, o ar quente sobe por cima do frio, formando nuvens e chuva. As frentes atlânticas trazem grande parte da chuva de inverno de Portugal, sobretudo ao Minho.

deep.x: An air mass is a huge body of air with similar temperature and humidity: cold and dry from the Arctic, warm and moist from the subtropics. Where two meet, they don't mix easily. The lighter warm air is pushed up over the denser cold air, cools, and builds clouds and rain.
Cold and warm fronts
A depression passes
Atlantic low-pressure systems usually carry a warm front followed by a cold one. You can often watch the sequence in the sky over a day or two.
Why the Minho gets so much

In winter the jet stream and its storm track sit further south, steering depressions towards Iberia. The northwest coast is first in line, and its hills squeeze extra rain from every front. Sometimes a long, narrow plume of tropical moisture, an **atmospheric river**, feeds a front and causes floods.
Norwegian meteorologists in Bergen named fronts around 1919, borrowing the word from the battle lines of the First World War.
A front is a battle line between air masses, and rain falls where the warm air is forced to climb.

cards.title: Trovoadas
cards.text: Correntes ascendentes fortes em ar quente, húmido e instável formam enormes nuvens cumulonimbus com 12 km ou mais. As cargas separam-se, produzindo relâmpagos, trovões, chuva forte e por vezes granizo.

deep.x: A thunderstorm needs three things: moisture, unstable air that keeps rising once it starts, and a trigger such as a hot afternoon, a hill or a cold front. As vapour condenses it releases heat, making the rising air even more buoyant. Updrafts can exceed 100 km/h and drive a cumulonimbus cloud up to the top of the lower atmosphere, 12 km or more.
Making lightning

Inside the cloud, small ice crystals and soft hail pellets collide. The light crystals tend to become positively charged and are carried to the top; the heavier pellets gather negative charge lower down. When the voltage reaches hundreds of millions of volts, a spark leaps across.
Thunder and distance
A bolt heats the air around it to about 30,000 °C, five times hotter than the Sun's surface, in a few millionths of a second. The air expands explosively: that is thunder.

x: Flash, then count seconds to thunder
Sound travels about 1 km in 3 s
9 s ≈ 3 km away

deep.w: Lightning never strikes the same place twice
deep.r: Tall objects are hit again and again; the Empire State Building gets struck about 20 times a year

deep.x: A thunderstorm is a giant engine that turns rising humid air into falling rain and an enormous electrical charge.

cards.title: Brisas marítimas

items: brisa da terra para o mar

cards.text: Nos dias de sol, a terra aquece mais depressa do que o mar. O ar sobe sobre a terra e entra ar mais fresco vindo do mar: uma brisa marítima. À noite inverte-se e passa a brisa terrestre. A Nortada na costa portuguesa é um vento de verão ligado a estes padrões de pressão.

deep.x: On a sunny morning the land warms quickly while the sea barely changes. Warm air over the land rises, pressure near the ground drops, and cooler, denser sea air slides in to replace it. By early afternoon the breeze can reach 20 km/h or more and push tens of kilometres inland.
Turning around at night
After sunset the land cools faster than the sea. The pattern reverses and a weaker **land breeze** blows offshore, often strongest just before dawn.
The Nortada

In summer, the Azores High sits to the west while heat builds a low-pressure area over inland Iberia. Between them, a strong north wind blows down Portugal's west coast, boosted each afternoon by the sea-breeze effect. It's why Viana do Castelo's Cabedelo beach is a favourite for windsurfers and kitesurfers.

x: The Nortada pushes surface water away from the coast, and cold deep water wells up to replace it
That **upwelling** keeps Portugal's Atlantic beaches chilly, often 16–19 °C even in August
It also feeds rich fisheries, including the sardine

deep.x: Cool upwelled water often chills the air above it into coastal fog on summer mornings, while it's hot and sunny just a few kilometres inland.
A sea breeze is a small-scale weather system: land and sea heat differently, pressure follows, and the wind does the rest.

cards.title: Previsão
cards.text: As previsões vêm de supercomputadores que resolvem as equações físicas da atmosfera numa grelha 3D, partindo de milhões de observações. Hoje, a precisão a 5 dias é mais ou menos a que as previsões a 1 dia tinham nos anos 1980.

deep.x: In 1922 Lewis Fry Richardson tried to forecast the weather by solving the physics equations by hand. A six-hour forecast took him weeks and came out badly wrong. In 1950 the ENIAC computer produced the first successful numerical forecasts. Since then, computing power and observations have grown enormously.
How it works today

Satellites, weather balloons, aircraft, ships, buoys and ground stations measure the atmosphere. Supercomputers split the globe into a 3D grid, with cells about 9 km wide in the best global models, and calculate how wind, temperature, pressure and moisture change, minute by simulated minute.
Chaos and ensembles

In the 1960s Edward Lorenz found that tiny differences in starting conditions grow until forecasts diverge: the **butterfly effect**. So forecasters run the model dozens of times, each with slightly different starts. If the runs agree, confidence is high; if they spread out, the forecast is uncertain.

deep.w: "40% chance of rain" means rain over 40% of the area
deep.r: It means a 40% chance of measurable rain at any given point

deep.x: Since 2023, AI models trained on decades of past weather have matched traditional models for many forecasts. The European Centre (ECMWF), of which Portugal is a member, began running one operationally in 2025.
Weather can be predicted because it obeys physics, but chaos limits detailed forecasts to roughly two weeks.

cards.title: Avisos do IPMA
cards.text: Em Portugal, o IPMA emite avisos meteorológicos amarelos, laranja e vermelhos para chuva, vento, calor, frio, agitação marítima e mais, por distrito.

deep.x: IPMA, the Instituto Português do Mar e da Atmosfera, is Portugal's national weather, sea and seismic service. It was created in 2012 by merging the old Meteorological Institute with the fisheries and sea research institute.
What gets a warning
Why by district?

The same weather affects places differently. A temperature that is normal in Évora in July may be dangerous in Viana do Castelo, and 50 mm of rain means more on dry ground than in the Minho. So thresholds are set for each district and region, including the Azores and Madeira.
From warning to action

x: IPMA issues the weather warning
The civil protection authority, ANEPC, turns it into advice and may alert phones by SMS
Warnings also feed Meteoalarm, a shared European map from national weather services

deep.x: Since 2017 IPMA has named major storms jointly with Spain's AEMET and France's Météo-France, so the public hears one name for the same storm across borders.
A colour warning tells you how much the coming weather could disrupt life where you are, not just how wild it will be.
